docs.name: 言談分析
docs.text: 1 DISCOURSE ANALYSIS Fall 2026 Instructor: Chen-Yu Chester Hsieh Email: hsieh.cy@mx.nthu.edu.tw Class time: Tuesday, 15:30~18:20 Office: HSS-B505 Office hours: By appointment Course Description Life is made up by various types and forms of discourse, from daily conversation, short videos, and social media posts to textbooks, lectures and PowerPoint slides. The ability to comprehend and generate discourse appropriately has influence over our daily routines, academic studies, career development and even interpersonal relationships. Analyzing discourse thus allows us to delve into the essence of language, text, interaction and society. In this course, which will be conducted primarily in English, we will study the major principles, methods and applications of discourse analysis (DA) in linguistics and applied linguistics and explore basic concepts of DA, features of different types of discourse, tools for DA research, and links of DA to various other domains and disciplines. Throughout this course, we will learn how to collect data, observe patterns, and analyze phenomena like a discourse analyst. By the end of this course, students should be able to (1) describe what discourse and discourse analysis are; (2) identify the connections between discourse and other domains of language and life; (3) utilize the methods discussed in class to analyze discourse data; and (4) conduct a research project based on the principles and methodology of discourse analysis. Textbooks and Readings 1. Johnstone, B. (2008). Discourse Analysis. (2nd Edition). Malden, MA: Blackwell. 2. Paltridge, B. (2012). Discourse Analysis: An Introduction. New York, NY: Continuum. 3. Strauss, S. & Feiz, P. (2013). Discourse Analysis: Putting Our World into Words. New York, NY: Routledge. 4. Other selected articles Grading 1. Attendance and participation 15% 2. Discourse and Language W03 09/22 Genre and Move Analysis 1: Foundations of Genre W04 09/29 Genre and Move Analysis 2: Move Structures in Academic and Professional Texts W05 10/06 Conversation Analysis 1: The Organization of Everyday Conversation W06 10/13 Conversation Analysis 2: Knowledge, Identity, Action, and Interaction in Talk IHA 1: Human-AI comparison W07 10/20 Genre Analysis Group Presentations DAE 1 W08 10/27 Corpus-based Discourse Analysis 1: Introduction to Corpus Tools and Techniques W09 11/03 Corpus-based Discourse Analysis 2: Corpus Approaches to Discourse Interpretation W10 11/10 Critical Discourse Analysis 1: Discourse, Ideology, and Social Practice W11 11/17 Critical Discourse Analysis 2: Critical Approaches to Media and Institutional Discourse IHA 2: Corpus- informed analysis W12 11/24 Project Proposal Presentations DAE 2 W13 12/01 Multimodal Discourse Analysis 1: Visual, Verbal, and Audio Meaning-making W14 12/08 Multimodal Discourse Analysis 2: Multimodal Analysis of Social and Digital Media W15 12/15 Final Project Discussion W16 12/22 Final Presentations Self-evaluation Written Report About Cheating and Plagiarism 1. Although the final results are important, integrity and true learning matter even more. If you have any difficulty about the exercises or assignments, always feel free to bring it up to the teacher. About the Use of Generative AI 1. Reasonable and responsible use of Generative AI such as ChatGPT is allowed or even encouraged in this class. 2. docs.text: National Tsing Hua University College of Humanities and Social Sciences Syllabus 11410FL 308700 English-Chinese Translation Practice Fall 2026 Instructor: Chen, Kuo-Hua Thursday, 1:20 PM - 3:10 PM chenkuohua@mx.nthu.edu.tw Course Description This course aims to provide students with a practical foundation in English-Chinese translation. Through a combination of lectures, discussions, and translation exercises, students will acquire the knowledge and skills necessary to effectively convey meaning and style between the two languages. As an introductory course in translation, the focus will be on translating from English to Chinese. The course will cover a range of topics related to translation, including syntax, semantics, cultural references, and idiomatic expressions. The course content will encompass an overview of fundamental translation concepts, a comparative analysis of Chinese and English, and a methodology section that addresses linguistic and cultural factors involved in language transfer. Course Objectives Students are expected to enhance skills of news translation through the course, to become news translators in the future. Upon successful completion of the course, the students will be able to: 1) Become familiar with the issues and challenges in translating English news stories. 2) Apply their translation skills to develop the concept of trans-editing. 3) Understand the process of journalistic translation in various news media. 4) Discover errors and problems found in the journalistic English translation. 5) Develop ability to collect and search information from diverse resources. Textbook & References There will be no textbook required for this course, but the following books are recommended should you feel a text would be helpful. 英中筆譯 1：基礎翻譯理論與技巧(廖柏森，眾文) 中英翻譯:對比分析法 (吳潛誠，文鶴) 英漢比較與翻譯(陳安定，書林) 筆譯精華（修訂版）(賴翠玲，文鶴) 新編譯藝譚 (黃邦傑，書林) Grading Policy Exercises 20% Participation 30% Assignments 50% Participation It is vital to participate in classroom activities, such as answering teacher’s oral questions promptly and acquire extra points counted to your final grade. Students are requested to focus properly on course content and classroom interaction. However, laptops, smartphones, tablet computers are permitted and encouraged in class to do note-taking or search for specific information. Students are even required to use an APP to submit their in-class translation exercises. Assignments Translation practice will be done constantly throughout the course, including timed in-class translation exercises and 6 assignments. Promptness in submitting assignments is required. Late submission is not acceptable. Failure to submit assignment on time will result in the deduction of final grade. Course Schedule 9/10 Course Orientation and Expectations 9/17 An Introduction to Translation 9/24 Choice of word meanings/Assignment 1 10/1 Language Comparison 10/8 Subjects Comparison/Assignment 2 10/15 Verbs Comparison 10/22 Pronoun Comparison/Assignment 3 10/29 Articles Comparison 11/5 Word Order Comparison 11/12 Voice Comparison/Assignment 4 11/19 Translation of Proper Nouns 11/26 Conversion/Assignment 5 12/3 Omission 12/10 Amplification/Assignment 6 12/17 Affirmative and Negative 12/24 Analysis of Translation Errors Please note that this schedule is subject to change. Ethics Statement on Generative Artificial Intelligence Grounded in the principles of transparency and responsibility, this course encourages students to leverage AI for self-learning to enhance the quality of course outputs. In accordance with the published Guidelines for Collaboration, Co-learning, and Cultivation of Artificial Intelligence Competencies in University Education, this course adopts the following policy：Conditionally open In the context of translation assignments, students are encouraged to incorporate AI tools to enhance the quality of their translations. Detailed guidelines pertaining to the use of AI tools in these assignments will be communicated and provided throughout the course. By utilizing AI technologies, students can improve their translation output and develop a deeper understanding of the translation process.

To help students cultivate self-development and personal growth at work, the course taps into advice from industry leaders, career coaches, self-help authors, management gurus, scholars, and psychologists. docs.text: Department of Foreign Languages and Literature Second Language Acquisition National Tsing Hua University Huang 1 Course description This introductory course provides students with a broad overview of theories and issues in the field of second language acquisition (SLA). Through lectures, discussions, activities, and projects, students will learn about theoretical issues and be familiar with research methods commonly used in SLA. Topics covered include (a) first language acquisition, (b) theories in SLA, (c) factors affecting SLA, (d) learner language, and (e) instructed SLA. Students are expected to critically draw on language learning theories and research to reflect on their own assumptions about language learning and teaching. Course Texts and Materials  Required Textbook  Lightbown, P. M., & Spada, N. (2021). How languages are learned (5th ed.). Oxford: Oxford University Press.  Required Material  An e-mail account ― it is essential that you check this e-mail account at least the day before class. Links to distance learning will be sent out on Wednesdays through this e-mail account.  A working account at the eLearn website. You will need to upload assignments to this e-learning platform (https://elearn.nthu.edu.tw/). Requirements and Major Course Projects  Attendance, engagement, and active class participation: Attendance and active class participation are vital to your success in this class. Students are expected to preview course content, attend all class sessions, and prepare for thoughtful discussions in class. Policy for absence and late attendance: **Students are required to notify the instructor in advance about missing a class. Please email at least one day before class time. You will fail this class if you have more than three absences even with prior notice. If absent, you are responsible 第二語言習得 Second Language Acquisition Instructor: Hung-Tzu Huang Office: 人社 B507, Phone: (03)574-2710 Office hours: by appointment Department of Foreign Languages and Literature Second Language Acquisition National Tsing Hua University Huang 2 for all notes and assignments. **Class will begin promptly. Late attendance will directly affect your grade. If you are more than 10 minutes late for class, you will be considered absent.  Weekly group discussion: Every week, you will be assigned into groups to discuss assigned questions. Your performance of the discussion will be evaluated by group members.  Commentaries and responses to discussion questions: You will write commentaries about the class content and answer discussion questions before joining the group discussion. In your writing, you need to summarize and reflect on interesting insights and issues. The purpose is to keep a record of weekly themes, to prepare for group discussion, and to help you place class discussion within the context of the entire course. You should submit your commentaries a day before the class.  Extending classroom learning (Choose at least two from the following) 1. Reflection of language learning related seminars/talks: You will attend language learning (or teaching) related seminars or talks throughout the semester. These talks could be in or outside of NTHU or online. In the reflections, you need to include summaries of the talks and relate the content to the SLA issues discussed in class. 2. Reflection of language learning news/articles/stories: You will read language learning, teaching, or policy related research articles or books throughout the semester. In the reflection, you need to include summaries of the reading and relate the content to the SLA issues discussed in class. 3. Reflection of learner/teacher/researcher/administrator interviews: You will interview successful language learners, teachers, researchers, or administrators. In the reflection, you need to include lists of the interview questions, summaries of the interviews, and reflect upon how the interviewees’ experiences relate to SLA issues discussed in the class.  Final exam: You will have a take home final exam. Policy for plagiarism and late assignments: *** Plagiarism is a type of academic dishonesty which may result in failing of the class or suspension from the university. Plagiarism includes but is not limited to submitting any work that has been copied in whole or in part from another Department of Foreign Languages and Literature Second Language Acquisition National Tsing Hua University Huang 3 individual’s work without citation and submitting the same written or oral material in more than one course without obtaining authorization from the instructors involved. Always cite the sources you use in all assignments. If you have any questions regarding plagiarism, please consult the instructor. *** Late assignments will not be accepted unless you discuss difficulties with the instructor in advance. Course information 課程代碼 Course Number 11510FL 327300 課程名稱 Title in Chinese 日語聽解 (一) 課程英文名稱 Title in English Japanese Listening (I) 全/半年 Two/one semester 全年 必/選修/通識 Required/ Elective/ General Education 選修 總學分數 Credits 2.0 每週上課時數/ 教室 Lecturing hours/ classroom 週一 T34 (10:10-12:00) / 人社院 C522 開課系所 Class standing 外語系 授課教師 Instructor 簡嘉菁 kankasei88@gmail.com 先修課程 Prerequisites 1. 建議修畢中級日語(二)或熟悉日語動詞活用變化與相關句型者 2. 因應下學期的教學進度, 建議同時選修高級日語（一） 3. 本課程進度較快，需在課外自行多加練習。請謹慎考量學習狀況不接受二退。 4. 以日語為母語者不能選修。外籍生請具備中文能力。 關鍵字 Keywords 日語 Japanese, 聽力 listening, 會話 conversation 課程簡介 Course Description 1. 教學目標：培養學生具有中級程度以上的日語聽解能力。透過討論、聽力練習與 會話演練來培養溝通表達能力。提升至日語 JLPT N5-N4 實力。 2. 指定教科書：上學期《大家的日本語初級 II 聽解タスク 25（改訂版）》、下學 期《大家的日本語進階 I 聽解タスク 25（改訂版）》。請自備課本。 3. 教學進度：搭配校內中高級日語的學習教材，採用同系列的聽力課本。以指定教 科書為主，輔以日語能力檢定的聽解內容。上學期進度《大家的日本語初 級 II 聽解タスク 25》第 13-25 課＋日檢 JLPT N5 聽解; 下學期進度《大 家的日本語進階 I 聽解タスク 25》第 26-35 課＋日檢 JLPT N4 聽解。 4. 課程說明：上課方式主要分為「授課」(老師補充詞彙句型)、「發表」(學生上台 報告 JLPT 聽解問題或指定教科書句型)、「聽解」(播放教科書與參考資 料 CD 做聽力與對話練習)。利用指定教科書與網路視聽教材的聽力練 習，輔以平時作業(日檢聽力)的寫作練習，培養日語的聽解、對話能力。 課程中適時加入相關日語句型的日語歌曲或新聞日文，以期有效應用本學 期所學習的內容。 5. 成績考核：期中考（35%）、期末考（35%）、作業與小考（20%）、出席（10%） 備註：教學方法、評量方式、參考書目、教學網頁、AI 使用規則等請參考課綱 附檔。第一週將詳細說明。 注意事項 注意事項： (1) 除特殊狀況，不開放加簽或申請二退（需當面晤談。未經同意，不審核二退的 電子簽單）。申請旁聽者請事先來信聯絡。 (2) 部分專有名詞與內容將以中文介紹。 115-1 NTHU 日語聽解 課程綱要 T34 簡嘉菁 2 (3) 詳細教學方法、評量方式、參考書目、教學網頁等將在第一週說明。 (4) 關於 AI 使用規則：有條件開放. 基於透明與負責任的原則，本課程可以利用 AI 進行查詢，以提升本門課品質。但是本課程的個人報告或分組報告中, 不得 使用生成 AI 工具撰寫報告. 若經查核使用卻未在作業或報告中標明，教師、 學校或相關單位有權重新針對作業或報告重新評分或不予計分。 (5) 出席: 重要考試或個人上台報告日，都必須出席。請假時請利用學校請假系統 的上網登記。除了緊急重大意外，請假時都必須在上課前完成請假。如果是公 假、喪假、病假、婚假、赴日（來回機票證明，一學期最多申請 2 次，1 次一 週為上限）需附上相關證明單。不需要再給紙本請假單。詳細規定請參考學校 請假系統通知。曠課達 3 次或請假達五週以上（或 1/4）不給予學期成績。 課程目標 Course Outcomes 此科目對應之系所課程規畫所欲培養之核心能力 Core capability to be cultivated by this course 1 培養扎實日語表達能力 溝通表達與語文能力、創作與創新能力 2 理解日本社會與文化 問題發掘與研究能力 3 透過與日本的比較, 提高對台灣的關心 全球化與國際視野及多元文化認知能力 二、教學大綱 II. 出席(10%): 請假需附上相關證明單與填寫假單 三、教學方法、評量方式、指定書目與參考書目等 教學方法 lecturing methodologies 方式 methods 說明 notes o 講述法 formal lecture 由教師引導發音･單字･句型練習。 授課內容以教科書為主,講義與線上網路報導為輔。 o 討論法 group discussion 由學生分組討論,共同解決發表的課題 o 合作學習 cooperative learning 分組口頭會話發表 o 媒體融入教學 media, audio, visual materials 使用電腦或多媒體播放相關日文,練習日語聽力與閱讀 o 專題研究 case studies 日語報告或詞彙整理等 評量方式 assessment methodologies:有 “等級制” 和 “百分制” 備註 notes: (1) 請掌握學習狀況,勿在考後要求補寫報告、調整成績等。 (2) 公佈成績:小考約 2 週後、期中考約 4 週後、學期成績約 2-3 週後。 (3) 可能會申請二退或應屆畢業生請留意成績出爐時間,再決定是否選課。 方式 methods 百 分 比 percentage 說明 notes o 期中考試 o 期末考試 midterm/ final exam 35% 35% docs.text: 1/3 【中級韓語一】課程教學大綱 課程資訊 (Course Information) 科號 Course Number 11510FL 328103 學分 Credit 3 人數限制 Class Size 中文名稱 Course Title 中級韓語一 英文名稱 Course English Title Elementary Korean I 任課教師 Instructor 李伶美 (Lee Yeongmi) 上課時間 Time F678 上課教室 Room 先修課程 Prerequisites 「初級韓語一」、「初級韓語二」 建議有修過「初級韓語一、二」或者具備韓文課時數達「96 小時」左右。 此科目對應之 系所課程規畫 所欲培養之核 心能力 Core capability to be cultivated by this course ■ 溝通表達與語文能力 (70%) The ability to communicate and express oneself in the English/a foreign language. (70%) □ 文學經典的分析與詮釋 The ability to analyze classic canons of literature. ■ 問題發掘與研究能力 (10%) The ability to look for problems and conduct research (including conducting linguistic analysis through scientific methods) (10%) □ 創作與創新能力 The ability to think creatively ■ 全球化與國際視野及多元文化認知能力 (20%) The ability to examine issues through global and multicultural perspectives (20%) 課程簡述 (Brief course description) 本課程通過充分運用中級詞彙及所學的文法，進一步提升學生聽、講、讀、寫的能力。本課程同 時著重加強口語訓練，讓學生能使用韓語進行簡短發表。主要課題包括打電話約時間、說明計 畫、介紹烹飪方式、聚會邀請和詢問交通工具及問路等。 課程大綱 (Syllabus) 一、課程目標 (Course Outcomes) 1. 能夠讓學生熟悉正確的韓語發音以及書寫方式，建立韓語學習的基礎。 2. 理解並且熟悉以個人主題所構成的對話。 3. 培養使用公共設施施和維持社會關係時所需的溝通能力。 4. 理解日常生活或社會現象中複雜的內容。 2/3 5. 學習韓語自然的發音，以及分辨随著句子意義的不同而改變的聲調。正確理解演講內容， 並且有效率地表達自己的想法。 二、教材 1. 指定書目 (Text Books)：《延世大學 韓國語1 (課本及 Workbook)》台北：聯經出版公司。 《延世大學 韓國語2 (課本及 Workbook)》台北：聯經出版公司。 2. 參考書目 (References)：《我的第一本韓語文法》新北市：國際學村。 3. 韓文學習網站 (web page) (1) https://dict.naver.com/ (Naver 詞典) (2) https://dic.daum.net/index.do (Daum 詞典) 三、教學方式 (Teaching Method) 1. 由教師引導發音、單字練習。 2. 講解韓文之基礎知識及句型。 3. 練習實用日常會話。 4. 不定時小考及作業、上課參與。 四、成績考核 (Evaluation) 1. 期中考試：35% 2. 期末考試：35% 3. 平時成績(包含小考及作業，上課參與情形，出席率及上課態度等)：30% 小考不開放補考（公假不在此限，但須於次週補考完成），上課參與不開放補參與!! 五、上課規範 (classroom rules) 1. 第一堂課不建議缺席！ 2. 準時到課，不建議提早離開，早退必須跟老師說一聲。 3. 不克出席上課須事先請假。 4. 缺課者必須主動向到課同學詢問當天的上課內容與作業，並且自行跟上進度。 5. 務必有教材以及抄寫筆記。 6. 參與課程所進行的活動。 7. 準時繳交作業(如需補交，請於一星期之內完成)。 8. 課程未達 2/3 出席者，會「被當」。 9. 爲了上課品質，不開放旁聽生。 10. 限非韓籍生修習。 3/3 六、教學進度 (Syllabus) ※每週課程進度可能視實際上課情況調整 週次 日期 教學內容 第 1 週 2026/9/11 課程介紹 第一堂課非常重要，不建議缺席！ 課程進度： 8-1 전화번호 좀 가르쳐 주세요 8-2 정민철 씨 계세요? docs.nameEn: Reading Literature Through Film: From Text to Context (II) - The Uncanny in Representations
docs.text: 1 Reading Literature Through Film: From Text to Context (2) The Uncanny in Representations 從書頁到影像：電影中的文學 (怪誕奇異篇) Instructor: Yi-hui Wang E-mail: wang.yh@mx.nthu.edu.tw Course Description: This course aims to introduce students to the intersection of literature and its cinematic adaptation within broader literary and cultural contexts. It offers a fundamental exploration of an interdisciplinary field regarding representations of the uncanny. Focusing on the works of Mary Shelley, Robert Louis Stevenson, and the Brontë sisters, this course examines how literature and the film adaptations engage with key themes such as an early imagining of artificial life, the duality of human nature, psychological horror, gothic romance, and the complexity of human experience. By the end of the semester, students will have developed the growth of Critical Thinking Skills (CTS) and heightened their sensitivity to language, dialogue, and visual representation. Required Text: All E-books and supplementary materials are available on the eeclass Course Methodology: (1) Using film as a gateway to classic literature: Using film adaptations to help students approach and engage with classic literary texts. (2) Comparing adaptations with the original texts: Examine the differences between different film adaptations and their original literary texts, and consider why directors make these changes. (3) Understanding the uncanny and its genre: Gain a deeper understanding of the concept of the uncanny and its relationship to the different literary genres. Jane Eyre. Edited by Margaret Smith, Oxford UP, 2000. Evaluation Methods: Class Attendance: 10％ Participation and Class Discussion: 10％ Presentation: 20％ Midterm Exam: 30％ Final Exam:30％ Requirements: Attendance & class participation are required. docs.name: 從《哈利波特》學英文
docs.nameEn: English Language Skills with Harry Potter
docs.text: Language Skills with Harry Potter Dr. Katchen TIME: Mon. 1:20 – 3:10 katchen@mx.nthu.edu.tw HSS C412 Rationale: The Harry Potter books have been extremely popular all over the world, including with young people in Taiwan. It is also known that the use of material of interest to students increases their motivation to learn. For these reasons, and because the teacher likes them, the Harry Potter books and films are used for this course. Moreover, language learning works best when we actually DO things with the language. Objectives: To advance students’ abilities in Reading, Writing, Speaking, and Listening. To expand students’ vocabulary in English. To increase students’ knowledge of British and English-speaking cultures. And, most of all, to reveal many of the hidden meanings in Rowling’s use of language, especially names. Prerequisite: This course is aimed at students with a relatively high level of English ability equal to the level of the students in the Department of Foreign Languages and Literature. Many students from other departments, and also international students, do meet these standards and they are welcome to take this course. If you do not feel that your level of English is comparable to that of FLLD students or higher, then this course is not for you and you will not do well in this course. Required Materials: Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone (the first book in English). Supplemental Materials: All seven Harry Potter books, all eight DVDs. Before taking the course, students should have either read all seven books (either in English or in your first language) or watched all the films because the vocabulary lectures and the essays will be based on all the materials. During the first third of the semester, we will spend time on the first and second books/videos . During the second third, we will be going through the materials from books/videos 3 – 4; during the last third books/videos 5, 6, 7/8. The focus will be on the vocabulary as well as the content of the stories. I do not expect you to re-read all the books, but you should review the films in order to answer the questions. Lists of content questions will be on eLearn, and some will appear on exams. Questions on vocabulary will be on the exams. Exams will contain multiple choice and matching, and each exam will contain three or four essays which will require you to think and support your arguments/reasons. Materials we will use in class, such as PowerPoint slides, will be uploaded to our class e- learning site (eLearn). For the out-of-class supplemental video, the URL is provided. Your role plays and group reports will be videod and you will be able to view them on eLearn. You are responsible for accessing the Harry Potter books and videos yourselves. Procedure: We will spend a lot of time in class looking at the vocabulary and cultural background from excerpts of the books and videos. You will be responsible for what you read in Book 1 (Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone) and watch on the accompanying videos; to assist you with the contents, you will find important questions on eLearn. These materials will be on the exams, so don’t ignore them. You will also be responsible for the content of the video “Harry Potter and Me.” You will create two role plays, give one oral report, and also write one out-of-class essay based on ideas taken from the books. You will also be given two listening quizzes in which you will fill in the blanks. All these materials and activities were made for native speakers, so your listening and speaking skills will be challenged, but I think you’ll have fun, too. NOTE: If we do not have enough class time to go through all the lectures in 16 weeks (we have two holidays, so we meet only 14 times), you can access all the lectures on eLearn. They are PowerPoint slides with audio. You can also use them for review before exams. Grading: You should be present and should participate every week. Whenever we have activities in class, your participation will be evaluated. The assigned activities, such as reports, role plays, essays, and quizzes, will, of course, receive definite grades. Quizzes will be based on listening to an excerpt of a scene from one of the films (fill in a cloze). If you come and participate and complete the assignments adequately, you should be able to pass the course. Midterm Exam 1, 20% Midterm Exam 2, 20% Final Exam, 20% Two Listening Quizzes, 5% each Two Role Plays, 5% each One Group Report, 10% One Outside Essay, 10% Attendance: I expect to see an official excuse using the university leave request system for missing a class. You must appear for the midterms and final unless you have an official serious excuse (in hospital, death in the family, or another important reason with official excuse). If you miss a listening quiz without an official excuse, you will get 0 for the quiz. The role plays and the group report can be made up in the following class. Use of AI: The out-of-class essay should be based on your own ideas. The topics are worded so that you MUST use examples from your own experience! If you use added materials in your essay to back up or to supplement your ideas, please add the reference(s) at the end of your essay. For the group reports, you will have to do some outside research. You must add the references/ URLs within or at the end of your ppt files. Calendar NOTE: We will attempt to follow this calendar, but sometimes we may get a little behind or even a little ahead. Unless something unusual happens, the activities will not change. Sept. 7 Introduction to the course and syllabus; Some general questions about Harry Potter; Lecture 1 Harry’s family; Lecture 2 places. Sept. 14 Lecture 3 Required Textbooks; Lecture 4 Weasley Family; Lecture 5 Classmates. Homework: Read Stone 1-5. Sept. 21 Lecture 6 Hogwarts Places; Lecture 7, Hogwarts Professors; Lecture 8 Creatures; Give out role plays. Sept. 28 HOLIDAY Homework: Read Stone 6-14. Review films 1 and 2. Oct 5 Student Role Plays (5%). Lectures 9 Objects. Perhaps begin Lecture 10. Homework: Read Chapters 15-17. Review Questions on Chamber at home. Oct. 12 Listening Quiz 1 (5%). Lectures 10 and 11 on Chamber. Give out Group Report Topics. Oct. 19 FIRST MIDTERM EXAM (20%). Oct. 26 HOLIDAY. Listen to J.K. Rowling interview (link on e-learn, also transcript and key questions). Review Prisoner and Goblet Questions at home. Review videos 3 and 4. Nov. 2 Lectures 12 and 13 on Prisoner. Lectures 14 and 15 on Goblet. Nov. 9 Student Group Reports (10%). Nov. 12 Finish Group Reports. Nov. 19 SECOND MIDTERM EXAM (20%) Nov. 26 Lectures 16 and 17 on Phoenix. Review Questions on Books 5, 6, 7 at home. Watch videos 5 - 8. Give out role plays. Dec. 7 Listening Quiz 2 (5%); Lecture 18 on Prince; Hallows. Questions at home. Give out role plays. Dec. 14 Student Role Plays (5%). Lecture 19 on Prince, Hallows. Dec. 21 FINAL EXAM (20%). Essay due by December 31 (10%). docs.text: 國立清華大學課程大綱【魯濱遜漂流記：全球脈絡下的多重文本】 <1050112 版> 科號 FL 350100 組別 學分 3 人數限制 30 上課時間 F2F3F4 Fall 2026 教室 人社院 C511 科目中文名稱 魯濱遜漂流記：全球脈絡下的多重文本 科目英文名稱 Robinson Crusoe: A Multilayered Text in Global Contexts 任課教師 紀元文 Chi, Yuanwen 擋修科目 無 擋修分數 請勾 選 Select 此科目對應之系所課程規畫所欲培養之核心能力 Core capability to be cultivated by this course 權重（百分 比） Percentage v 溝通表達與語文能力 The ability to communicate and express oneself in the English/a foreign language. 20% v 文學經典的分析與詮釋 The ability to analyze classic canons of literature. 20% v 問題發掘與研究能力 The ability to look for problems and conduct research (including conducting linguistic analysis through scientific methods) 20% v 創作與創新能力 The ability to think creatively 20% v 全球化與國際視野及多元文化認知能力 The ability to examine issues through global and multicultural perspectives 20% 課程簡述(必填) Brief Course Description (required) 本欄位資料會上傳教育部課程網 Character limit: 20-1000 characters. Aim for a concise 50-200 words, as this information will be uploaded to the Ministry of Education's curriculum website. Daniel Defoe’s (1660?-1731) Robinson Crusoe is a trilogy of adventure stories consisting of three novels--The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1719), The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1719), and Serious Reflections of Robinson Crusoe (1720). In these texts, the novelist embodies the ideology of mercantilism and colonial expansion which, in turn, intersect and re-enforce each other. Therefore, we can clearly see that the protagonist is a typical colonizer, who roves all over the globe to go on expeditions, to cultivate plantations, and to accumulate capitals. Being at the threshold of the industrial revolution, the English society was driven to explore new territory, to secure the supply of raw materials, and to search for new markets. To be sure, Crusoe has no scruples about betraying his own ideas or upholding contradictory doctrines, insofar as his interest is concerned. As Maximillian E. Novak has pointed out that Defoe is “a propagandist for social schemes, colonial expansion, economic projects and political factions and a satirist working for reformation of manners”(“Defoe’s Theory of Fiction.”) 請輸入課程內容「中文暨英文關鍵字」至少 5 個, 每個關鍵字至多 20 個中文, 以半形逗點分 隔 (必填) Please fill in at least 5 course keywords (up to 40 letters for each keyword) and use commas to separate them.(required) Daniel Defoe, Robinson Crusoe, adventure story, providence, prudence, nature, mercantilism, colonialism, prose fiction, eighteenth-century, English literature 一、課程說明 Daniel Defoe’s (1660?-1731) Robinson Crusoe is a trilogy of adventure stories consisting of three novels--The Life and Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1719), The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1719), and Serious Reflections of Robinson Crusoe (1720). In these texts, the novelist embodies the ideology of mercantilism and colonial expansion which, in turn, intersect and re-enforce each other. The full title of the first serial is as follows: The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe of York, Mariner, who lived Eight and Twenty Years, all alone in an un-inhabited Island on the Coast of America, near the Mouth of the Great River of Oroonoque; Having been cast on Shore by Shipwreck, wherein all the Men perished but himself. With an Account how he was at last as strangely deliver’d by Pyrates. Written by Himself. London: Printed for W. Taylor at the ship in Pater-Noster-Row. MDCCXIX. Therefore, we can clearly see that the protagonist is a typical colonizer, who roves all over the globe to go on expeditions, to cultivate plantations, and to accumulate capitals. Being at the threshold of the industrial revolution, the English society was driven to explore new territory, to secure the supply of raw materials, and to search for new markets. To be sure, Crusoe has no scruples about betraying his own ideas or upholding contradictory doctrines, insofar as his interest is concerned. As Maximillian E. Novak has pointed out that Defoe is “a propagandist for social schemes, colonial expansion, economic projects and political factions and a satirist working for reformation of manners”(“Defoe’s Theory of Fiction.”) In the story, Defoe dwelled upon the voyages and adventures—a popular leitmotif among the writers in the Eighteenth Century. Crusoe even narrates his voyage to Formosa: “… [W]e came to the Latitude of 22 Degrees, 30 Min.; by which Means we made the Island Formosa directly, … the People there, who are very courteous and civil in their Manners, supply’d us with willingly, and dealt very fairly and punctually with us in all their Agreements and Bargains; which is what we did not find among other People; and may be owing to the Remains of Christianity, which was once planted here by a Dutch Missionary of Protestants, and is a Testimony of what I have often observ’d, viz. That the Christian Religion always civilizes the People, and reforms their Manners, …”(Robinson Crusoe [The Shakespeare Head Edition] Vol. III:130-31). In a certain sense, this text has also witnessed the plunging into, and involvement of, the island of Formosa in the global geo-political encounters and conflicts since the Age of Discovery. The fact that the first serial of the story became a best seller immediately after its publication indicated that the subject matter struck deeply at the structure of English sentiments collectively. In a word, Crusoe’s detailed accounts and enumerations of expeditions, businesslike transactions, and adventuresome spirits embodied the emblems of Geistegeschichte of “true-born Englishmen” in the Eighteenth Century. 二、指定用書 Daniel Defoe. Robinson Crusoe. Ed. Michael Shinagel. New York: Norton, 1994. 2nd ed. Supplementary readings from this text are indicated as “Norton: xx.” （Information of textbook in the campus bookstore: 水木書店 03-5716800.） 三、參考書籍 Supplementary readings are primary and secondary sources related to the trilogy of Robinson Crusoe. In addition, we will also read quintessential criticism about Robinson Crusoe. Excerpts from these sources are indicated with the symbol of an asterisk “  ”. The instructor will give out these excerpts as handouts in the class. Primary Sources Defoe, Daniel. The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1719). Vol. II of The Novels and Miscellaneous Works of Daniel De Foe. Ed. Sir Walter Scott. Oxford: Thomas Tegg, 1840. 247-254. ---. The Farther Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1719). Vol. 2 of The Novels of Daniel Defoe (10 vols.). Ed. W. R. Owens. London: Pickering & Chatto, 2008.155-167, 235-237. ---. The Life & Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1719). Shakespeare Head Edition. Oxford: Basil Blackwell, 1927. 3 vols. ---. The Life and Strange Surprizing Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1719). Vol. 1 of The Novels of Daniel Defoe (10 vols.). Ed. W. R. Owens. London: Pickering & Chatto, 2008. ---. Serious Reflections during the Life and Surprising Adventures of Robinson Crusoe (1720). Vol. 3 of The Novels of Daniel Defoe (10 vols.). Ed. G.. A. Starr. London: Pickering & Chatto, 2008.129-144, 340-353. ---. Serious Reflections during the Life and Surprising Adventures of Robinson Crusoe with His Vision of the Angelic World (1720). Vol. III of Romances and Narratives by Daniel Defoe. Ed. George A. Aitken. London: J. M. Dent, 1895.104-126. Gildon, Charles. Robinson Crusoe Examin’d and Criticis’d (1719). Ed. Paul Dottin. London and Paris: J. M. Dent & Sons, 1923. Secondary Sources Ellis, Frank H, ed. Robinson Crusoe: A Collection of Critical Essays. Englewood Cliffs, N.J.: Prentice-Hall, 1969. Hunter, J. Paul. The Reluctant Pilgrim: Defoe’s Emblematic Method and Quest for Form in Robinson Crusoe. Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1966. Ian Watt. “Realism and the Novel Form.” The Rise of the Novel: Studies in Defoe, Richardson and Fielding (1957). Harmondsworth: Penguin Books, 1979. 9-37. Novak, Maximillian E. Daniel Defoe: Master of Fiction. New York: Oxford UP, 2008. Rogers, Pat. Robinson Crusoe. London: George Allen & Unwin,1979. 25-50. Spaas, Lieve and Brian Stimpson, ed. Robinson Crusoe: Myths and Metamorphoses. New York: St. Martin’s Press, 1996. 中中文文 林紓、曾宗鞏譯，達孚著。《魯濱孫飄流記》（光緒三十一年，1905 年）。 臺北：臺灣商務印書館,，1973 年。二版。1-2。 林紓、曾宗鞏譯。《魯濱孫飄流續記》（光緒三十二年，1906 年）。上海： 商務印書館，1914 年。1-6。 狄福著，戴維揚導讀。《魯濱遜飄流記》。臺北：桂冠圖書公司，2005 年。 黃杲炘譯。《魯賓孫歷險記》。上海：上海譯文出版社，1997 年。 齊霞飛譯，迪福原著。《魯濱遜飄流記》。臺北：志文出版社，1984 年。 四、教學方式 Lectures and discussion are the major pedagogy in the class. The instructor will lecture on the topics and issues concerning the rapports between the evolution of the socio-cultural contexts and the text as an embodiment of mercantilism in England in the Eighteenth Century. Students are expected to read closely the designated materials and participate in class discussions so as to articulate their understanding and critiques of materials under study. As England stood at the threshold of the industrial revolution in the early Eighteenth Century, Defoe’s experiments with prose fiction and his attempts to represent the prevailing ideologies of mercantilism and monarchism had a significant impact on shaping the form and development of the genre of the novel. It is believed that the progress of material culture and economic growth has to do with the evolution and formation of literary genres. Thus the pedagogy of this class attempts to explore how Daniel Defoe utilized prose fiction to represent the agenda of social changes in the contexts of global exploration and exploitation in Eighteenth-Century England. 五、課程進度 A Tentative Syllabus* Week Readings Supplementary Readings 1 (Sept. 11) Introduction to the Course & the Long Eighteenth Century. 8:00-12:00 The implication of the long eighteenth century in the contexts of pre-modern global era. Daniel Defoe’s life and his writing career. Defoe as a merchant, spy, pamphlet writer, and the pioneer of prose fiction. 2 (Sept. 18) Robinson Crusoe: 2-18 8:00-12:00 The protagonist Crusoe’s account of himself and his captivity by the Turkish pirates in his first voyage. 3 (Oct.2) Robinson Crusoe:19-40 Norton: 230-235. 8:00-12:00 Crusoe’s escape and his plantation in Brazil. Going on a voyage to the coast of Guinea to traffic Negroes. Shipwrecked and stranded in an isolated and lonely island. 4 (Oct.16) Robinson Crusoe: 41-60 Norton: 262-264 8:00-12:00 Rescue necessities and tools from the shipwreck. The practice of Puritan reflections in the form of bookkeeping: assets and liabilities. Reflections on his conditions: to set the good against the evil. 5 (Oct. 23) Robinson Crusoe: 61-73 8:00-12:00 Keep a journal and make furniture. Management and maintenance of his house. Reflections on religion in misery. Solemn fast on the anniversary of Crusoe’s landing on the island. 6 (Oct. 30 ) Robinson Crusoe: 74-113 Defoe, Farther: 154-167 & 8:00-12:00 Cultivate crops, mould 235-237 (W.R.Owens ed.) some pots, and prepare stuffs for making bread. The 11thyear on the island. Raise some goats for milk, butter, and cheese. Footprints on the beach. 7 (Nov. 6 ) Midterm Exam 9:00-12:00 8 (Nov. 13) Robinson Crusoe: 114-130 9:00-12:00 Fortify his castle against the cannibals and nauseated at the sight of anthropophagy. 9 (Nov. 20) Robinson Crusoe: 131-150 9:00-12:00 Reflections on providence and cannibalism. Crusoe’s household on the island in the 23rd year. 25th year on the desolate island and the implications of Friday as “noble savage.” 10 (Nov. 27) Robinson Crusoe:151-175 Defoe, Serious: 204 -211 & 8:00-12:00 Crusoe tries to “civilize” Friday 392-397 (G.A.Starr ed.) and their discourses on Christianity. Crusoe’s war against the savages and the rescue of Friday’s father. 11 (Dec. 4) Robinson Crusoe: 176-200 8:00-12:00 Crusoe’s preparations to rescue the Spaniards detained in the Mainland. The recapture of the mutinied English ship and leaving the island on December 19, 1686. A Topic on Translation: Lin Shu. and Travel Theory in Cultural Translation. Lin Shu’s Contribution to the Making of Modern Chinese Literature.Excerpts of Lin Shu’s Translation of Robinson Crusoe in Classical Chinese: 林紓《魯濱孫》：1-10; 林 紓《魯濱孫續記》：上 1-10。林紓《魯濱孫續記》：下 40-50。 12 (Dec. 11) Robinson Crusoe: 201-220 8:00-12:00 Crusoe’s lonely voyage back home and his claims of the property in Brazil. Crusoe’s assets, his journey through Spain and France to go back to England. Crusoe’s revisit of his island in 1694. Review of the materials under study in the class. 13 (Dec. 18) Final Exam 9:00-12:00 *ATTENTION! Class hours are adjusted to two sets of time periods owing to National Holidays on February 27, April 3, and May 1. Please consult each one of the class sessions, respectively. To be more specific, class sessions begin at 8 o’clock sharp in the morning, except for Nov. 6 (Midterm Exam), Nov. 13, Nov. 20, and Dec.18 (Final Exam). 六、成績考核 There are two exams in this course—the midterm and final exams. The exam is a test of basic knowledge about the text and quintessential ideas about the social and cultural contexts of this period in the formats of Identification, Essentials of Robinson Crusoe, Explication of Literary Terms, and Essay Questions. (See the Test Sample attached). To be more specific, Identification refers to the understanding of the lexicons in the text; Essentials are the major events and episodes in the story per se; explication of literary terms aims at training and expanding students’ knowledge about Western culture, whereas Essay Questions serve to test students’ capabilities to analyze, organize, and critique the text and some materials related to this field. All of these serve for the instructor to understand the validity of the pedagogy, to train the students’ capabilities to organize their perception of the text and some related materials, and to articulate their knowledge of the field in verbal and written forms both logically coherent and grammatically correct. Students who actively participate in class discussions will have some credits for their performance and have favorable consideration for their grades (GPA). 1. Active participation in class discussion and oral conversations (Questions and Answers) are required (10%). 2. Midterm exam (40%) and final exam (50%).

docs.text: Studies in Poetry 1. Course Description: This course aims to acquaint students with practices of poetry, generally in terms of the shorter verse forms, and explore the idea of poetry as a genre. The students will be familiarized with various verse forms established in the course of history, read a variety of poetic endeavors, and discuss how these works variously explore the multiple aspects of the self and boldly imagine and invent ways of living and acting in the society and the world. 2. Textbooks: Selections from various sources, including Harold Bloom’s How to Read and Why ; Edward Hirsch’s How to Read a poem and Fall in Love with Poetry; W. R. Johnson’s The Idea of Lyric: Lyric Modes in Ancient and Modern Poetry 3. Teaching Method: Lecture, class discussion and group presentation. 4. Syllabus: Week 1 9/7 General introduction: the idea of lyric; e.e. cummings’s “i carry your heart with me,” Tennyson’s “The Eagle,” Craig Raine’s “A Martian Sends a Postcard Home.” Week 2 9/14 Sappho’s fragments, William Blake’s “The Sick Rose.” Hirsh, Chapter 1“Message in a Bottle” p.1-15. The Dramatic Monologue: Robert Browning’s “My Last Dutchess” Week 3 9/21 Presentation 1: Tennyson’s “Ulysses” and “Crossing the Bar.” Hirsh, Chapter 1 p15-30 Week 4 9/28 Holiday Week 5 10/5 Dylan Thomas’s”Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night” Ballads: “Sir Patrick Spence”; “The Unquiet Grave.” Week 6 10/12 Presentation 2 : Hirsh,: Chapter 2 “A Made Thing” P30-45 (and more Concrete poems) Week 7 10/19 Chapter 3 “A Hand, a Hook, a Prayer” p46-60. Elizabeth Bishop’s “Sestina” Week 8 10/26 Holiday Week 9 11/2 Midterm exam Week 10 11/9 Shakespeare Sonnets 18, 73; Mallarme’s “A Toast,” Baudelaire’s “To the Reader” and more about French Symbolist poems Week 11 11/16 Presentation 3: Chapter 4 “Three Initiations” p 61-87. Week 12 11/23 Presentation 4: Hirsh, “Reverberations of an Ode” in Chapter 9 (213-225). Keats’ “Ode to a Nightingale” and “Ode on a Grecian Urn.” Week 13 11/30 Film: Il Postino. Film response due 12/5 23:00 Week 14 12/7 Metaphysical Poems: John Donne’s “The Flea,” “A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning” ; Andrew Marvell’s “To His Coy Mistress.” Week 15 12/14 Confessional Poetry: Sylvia Plath’s “The Applicant,” “Daddy,” “Lady Lazarus,” “Morning Song,” “The Edge.” Week 16 12/21 Final 5. Evaluation: Midterm 30% Final 40% Class Discussion and Presentation 30%

docs.text: COURSE SYLLABUS National Tsing Hua University Journalistic English Fall 2026 Instructor: I-Tsen Huang Email: itsen1213@gmail.com Course Description The course is designed to introduce students to the characteristics and conventions of journalistic writing. Great emphasis is placed on honing reading and language skills that students need most in comprehending news reports and articles in English. Training in key vocabulary skills and knowledge includes connotations, loanwords, metaphors, allusions, and idioms. Training in reading is aimed at inferring word meaning from context, identifying contextual clues, and grasping main ideas. A selection of texts will be used to sharpen students’ abilities to detect hidden bias and to raise students’ awareness of cohesive and discourse features that tie a text together. Course Objectives 1. Learn and practice the fundamentals of news writing 2. Understand headlines through contextual clues 3. Infer meanings and learn new words through context 4. Analyze the content and viewpoint of a text 5. Recognize and practice rhetorical devices Office hours by appointment only Monday 13:00 - 15:15 Required course materials The course materials are available in each of the weekly folder on the eLearn learning platform. Students are required to access the files and print them out. Grading policies 1. Attendance and coursework – 10% a. Success in this class depends on regular and punctual attendance. Each late arrival will result in a 2-point deduction of the semester grade. b. Each unexcused absence will result in a 5-point deduction of the semester grade. c. Students are required to email the instructor to request a leave of absence. The grant of a leave of absence is within the discretion of the instructor. d. Two unexcused absences will result in a failing grade. A total of three absences will result in a failing grade. e. Missing 15 minutes of class—arriving late, departing early, or leaving during class—counts as half an absence. 2. Active in-class participation and contributions – 15% a. Cell phones, laptops, tablets, earphones, headphones, or earbuds are not allowed in class. b. Please seek permission to leave the classroom. 3. Midterm exam (Journalese and headline grammar) – 15% a. A makeup exam is not offered. 4. Assignments (vocabulary, reading, speaking, and listening) – 25% 5. Headline and news writing – 10% 6. Newscast project – 15% 7. Headlines in The Economist – 10% Information about AI use, assignments, and classroom activities 1. Please note that late submissions will not be graded. 2. An excused absence does not negate the student’s responsibility for classroom activities or assignments due during his or her period of absence. Students are obligated to email any due assignments to the instructor before the deadline. 3. No use of generative AI tools permitted This course assumes that work submitted by students will be generated by the students themselves, working individually or in groups as directed by class assignment instructions. Weekly Schedule Week Date Topics 1 9/7 Grammatical features of newspaper headlines Journalese and short words 2 9/14 Key words in headlines and contextual clues in leads 3 9/21 Business 4 9/28 Holiday 5 10/5 Diplomacy and wars 6 10/12 Headline and news writing (1) 7 10/19 Politics 8 10/26 Holiday 9 11/2 Midterm exam 10 11/9 Detecting bias in texts 11 11/16 Headline language devices in The Economist 12 11/23 Headline and news writing (2) 13 11/30 Crimes 14 12/7 Newscast project: Studio recording 15 12/14 Technology 16 12/21 Headline and news writing (3)

docs.name: 美國文學-1865年之後
docs.text: American Literature Since 1865 This course studies American literature from the end of the 19th century to the present day. We will explore some of the major issues which the literary works in these periods have distinctively articulated and/or born witness to. Our reading of the literary texts will build on critical and historical contexts in order to acquire a general knowledge of the literary developments in the U.S. since 1865 with attention to their historical (dis)continuities and their relation to social changes. Teaching Method: a mix of lectures, student discussion and group presentations. Textbooks: The Norton Anthology of American Literature 1865 To The Present ( Tenth Edition) Reading Schedule: 日期 週次 內容 9/9 1 General Introduction. Course information 課程代碼 Course Number 11510FL 421100 課程名稱 Title in Chinese 商用日語 課程英文名稱 Title in English Business Japanese 全/半年 Two/one semester 半年 必/選修/通識 Required/ Elective/ General Education 選修 總學分數 Credits 2 每週上課時數/ 教室 Lecturing hours/ classroom 週四 R34 (10:10-12:00) 人社院 C522 開課系所 Class standing 外語系 授課教師 Instructor(s) 簡嘉菁 kankasei88@gmail.com 先修課程 Prerequisites 1. 具備 JLPT Ｎ4 以上或修畢高級日語 (約「大家的日本語」50 課) 程度 2. 推薦選修下學期「新聞日語」課程（加強專有術語） 3. 本課程進度較快，需自行多加練習。請謹慎考量學習狀況不接受二退。 4. 以日語為母語者不能選修。外籍生請具備中文能力。 關鍵字 Keywords 日語 Japanese, 商用禮儀 business manner, 敬語 honorific, 商用文書 business document, 致電＆接電話 telephone, 訪問&接待 reception 等各種主題 課程簡介 Course Description 1. 教學目標：教授日語商務禮儀、慣用表現等相關會話。透過討論與演練來培 養溝通表達能力。提升日語 JLPT N3~N1 實力。 2. 指定教科書：《30 小時快速學習職場日本語》台北：大新書局。 3. 教學進度：以指定教科書為主，輔以自編商務日語教材與網路教學影片等。 4. 課程說明：內容涵蓋日本職場中常用的尊敬語・謙讓語等敬語、自我介紹、 社外・社內商用文書、撥打電話、接聽電話與相關會話、訪問禮儀、接 待禮儀、面試技巧、服裝儀容等相關商務內容。透過上台發表與會話演 練，來培養升學或就業時候所需的面試技巧與商務技能。教學方式將由 教師引導專業術語、慣用句或商務背景知識的學習。透過相互會話練習 以及上台發表，讓學生加強商用日語的熟練度。 5. 成績考核：期中考（35%）、期末考（35%）、上台報告（10%）、作業（10%）、 出席（10%） 註：教學方法、評量方式、參考書目、教學網頁、AI 使用規則等請參考課綱 附檔。第一週將詳細說明。 注意事項 Please note 注意事項： (1) 除特殊狀況，不開放加簽或申請二退（需當面晤談。未經同意，不審核二 退的電子簽單）。申請旁聽者請事先來信聯絡。 (3) 部分專有名詞與內容將以中文介紹。 (4) 詳細教學方法、評量方式、參考書目、教學網頁等將在第一週說明。 (5) 關於 AI 使用規則：有條件開放. 基於透明與負責任的原則，本課程可以利 用 AI 進行查詢，以提升本門課品質。但是本課程的個人報告或分組報告 中, 不得使用生成 AI 工具撰寫報告. 若經查核使用卻未在作業或報告中標 明，教師、學校或相關單位有權重新針對作業或報告重新評分或不予計分。 (6) 出席: 重要考試或個人上台報告日，都必須出席。請假時請利用學校請假 系統的上網登記。除了緊急重大意外，請假時都必須在上課前完成請 假。如果是公假、喪假、病假、婚假、赴日（來回機票證明，一學期最 113-1 NTHU 商用日語 課程綱要 R34 簡嘉菁 2 多申請 2 次，1 次一週為上限）需附上相關證明單。不需要再給紙本請假 單。詳細規定請參考學校請假系統通知。請假達五週以上（或 1/4）不給 予學期成績。曠課（沒有提早請假）達三週以上不給予學期成績。 課程目標 Course Outcomes 此科目對應之系所課程規畫所欲培養之核心能力 Core capability to be cultivated by this course 1 培養扎實日語表達能力 溝通表達與語文能力、創作與創新能力 2 理解日本社會與文化 問題發掘與研究能力 3 透過與日本的比較, 提高對台灣的關心 全球化與國際視野及多元文化認知能力 二、教學大綱 II. docs.nameEn: Fiction and History: Survey of Literature from the Middle Ages to the 17th Century
docs.text: 1 Zrinka Stahuljak, Prof. 課程相關問題請洽清大外語系 fl@my.nthu.edu.tw Course description: This course explores European literature from the Middle Ages to the Golden and Classical Age. Its objective is to introduce you to some of the most important literary and cultural concepts, forms, and genres. World-making and social organization of the world are at the core of this class, and we will observe them through the prism of literature, religion, government, the military, travel, and science. In each unit of the course, we focus on continuities and transformations between periods and genres. While the focus is on the written sources from European culture, as Europe opens up to the globe through travel and exchange of ideas, we will also observe how the world questions the justification of social organization of Europe as that of “the best of all possible worlds” (Leibniz, 1710). The course therefore incorporates a critique, internal and external, of the Eurocentric organization of the world. 2 The arc of this class follows the role of fiction (dreams, allegory, imagination) in the making of history. From the birth of literature in European vernacular languages to the European arrival to the Americas to the major rational moment of the Cartesian break, dreams, allegories, and imagination drive the people and ideas. For example, maps regularly included fictional places and monstrous races, and Hobbes’s Leviathan was an allegory. Fiction is implied at every moment of the past, but is not usually told as part of history, that is, as a major force in the making of history. At the same time, fiction does not imply the absence of truth. Throughout the class, fiction is a major tool of showing the truth and creating truth-regimes. Therefore, the class will carefully nuance the usual opposition between fiction and history to provide a richer reading of fiction as instrumental in the making and thinking of the world that history describes. Learning outcomes: - to master basic and intermediary skills of critical and analytical thinking - to master advanced writing skills - to gain critical insight into the history of Europe and its culture - to reflect on learning in an AI-assisted environment Course requirements: The requirements are threefold. They involve both research/writing, analysis, and discussion/debate. This course aims to improve both written and oral skills. 1. Verbal Requirements: Class discussions and debate Your participation will be graded (35% of the grade). 2. Written Requirements: The Three Papers The requirement for this course takes the form of three papers. Papers #1 and #2 are submitted only in draft form. Paper #3 (or final paper) submitted twice, in draft form, and following instructor comment period, in final version. All papers are to be submitted on Kudu. NO LATE WORK WILL BE ACCEPTED. The first paper is 1200 words (ca. 4 pages), the second 1500 words (ca. 5 pages), and the third paper 1800 words (ca. 6 pages) in length. Each paper should be double-spaced and in Times New Roman, 12 point, with 1 inch margins. Please do NOT create a cover page for the papers. 3. Learning Checkpoints 3 To be completed at the end of each week’s reading sections. They are due by 11:59PM on Saturday of each week. They will not be graded and you have unlimited attempts to answer the multiple choice questions and receive full credit. Grading: • Paper One: 15% • Paper Two: 20% • Paper Three: 30% Draft 5% Final 25% • Discussion 35% Class readings: All readings, textbook and primary sources, are available online via the Kudu platform. Academic integrity and AI policy: Plagiarism, cheating, and fabrication are strongly prohibited in this course. These violations include the unattributed use of another’s work and the misuse of AI to generate academic content. The use of AI is permitted in working through outlines and ideas, as part of the closed-loop Kudu platform and chatbot. However, the general use of AI does not substitute for one’s original research and thinking. Students may be asked to work on drafts in class and to show subsequent drafts of their work as proof of their originality. Presenting AI-generated material as one’s own creation, without appropriate citation, constitutes a breach of these rules. All students are expected to adhere to these standards, ensuring that their academic work is genuinely their own and maintaining the integrity of their scholarly work. * Please note that the class syllabus may be subject to change.* COURSE SCHEDULE Week 1: Making Worlds: Language, Writing, Translation Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “Historical Periods and Concepts,” “The Medieval World,” and “From Latin to Vernacular French” - Primary sources: - William IX, “I’ll Write a Verse About Nothing at All” - Marie de France, “Prologue,” “Laustic” 4 Week 2: Making Worlds: Translation Required readings: - Primary sources: - Chrétien de Troyes, Prologue to Cligés - Anonymous, Prologue to The Book of Deeds of Jacques de Lalaing - Leonardo Bruni, from “On the Right Way to Translate” Week 3: Story Worlds: World and Storytelling Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “Book Forms” (manuscripts, incunabula, print books)” - Primary sources: - Petrarch, Letter from Familiarum Rerum Libri (Letters on Familiar Matters), "On the Study of Eloquence,” I, 9 to Tommaso de Messina; and “On Quotations,” VI, 4 to Giovanni Colonna - Petrarch, Letter from Seniles (Letters of Old Age), Book XVII, Letter 2 to Giovanni Boccaccio - Petrarch, Letter from Seniles, Book XVII, Letter 3 that explains Petrarch’s approach to writing Griselda Week 4: Story Worlds: World and Storytelling Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “Frame Narratives and Translation” - Primary sources: - Boccaccio, from The Decameron: “Prologue” - Chaucer, from The Canterbury Tales: “Prologue” - The Thousand and One Nights, “Prologue” - Marguerite de Navarre, Prologue to The Heptameron Week 5: Story Worlds: World and Storytelling Required readings: - Primary sources: - Boccaccio, “Day 10, Tale 10 (Griselda) - Chaucer, “The Clerk’s Tale (Griselda)” - Petrarch, “The Tale of Griselda” 5 Week 6: World Views (Chivalry) Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “The Long Tradition of Allegory and Chivalry” - Primary sources: - Chrétien de Troyes, from The Story of the Grail (Perceval), vv. 69-154, vv. 1416-1696, vv. 3153-3344, vv. 4579-4693, vv. 6152-6222 - Anonymous, from The Quest of the Holy Grail, chapters I and XV Week 7: World Views (Chivalry) Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “Chivalry and the Crusades” - Primary sources: - Urban II, Call to the First Crusade (1095) - Ramon Llull, Crusade Treatises: De fine (1305) and De acquisitione Terrae Sanctae (1309) - Chrétien de Troyes, Yvain: vv. 269-580 Week 8: World Views (Chivalry) Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “Reading Don Quixote with Chrétien de Troyes” - Primary sources: - Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part I: Prologue, chapters 1, 2. 3, ch.5, ch.7, ch.8, ch.9. Part II: ch. 3 (first paragraph) - Cervantes, Don Quixote, “The Captive’s Tale” Week 9: World Views (Religion) Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “Creation Narratives Across Cultures,” “Artistic and Literary Representations,” and “Dante’s Italy and Vernacular Literature” - Primary sources: - Genesis, Chapters 1-3 - Popul Vuh (excerpts) - Anonymous, The Play of Adam (excerpts) 6 Week 10: World Views (Religion) Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “Dante and Milton, the Fall and Free Will” and “Free Will and the Reformation” - Primary sources: - Dante, Comedy (Inferno), Cantos 1-5, 12, 15, 19, 26, 28, 34 - Milton, Paradise Lost, Book 4 Week 11: Traveling the World Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “Journey and Travel Narratives in the Middle Ages,” “Maps and Cartographic Traditions,” and “Missionaries and Religous Encounters” - Primary sources: - Benjamin of Tudela, from Travels, Saragosa-Rome, Constantinople, Jerusalem-Damascus, Baghdad, China-Africa-Europe - Ibn Battuta, from Travels: on Constantinople and Jerusalem Week 12: Traveling the World Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “Marco Polo and the Discovery of the World” and “Pilgrimage and Religious Travel” - Primary sources: - William Wey, from The Pilgrimage - Giorgio Gucci, from Visit to the Holy Places, chapters 75, 84, 110-111 - Marco Polo, The Description of the World, chapters 1-19, 96-100, 168, 171-172, 189 Week 13: Exploring and Colonizing the World Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “Encounter and Colonization” - Primary sources: - Christopher Columbus, “Letter concerning the First Voyage” - Hernán Cortés, from “The Second Letter” - Florentine Codex (excerpt) 7 Week 14: The “New” Worlds: Empires and Utopias Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “Empires and Utopias,” The Civilized and the Savage,” and “Utopias, Ideals and Philosophical Questions” - Primary source: - Thomas More, from Utopia - Michel de Montaigne, “To the Reader,” “Of Cannibals” - Christine de Pizan, from The Book of the City of Ladies, chapters 1-4 - Calderón, Life is a Dream, Act II Week 16: The World as a Dream: Dreams and Science Required readings: - History and Fiction Textbook: “The Cartesian Break and Hobbesian Representation” and “Interpretation of Dreams” - docs.text: 1 Research Methods Fall, 2026 Class Time: Monday 13:20-16: 20 Location: HSS B304 Instructor: Huifen Lin Email: huifennthu@gmail.com Office: HSS C630 Office hours: by appointment Learning management platform: elearn.nthu.edu.tw Course description This course is an introductory course in research methodology and it aims to develop graduate students’ abilities in conducting research in areas such as second/foreign language acquisition, computer-assisted language learning/teaching and general behavioral and social sciences. Basic skills and approaches to conduct experimental/non-experimental research will be introduced with a pedagogical focus. The instructor will guide students step by step from selecting a research topic, reviewing relevant literature, designing research method, collecting data to the end of putting together a research proposal. Each research method will be introduced by reference to studies using that method. It has to be noted that data-analysis and qualitative research paradigm will NOT be covered in this class due to time constraint. Student learning outcomes Upon completion of this course, students will be able to do the following: 1. Conduct a literature search and write a review on a research topic 2. Define and design important terms related to experimental designs. 3. Design a research study and determine an appropriate method of investigation 4. Apply concepts and theories they learn in class to develop a research project 5. Be familiar with research methodology and tools in second language studies 6. Critically evaluate a published research study 7. Learn to write a research proposal in APA style Required Textbook Jhangiani, R. S., Chiang, I. C. A., Cuttler, C., & Leighton, D. C. (2019). Research methods in psychology. Kwantlen Polytechnic University. NOTE: This is an online, open text that is free of charge to you. Textbook chapters are available online in the learning management platform. You could also download the book here. 2 Assessments Your grade will be determined on the basis of your performance of the following assignments/activities: Annotated bibliography of at least 15 studies on a selected topic-20% Once selecting a topic for your research project, you are encouraged to review studies on that topic. This assignment requires that you review at least 15 studies, create an annotated bibliography and write a summary of the studies, which should then lead to the gaps of previous studies that you intend to fill and the research questions of your study. Midterm exam-20% There will be multiple-choice and short essay questions in the midterm exam. The exam questions will come from the textbook and supplementary materials covered in class. Non-graded Chapter Exercises - 18% Throughout the course, there will be several chapter exercises that are not graded. However, you will receive credit points based on the complexity of the exercise if you submit it on time. Each exercise will cover one or more chapters and is designed to assess your comprehension of the material, as well as provide a hands-on opportunity to apply the knowledge in a practical way. Exercises are due every Saturday at midnight, before our class meeting. Presentations-10% You will give two presentations, the first one on your literature review, second one on your research project. Each presentation will be followed by my feedback and your peer’s questions. You would incorporate these feedbacks into your final research project. Peer feedback-10% During the course, you will be asked to evaluate your peer’s work and provide suggestions/feedback both in oral and written form. Research proposal-22% You will write a 15-20-page research proposal, excluding references and appendices. The research project should be prepared in APA format. Three major components are Introduction, Literature review and Methodology. Each major section should include relevant details. Full details of the research project will be announced in class. 3 Course schedule Week # Date Topic Due 1 9/7 Introduction AI Ethics and Policies 2 9/14 Chapter I. The Science of Psychology Chapter II. Overview of the Scientific Method Chapter exercise 1 3 9/21 Literature review I University Library: AI-assisted database (Literature search). Factorial Designs I Chapter exercise 7 15 12/14 Chapter XI. Presenting your research Chapter exercise 8 16 12/21 Research proposal presentation Peer review 2 Use of AI Tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, etc.) Students may utilize generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT, for specific purposes in this course. The fundamental principle is that the core intellectual work and initial drafting of all submissions must be entirely your own. You may use AI as a conversational partner to explore concepts, clarify methodologies, or discuss course topics. 4 You may also use AI to refine the grammar, syntax, and clarity of text that you have already written yourself. However, you are violating academic integrity if you use AI to generate foundational drafts, outlines, or any substantive text for your assignments. Whenever an AI tool is used for the acceptable purposes, you must explicitly disclose this in your assignment. Instructions of how to disclose AI use will be given in class.

docs.text: National Tsing Hua University, Department of Foreign Languages and Literature Fall semester 2024 11310 FL 560500 論文寫作 Thesis Writing Thursday 9:10 AM – 12:00 PM, Room HSS B304 Instructor: Viphavee Vongpumivitch (張寶玉) (viphavee@gapp.nthu.edu.tw) Course Descriptions: This course aims to teach Master’s degree students to write a proposal for their thesis research. The course takes the students through each part of a thesis, from the abstract to the introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion, and conclusion chapters. Students will also learn the APA Style of the American Psychological Association. There will also be a review of research methodology in applied linguistics that applies to individual students’ thesis. Throughout the semester, each student will focus on only one research topic and draft the abstract as well as the three chapters of their thesis proposal. The accumulated written products will be the first draft of a thesis proposal that is ready to be presented to each student’s thesis supervisor for future revisions and expansion. It is strongly recommended that the students only take this course when they are ready to start working on their own thesis. It is best for the students to take this course while consulting with their own thesis supervisor. FLL Department’s Core Capabilities to Be Cultivated by this Course: • Familiarity with theories and practices of applied linguistics and related topics of research. (35%) • The ability to conduct applied linguistic research and analyze research data. (35%) • The capability of thinking and conducting research professionally and independently. (30%) Required Textbook: • Bitchener, J. (2010). Writing an Applied Linguistics Thesis or Dissertation: A Guide to Presenting Empirical Research. Palgrave Macmillan. o [Relevant paper] Cao, Y. & Philp, J. (2006). Interactional context and willingness to communicate: A comparison of behavior in whole class, group and dyadic interaction. System, 34, 480-493. • Three Award-Winning MA Theses (one quantitative study, one qualitative study, one mixed-method study) https://alanz.org.nz/best-thesis/ Reference Books: • American Psychological Association (APA). (2020). Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association (7th Edition). Washington, CD: American Psychological Association. • Creswell, J.W. & Guetterman, T.C. (2019). Educational Research: Planning, Conducting, and Evaluating Quantitative and Qualitative Research (Sixth Edition). NY: Pearson. • Dornyei, Z. (2007). Research Methods in Applied Linguistics: Quantitative, Qualitative, and Mixed Methodologies. Oxford University Press. • Paltridge, B. & Phakiti, A. (2015). Research Methods in Applied Linguistics: A Practical Resources. Sydney: Bloomsbury. Teaching Methods: Lecture, Class Discussion, Reading Assignments, Writing Assignments, Peer Review Evaluations: Class participation (weekly paper summary) 50% The thesis proposal 50% • Abstract, Introduction, Literature, Methodology, Expected Results and Conclusion Course Rules: • Active participation is expected from all students. Please complete the Reading Assignments before coming to class. • All written works are submitted onto EEClass. You must put your name and a title of your work on the first page and include a page number on each page. Use Times New Roman font size 12, double spaced. Save your work as a Microsoft Word file, NOT a PDF file. Work that does not follow these formats will not be graded. • We will have a class group Line. Please take the initiative to contact the teacher whenever you have problems/questions about the course. It is unwise to guess or ask classmates without a confirmation from the teacher. Messages written to the teacher must be written in English. docs.text: 課程名稱 (中文) 內隱與外顯語言學習 (英文) Implicit and Explicit Language Learning Fall 2026 Time: Fri 13:20 – 16:10 Location: HSS B304 Instructor: 陳宗穎 Office: HSS B506 Office Hours: 12:00 – 13:00 Wednesdays Last Updated on Aug 30, 2026 課程大綱內容 一、課程概述 Language learning is either implicit or explicit, depending on learners' awareness of the process. This distinction has been commonly extended to explain the fundamental difference between L1 acquisition and L2 learning; the former occurs with leaners' "instinct" in natural language learning settings in their early infancy and childhood, whereas the latter could involve more explicit motivations and instructions. These qualitative differences have inspired an ongoing discussion of L1 language acquisition models, the extension of these models in L2 language learning, and the roles of implicit and explicit learning / knowledge for both L1 and L2 learners. In this course, we will join this discussion by reviewing crucial theoretical proposals as well as experimental findings in hopes of contributing to our understanding of language learning as a whole. 二、課程目標 In this course, students are expected to (i) learn/review different linguistic aspects (semantics, syntax, morphology, phonology, etc.), (ii) further their understanding of different L1/L2 language learning theories, (iii) explore various experimental approaches to examine various implicit/explicit language learning hypotheses, (iv) develop their own research insights and topics related to the course theme, and (v) complete a term research project and report initial findings and contributions. 三、課程進度表 週次 主題 閱讀範圍 1 Overview & Definition Hulstjin (2005), Andringa & Rebuschat (2015) 2 Conscious Measures Ellis & Roever (2021), Maie & DeKeyser (2020), Chen (2026) 3 Mid-Autumn Festival (No Class) 4 Similarity/Differences between L1 and L2 Learning Lichtman (2013), Hulstjin (2015) 5 National Day (No Class) 6 Lexicon Sonbul & Schmitt (2013), Ender (2016), Yeung et al. (2020) 7 Phonology Chan & Leung (2018), Bryfonsky & Ma (2019), Ge et al. (2025) 8 Morphology/Syntax Cipitria et al. (2026), Kidd (2012), Rogers et al. (2016) 9 Semantics Ionin et al. (2009), Blais & Gonnerman (2013), Cantemori et al. (2022) 10 Pragmatics Haselow (2021), Sperlich et al. (2019) 11 Advanced Approaches Morgan-Short et al. (2012), Godfroid et al. (2015) 12 Cognitive Factors Erçetin & Alptekin (2013), Serafini & Sanz (2016) 13 L2 pedagogy Ellis et al. (2006), Cerezo et al. (2016) 14 Topics and Papers of Your Choice 15 Course Project Presentation 16 Constitution Day (No Class) 四、評量方式 Paper Presentation and Discussion (40%) At least two students per week present a research article in 20-30 minutes. Oral presentations will be assessed based on their clarity, organization, and content. Non-presenters are required to ask clarification questions regarding each presentation and critical content-based questions regarding a research paper. The quality of the questions and the presenters’ replies to these questions will be considered for grading this item. Research Abstract (10%) This course requires individual students to work individually on a research topic related to L1/L2 and implicit/explicit language learning. Each student must have their term project topic approved by Oct 16, 2026. Each student will then have to complete a research proposal no longer than two pages based on the approved topic by Oct 30, 2026. The proposal should briefly summarize the research background, methods, as well as the expected research outcome, if applicable. Final Presentation (10%) On Dec 25, 2026, the last class of the semester, each student must give a 15-minute presentation of their term research project, which will be assessed with the same criteria applied to the students’ oral presentations. Students are expected to review a collection of related studies, primary research questions, research methods, and the (expected) findings. Non-presenters will also have to ask questions regarding each presentation, and their performance are also taken into account when grading this item. Research Proposal (40%) A research paper with a length between 10 and 15 pages (references not included) is due Dec 28, 2026. Clear statements of the research goals/methods and logical arguments are considered essential in this work. PAPERS CONTAINING PLAGIARISM (i.e., ≥ 20% in Turnitin) WILL NOT BE ACCEPTED AT ALL. Late research papers are NOT ACCEPTED without extremely good reasons. AI Policies Students in this course are allowed to use generative AI (e.g., ChatGPT) to help edit their English writing. If the students choose to edit their work using generative AI, they must submit both an initial draft and its AI- edited version, and both works must pass the Turnitin plagiarism check. The students must be aware of the limits of generative AI and carefully proofread/improve the AI-edited version. The students are still fully responsible for the quality of writing in the ultimate product and the originality and logic of their AI-edited proposal. 五、課堂閱讀 Andringa, Sible & Rebuschat, Patrick. 2015. docs.name: 語言習得專題
docs.text: Topics in Language Acquisition Fall, 2026 Time: Tuesday 15:30-18:20 Classroom: B304, HSS Building Instructor: Chun-Chieh Hsu (許淳潔) Contact: cchsu@mx.nthu.edu.tw  Course Description This course takes a linguistic/psycholinguistic perspective to study grammar acquisition. Relevant linguistic theories, experimental methods, and empirical evidence will be introduced and discussed. Specifically, this course focuses on the aspects of syntax, semantics, and pragmatics, asking “why” questions instead of “how” questions. Students are expected to learn how linguistic/psycholinguistic theories can be relevant to L2 acquisition as well as how theories can be tested empirically. Most importantly, this course will enhance students’ knowledge of various linguistic constructions, helping them not only to identify but also to explain interesting phenomena or errors observed during language learning/teaching experiences. Such knowledge is particularly useful for developing new insights that can be incorporated into future language learning and teaching practice. Some of the questions to be addressed are listed below:  Why is it so difficult for L2 learners to use English articles (the/a) correctly?  What is the difference between “Lions are usually dangerous” vs. “A lion is usually dangerous” in English generic expressions?  Do L2 learners interpret pronouns and reflexives the same way as native English speakers?  Why do L2 learners of English often make mistakes in using tense markers? How is the completion of an event expressed in English and in other languages?  Course website: NTHU eeclass https://eeclass.nth.edu.tw All announcements and assigned readings will be posted on the website for you, and so please be sure to check out the website regularly.  Textbook No textbook for this course. Relevant articles from various journals and books will be selected and assigned for each topic. We will be reading 2-3 selected articles every week.  Course requirement and evaluation Class participation & discussion 10% Weekly reading questions 15% Article presentation & discussion 25% Overall Learning Reflection Report 15% Research term paper 35%  Planned Syllabus (tentative) W Date Theme HW Due 1 09/08 Orientation & Some basics 2 09/15 Theoretical Framework 3 09/22 Nominal phrases (I): Article system / Genericity 4 09/29 Nominal phrases (II): Mass-count distinction 5 10/06 Interpretation of reflexives 6 10/13 Interpretation of pronouns 7 10/20 Tense & Aspect 8 10/27 Verb subcategorization 9 11/03 Negation & Polarity Item 10 11/10 Relative clauses 11 11/17 Wh-questions 12 11/24 Scalar implicature & Scope Interpretation 13 12/01 Overall Learning Reflection Report Discussion on the term paper topic (Learning Reflection Report DUE) 14 12/08 Student research term paper Meeting & discussion Term Paper Topic Proposal (2-3 pages) 15 12/15 Student-selected articles presentation 16 12/22 No class (Research term paper DUE) ● Class regulation and academic integrity: 1. Cheating and plagiarism are strictly prohibited. If you are found to copy-paste words and ideas without indicating the sources, you will get ZERO for this course. docs.text: 國立清華大學課程大綱 一、課程說明 在大洪流的環境中許多發燒的議題都隨時間消逝，工業 4.0 是少數仍受到 重視與討論的議題，近兩年 ChatGPT 更是火熱，使用與否都受到放大鏡 的審視，但這背後代表的意義為何?科技領域討論實體虛擬、經濟領域討 論產業戰略、文化領域討論人類和諧共榮等，無論是哪個論述，或許都 離不開機器與人或是人與人彼此的融合。這場全世界都爭相競爭追逐的 科技夢，現在已經改變人類的生活方式(通訊溝通)，未來勢將帶來更大的 改變。 本課程旨在結合工業 4.0 理論與情境應用，以期讓各科系學生能 1.了解何 謂工業 4.0；2.工業 4.0 對製造業的影響；3.以實務案例說明工業 4.0；4. 實作展示自走車設計、基礎 DNN/CNN 以及 PLC 自動控制，修習本門課 將對工業 4.0 整體領域建立初步的了解，並一同探討在科技、經濟與人文 在 4.0 中的衝擊與領悟。 二、指定用書 自編講義(PPT)。 三、參考書籍 書名: 工業 4.0 理論與實務 (ISBN: 9789865030407) 作者: 臺北科技大學 出版社: 全華圖書 四、教學方式 本課程的授課方式主要有講授、課堂互動討論方式與報告進行，並鼓勵 同學參觀各大展覽藉以吸收最新國內外相關領域資訊。 五、教學進度 第一週 : 課程大綱與教學內容及教學方式說明 第二週 : 科技對人與生產方式改變：淺談各階段工業發展史 第三週 : 由消費者需求與生產方式改變談起：什麼是工業 4.0？ 第四週 : 製造業的衝擊與戰略思考：工業 4.0 技術與思維導向 第五週 : 從各行各業的科技化到智慧化：活絡科技運用思維 第六週 : 智慧城市與生活之應用：無所不在的物聯網 第七週 : 機器與零件對話：看 AI 機器如何使命必達 第八週 : 知識與技術擴散：參觀展覽 第九週 : 世界各國工業 4.0 差異性 [經濟發展策略] 第十週 : 世界各國工業 4.0 差異性 [文化發展策略] 第十一週 : 實作展演：PLC 自動控制介紹 [計時器應用] THINGSPEAK 系統介紹 IoT 簡易系統 第十二週 : 案例介紹：實作展演：PLC 自動控制介紹[停車場] 第十三週 : 實作展演 : 人工智慧的危與機 [mini car 系統] 第十四週 : 案例介紹: 工業 4.0 產生的衝擊 [產業區塊與人類文明衝突] 第十五週 : 期末報告: 分組報告 1 第十六週 : 期末報告: 分組報告 2 六、成績考核 (1)平日課堂考核: 10% (到課率）。 (2)課堂參與互動性: 20% (課堂分組討論—老師與學生課堂討論互動/申 論簡答等)。 (3)期中報告: 30% (參觀展覽心得報告與攤位資料；展覽主題包括：未來 科技、智慧科技運用、工具機、自動化、物聯網、AI 人工智慧等)。 替代方案：將於第一堂上課說明。 (4)期末報告: 40% (以分組製作 PPT 方式口頭報告並有 Q&A(15 分鐘報告 5 分鐘 Q&A)；成績考核標準為: PPT 與口頭報告內容、口頭報告清晰度 與脈絡及 Q&A 表現等。 (5)加分：鼓勵同學參與大師講座與論壇(不限本課程主題)。 七、課程備註說明 (1)本課程採 16 週上課。 (2)依據本校發佈的「大學教育場域 AI 協作、共學與素養培養指引」 （2023.5.1），本課程採用：(2)有條件開放，請註明如何使用生成式 AI 於 課程產出。  同學可於課堂作業或報告中的「標題頁註腳」或「引用文獻後」簡 要說明如何使用生成式 AI 進行議題發想、文句潤飾或結構參考等使 用方式。  若經查核使用卻無在作業或報告中標明，教師、學校或相關單位有 權重新針對作業或報告重新評分或不予計分。  本門課授課教材或學習資料若有引用自生成式 AI，教師也將在投影 片或口頭標註。  修讀本課程之學生於選課時視為同意以上倫理聲明。 (3)課程若遇國定假日或學校停課則課程進度順延。 (4)課程加簽：必須參與學期第一堂上課，且加簽總人數須為教室容留人 數上限以下。 八、額外學習資源 (1)通識教育中心每學期皆會舉辦全校性通識論壇，本課程將配合學校鼓 勵同學實體/線上參與。 (2)本課程採跨領域與多元教學方式，期中將請同學參觀工業 4.0 相關議 題展覽，增加同學知識與技術擴散應用。 (3)課程將視實際情況或是否有計畫經費補助，於課程中邀請校內外專 家、講師進行演講。 (4)課程中增加實務實作的介紹。
