docs.text: 1 ISS4066: Programming for Business Analytics (Undergraduate) Jaewon Yoo Assistant Professor Institute of Service Science National Tsing Hua University Fall 2026 Course Duration: Sep. 2026 – Dec. 2026 Classroom: TSMC Bldg. R421 Class Time: Monday, 14:20 pm- 17:20 pm TA: TBD Office number ：(03) 5162543 Instructor email: jaewon.yoo@iss.nthu.edu.tw COURSE DESCRIPTION: This introductory undergraduate-level course leverages R to equip students with the fundamental skills required for robust business data analysis. The course is designed to address both practical programming skills and the conceptual understanding necessary to apply data science effectively in business contexts. Specifically, at the end of the semester you should be able to: • Data Visualization and Wrangling: Students will learn to summarize and visualize data, transforming messy data into tidy, analyzable formats. In practice this covers filtering, summarizing, grouping, joining, and reshaping data, and building clear exploratory graphics such as histograms, boxplots, and layered plots. • Causality and Regression Analysis: The course emphasizes evaluating claims about causality and using linear regression to conduct data analysis, crucial for drawing meaningful conclusions in business. It distinguishes randomized experiments from observational studies and builds from simple to multiple linear regression, including categorical predictors and model fit. • Statistical Uncertainty: Understanding and quantifying uncertainty in data analysis are core components of the curriculum, enabling students to make informed decisions. This includes sampling distributions and the central limit theorem, the bootstrap and confidence intervals, hypothesis testing (including permutation tests and power analysis), and inference for regression. • Professional Tools: Mastery of professional tools such as R, RStudio, git, and GitHub will be developed, ensuring students are well-prepared for real-world data analytics tasks. You will also write your own functions in R and produce reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto. By the end of this course, students will not only be proficient in handling complex business datasets but will also appreciate the importance of meticulous data analysis. Even as agentic AI now writes much of the code, the essential skill has shifted from writing it to directing and verifying it: without the underlying building blocks, you cannot tell when an analysis is wrong, and you end up steered by the tool rather than steering it. The course thus builds programming and visualization foundations first, then turns to statistical inference for business analytics. This course welcomes students from any background who are interested in developing foundational data analysis skills applicable to the business sector. A graduate-level section (ISS5066) is also offered, with higher expectations for independent, research-grade work. Students may not receive credit for both sections. 2 RECOMMENDED TEXTBOOKS: We will use the following books in this class. Students are expected to complete the assigned reading before joining class, which will assist in understanding the lecture materials and foster in-class discussions. Students can purchase either a hard copy or e-book version of the books. Be aware that it might take time for the textbooks to be delivered so if you plan to take the course, please make sure to place your order early enough so the books arrive in time. 1. [MD] Ismay, Chester and Albert Y. Kim. 2022. Statistical Inference via Data Science: A ModernDive into R and the Tidyverse. 2. [QSS] Imai, Kosuke and Nora Webb Willaims. 2022. Quantitative Social Science: An Introduction with Tidyverse, 2022. Princeton University Press. 3. [IMS] Mine Cetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. 2021. Introduction to Modern Statistics. OpenIntro. 4. [AAG] R for Everyone: Advanced Analytics and Graphics, 2nd Edition by Jared P. Lander, O'Reilly Media, 2017. 5. [VT] Visualize This: The Flowing Data Guide to Design, Visualization, and Statistics by Nathan Yau, John Wiley & Sons, 2011. SOFTWARE TOOLS: Students will use the R statistical programming language to write and run the codes for the assignments and in-class exercises. R is an open-source language that can be used free of charge and can be downloaded from https://www.r-project.org/. For improved productivity and convenience, students will also use RStudio, a widely used integrated development environment (IDE) for R which is available at https://www.rstudio.com/products/rstudio/ for download. You can also use Visual Studio Code to edit your code, which can be downloaded at https://code.visualstudio.com/. COURSE EVALUATION: Grading Policy Performance in this course is assessed through a blend of practical assignments, participation, and quizzes, designed to gauge your proficiency in understanding of the materials we will cover throughout the semester. Here are how each portion of course contributes to the overall grade: Category Percent of Final Grade Final Project 40% Assignments 20% Problem Sets 15% Quizzes & In-Class Exercises 5% Attitude/Participation 10% 3 Attendance 10% Course Requirements 1. AI Use Policy*: Students are permitted and expected to use AI tools, including large language models and agentic coding assistants (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini), for assignments and the final project. You are fully responsible for everything you submit. The final project is designed so that a high-quality result requires genuine understanding; AI accelerates competent work but does not substitute for it. However, it is imperative that the final submission predominantly reflects the student's understanding and personal input. To maintain academic integrity, students who choose to use AI tools must adhere to the following guidelines: a. Thorough Explanation: Students must provide a detailed explanation of how the AI tool was used in the completion of the assignment. b. Original AI Responses: Alongside their submission, students are required to submit the original responses generated by the AI tool. c. Critical Evaluation and Personal Input: Students should critically evaluate the AI- generated content and clearly indicate the portions of the work that have been modified or expanded upon with their own insights and understanding. d. Proper Attribution: Proper attribution should be given to the AI-generated content used, clearly indicating the sections that are AI-generated. ** Remember, attempting to cheat the system by heavily relying on AI-generated content without substantial personal input is ultimately the student's loss, as it undermines the learning process and personal growth. 2. Academic Honesty and Plagiarism*: All work submitted for academic evaluation must be the student’s own. The penalty for violation of academic integrity will result in a zero for that assignment for the first time. Subsequent violation(s) will result in a failing grade for the course. Plagiarism will also not be tolerated. Academic dishonesty comprises of, but is not limited to, the following: • Cheating: Copying from other students’ quizzes and assignments or allowing others to copy from one’s own. • Plagiarism: Using other people’s original work without giving appropriate credit or acknowledgment to the authors or sources. • Self-plagiarism: Submitting a piece of work in more than one course without the explicit permission of the instructors involved. • Misrepresentation of authorship: Submitting work as one’s own, which has been prepared by or purchased from others. Students will be asked to upload their submission materials to Turnitin.com, an online plagiarism checker, to ensure academic integrity. Read more about online submission on http://learning.site.nthu.edu.tw/p/412-1319-7120.php?Lang=en. 3. Attendance: All students are expected to attend every class. Please bring your own hard copy of the course materials, which will be distributed by the instructor before class. If you have any urgent reason to miss a class, you are still responsible for the materials covered during the class and are 4 expected to complete the required work. Attendance will be taken on a regular basis and will count towards your participation score (10%). Class missing will cause about 1% loss of final grade. Students who miss a class should inform me or the TA prior to the class via email or phone call. 4. Final Project*: In lieu of in-class examinations (typically two midterms and a final), the final research project is the primary summative assessment of this course. It is completed in teams and includes a final in-class presentation with Q&A; a grading rubric will be provided. This is an open- ended data analysis project on a topic of your interest. Whether you are fascinated by voting trends in presidential elections, racial disparities in policing, NBA salary distributions, or the box-office economics of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, the core steps should involve: 1) develop a clear research question; 2) locate and prepare data that can address that question; 3) apply the analytical techniques covered in the course to answer the question. You should be able to present your findings in a format suitable for a general audience. The aim is to produce a polished, portfolio-ready project that demonstrates the skills you’ve acquired to prospective employers. Your deliverable will be a publicly accessible article or webpage that includes: a concise overview of the research question and dataset; a visualization that directly addresses the question; a table or figure presenting a regression model and a plain-language explanation of the results; and a brief paragraph discussing the study’s limitations, threats to inference, and how the analysis could be improved (for instance, by collecting better data). Finally, the piece must link to a GitHub repository containing all code used to load, clean, analyze, and visualize the data and to generate the article. The data collection and cleaning must be meaningful -- it’s not sufficient to simply use a pre- cleaned data from an R package. Self-collected data is allowed and even encouraged, though beware you may need to undergo the Institutional Review Board (IRB) review process to be able to use the data for your final project. Milestone Course Week Creating a GitHub Repository 4 Data and Proposal 6 First Visualization 9 First Analysis 11 Final Report 15 5. Assignments: There will be a total of FIVE assignments throughout the semester. The assignments will be relevant to our class topic and most likely will require you to run and report a statistical method we will cover in class. For instance, after we cover ordinary least squares (OLS) estimation, students will be asked to run a dataset (to be provided by the instructor) and report the results in a simple article format. Students will be required to write a brief report using R Markdown/Quarto for the assignment. Each assignment is worth 4% of the final grade. Assignments are to be submitted on the due date. Late submissions will be penalized 1 percentage point of the assignment’s weight per day (e.g., for an assignment worth 4% of the course grade, turning it in 2 days late caps the attainable score at 2%). 6. Problem Sets: Throughout the semester, you will be required to complete problem sets that make up 15% of your final grade. These problem sets will consist of a mix of exercises taken from the 5 recommended textbooks and are designed to reinforce your understanding of key concepts covered in class. 7. Quizzes & in-class exercises: To keep the learning momentum going, students will be asked to complete multiple quizzes about the course materials throughout the semester. In order to foster learning, students will also be given in-class exercises, some of which will be graded & will count towards the final letter grade. 8. Attitude/participation: In class, the most important thing for the students is to stay active and engaged about the topic being discussed. Positive contributions to class discussions will increase your score towards attitude. When we discuss a topic in class, effective discussions are only possible if everyone is well prepared. Please, be prepared to open and engage in discussions with your opinions and thoughts. TENTATIVE WEEKLY SCHEDULE: Week Topics Prepare before class In-class deliverable #1 The nuts and bolts of R programming: • Review of programming structures • Different types of programming errors • Let’s take a touR! • Operators for R programming • What can we do with R? Recap of Basic Statistics: • Probability and inference • Random variables (r.v.s) • Probability distributions • Expectations? Spread? * Read AAG Chap 1 and 2 after class. Read: MD Ch 1 AAG Ch 4.3, 5, and 6 VT Ch 1 and 2 Install R & R Studio Self-introduction on Canvas general discussion board Complete Swirl R Tutorials 1: Basic Building Blocks 2: Workspace and Files 3: Sequences of Numbers #2 Data Types and Structures: • Numeric, character/string, logical, dates & times • Vectors, Matrices, and arrays • Lists and data frames Data Visualization for Exploratory Analysis I: • Building plots by layers • Histograms and boxplots • Grouped data * In-class group exercises Read: MD Ch 2 AAG Ch 3, 4, 7.1, 9, & 10 AAG Ch 27 and 28 VT Ch 3 and 4 Read a handout for ‘Reporting Tools (R Markdown and Quarto)’ 6 #3 User-Defined Functions in R: • Creating & nesting fn. • Local vs. global var. • Scoping rules in R • Creating binary operators Data Visualization II • Principles of analytic graphics * In-class group exercises Read: AAG Ch 7.2 and 11 VT Ch 5 and 6 AS1 (The Nuts and Bolts of R Programming for Business Analytics) Complete group formation survey #4 Data Wrangling: • Operating on rows • Operating on columns • Operating on groups • Creating barplots Read: AAG Ch 14, 15, and 16 VT Ch 7 MD Ch 3 #5 Causality: • What is it? • Randomized experiments • Calculating effects • Observational studies Read: QSS Ch 2.1-2.5 #6 Relationships and Importing/Tidying Data: • Z-Scores and standardization • Correlation • Pivoting data longer • Joining datasets Read: AAG Ch 11 MD Ch 4 QSS Ch 3.5-3.6 AS2 (Visualization & Causality: Air Pollution and Job Training Program) #7 Prediction: • Predicting election outcomes • Loops • Evaluating the predictions • Time-series plot * Review: causal effect estimation for AS2 Read: AAG 4.7 and 12 VT Chap 8 and 9 #8 Regression: • Prediction • Modeling with a line • Linear regression in R • Model fit Read: MD Ch 5 QSS Ch 4.1 and 4.2.1- 4.2.4 #9 More on Regression: • Multiple regression • Categorical independent variables * In-class group exercises Read: MD Ch 6.1-6.2 QSS Ch 4.2.6-4.3.2 AS3 (Regression & Prediction: Ethnic Bias and Voter Turnout) #10 Sampling and Sampling Distribution: • Sampling exercise and framework • Random var. and probability distributions • Normal variables and the central limit theorem Read: MD Ch 7 7 #11 Bootstrap and Confidence Intervals: • Resampling from our samples • Bootstrap CIs for a difference in means • Bootstrap CIs for a difference in ATEs • Computing and interpreting CIs Read: AAG Chap 18 and 19 MD Ch 8 IMS Ch 12 #12 Hypothesis Testing: • Hypothesis testing using [infer] • Two-sample tests • Two-sample permutation tests • Issues with hypothesis testing • Power analysis Read: MD Ch 9 IMS Ch 11 AS4 (Bootstrapping: Rags to Riches TV & Economic Mobility) #13 Individual meeting by appointment. (no in-class meeting) #14 Models of Uncertainty: • Using the normal for inference • CI for experiments • Inference for linear regression Read: IMS Ch 13 AS5 (Hypothesis Testing) #15 Inference for Linear Regression: • Uncertainty estimation for regression • Presenting OLS regressions • Wrapping up the class Read: QSS Ch 7.3 #16 Final Project Showcase and Course Wrap-up: • Teams present their projects at stations in a showcase (gallery) format • Peers visit and evaluate other teams Showcase materials ready Final project showcase; peer evaluations Notes: The course schedule is subject to change if necessary (AAG, VT, MD, QSS, and IMS, refer to ‘Recommended Textbooks’ in Page 1; AS: assignment). Assignments are due at the beginning of the class on the submission date.

docs.text: 115.03.10 114 學年度第 5 次所務會議討論修正 暑期產業實習辦法 課程目標 希望落實研究論文兼具有學術嚴謹性與產業相關性，提供學生接觸產業實際運作的機會，學習融入 實習產業文化之訓練，藉此從產業實習中找出潛在的服務創新研究方向，同時研究成果亦可更貼近 產業需求，促進產學合作與交流。 課程說明 一、 修課對象:服務科學研究所碩士生必修 二、 開課學期:碩士修業第二學年上學期 三、 修課涵蓋 （1） Yes Party 產業實習始業式:實習前於碩一下學期辦理 （2） 實習期間：以碩一升碩二暑假 7、8 兩個月為原則，或於碩一下學期學期結束後至碩二上學期 開學前至少八週以上。 （3） 實習成果發表：實習結束後於碩二上學期開學後辦理。 課程規劃 面試及媒合 (6 月 30 日前) • 尋求有意願合作企業，提供實習工作機會，由企業主提供產業實習內容 之架構規劃與需求內容，必要時由本所教授提供建議。 • 職缺來源：企業主、本校/院職涯辦公室及系所辦公室公告。 • 媒合：確實掌握學生狀況提供諮詢，實習單位以學生意願及指導教授建 議為原則，媒合完成需請企業協助指派企業導師。 Yes Party 實習始業式 (6 月 30 日前) • 透過學長姐座談經驗傳承，並提供職場安全宣導。 • 拍攝個人形象照，製作實習個人海報。 • 辦理活動凝聚共識，作為開始實習的充電，踏出實習旅程的第一步。 實習期間 7 月 1 日~8 月 31 日 或學期結束後至下學 期開學前至少八週 • 上班時間依實習單位規定。 • 學生於實習後一週內回覆個人企業導師及單位主管之聯絡方式，以利掌 握實習狀況。 • 實習期間安排訪視，瞭解實習狀況。 評量 (9 月 30 日前) • 實習結束後一個月內完成成績評量。 • 企業主依學生實習期間表現提供企業單位評分表，學生填寫實習自評表。 成果發表會 (9 月 30 日前) • 實習結束後一個月內舉辦展現實習成果，如有特殊狀況檢送所務會議討 論核定。 • 邀請企業主與產業導師參加，由本所教授依發表成果內容進行評比。 115.03.10 114 學年度第 5 次所務會議討論修正 工作項目 一、系所辦公室 1. 協助授課教師規劃實習機制、草擬實習辦法、設計實習期間所需之各類表單文件等。 2. 協助安排相關會議(如：規劃會議、實習始業式、實習期間之討論會議、實習成果發表及相關 檢討會議等)。 3. 協助向學生及分發企業說明產業實習課程實施之辦法、時程、應繳資料及應注意事項等。 4. 溝通、協調實習期間各參與者間之意見、協助處理紀錄突發狀況。 二、授課教師: 服務科學研究所全體教師共同擔任，並推派一位擔任總召集人 1. 協助徵求有意合作企業。 2. 與企業導師共同規劃實習內容，確保實習品質。 3. 輔導、評量學生實習前之準備工作。 4. 於實習階段對學生的輔導與對企業導師的聯繫。 5. 會同企業導師對學生實習成效進行考核評量。 6. 提出實施成效建議。 三、合作企業: 1. 提供暑期實習專案之需求條件並指派企業導師與授課教師共同規劃與執行產業實習課程。 2. 於實習階段依政府相關法令及分發企業聘用標準，給予薪給津貼、安排學生實習所需各項資 源與保險等等，並與學生訂立僱用契約。 四、企業導師 1. 與授課教師共同規畫實習內容，與學生就選定課題設立階段目標、評估實習成效等項目進行 討論，協助輔導學生進行實習前之準備工作。 2. 於實習階段對學生達成階段目標及完成實習課題提供相關諮詢、輔導與協助。 3. 參與實習課程期間之相關會議、提供對學生及實習課程之意見回饋或改善建議。 4. 實習結束後提供學生實習成效進行考核評量績效考核。 五、學生 1. 在充分瞭解各企業之實習內容及架構，選定前往實習企業後，須配合與授課教師、其分發企 業導師就實習課題設立階段目標、評估實習成效等項目進行討論，並進行相關準備工作。 2. 按時繳交本實習課程所要求之相關報告與本所為評估瞭解實習成效所做之意見調查。 3. 實習課程進行期間，與授課教師、企業導師及本所保持密切聯繫，並充分告知實習進行情 形，如有突發狀況致可能影響原訂實習課題或目標，應隨時反映。 4. 實習期間切實遵守國立清華大學及本所及合作企業之相關規定。 5. 實習階段所產出研發成果之智慧財產權悉歸合作企業所有，並應遵守本校及合作企業有關智 慧財產權之規範。

This course studies how managerial decisions perform once they meet the realities of markets and operating systems. The course is organized into two modules: marketing and supply chain. In these two contexts, students examine how choices about demand creation, customer response, fulfillment, capacity, timing, and coordination generate outcomes that are often uncertain and delayed. Through case-based simulations, students step into decision-making roles, make choices under incomplete information, observe responses, and diagnose the mechanisms behind performance. Learning Objectives: By the end of this course, students will be able to: • Frame managerial decisions under uncertainty. • Use simulation and AI-assisted tools as decision-support aids. • Diagnose performance outcomes. • Evaluate the robustness of business decisions. • Communicate recommendations with managerial judgment. Prerequisites: This course welcomes students from diverse academic and professional backgrounds. No prior programming experience is required. Familiarity with introductory statistics concepts such as probability, random variables, and basic regression is recommended. Evaluations: 1. Entry and Exit Quizzes (20%) 2. Midterm Exam (30%) 3. docs.text: 1 SYLLABUS ISS5065: Quantitative Research Methods in Marketing Fall Semester 2026 Instructor: Yi-Chun Ou Class time: 9.00 – 12.00 Thursdays email: ycou@iss.nthu.edu.tw Class location: 406 TSMC Building Office location: 828A TSMC Building Office hour: by appointments COURSE DESCRIPTION This course provides an opportunity for students to work in small groups to complete and present a marketing project. To successfully complete the project, students will apply appropriate quantitative analytical methods and demonstrate a solid understanding of relevant marketing theories. In addition to the group project, the course includes three individual assessments designed to evaluate students’ understanding and application of the course material. COURSE OBJECTIVES The course aims to develop students’ teamwork skills and their ability to design and implement a marketing research project using quantitative methods. Students will learn how to apply marketing knowledge and analytical techniques to generate meaningful managerial insights and maximize the practical value of research findings. Specifically, the course objectives are to enable students to: 1. Develop a conceptual framework and formulate research hypotheses; 2. Design a questionnaire and collect data; 3. Assess the reliability and validity of measurement items; 4. Conduct statistical analyses involving moderating and mediating effects; and 5. Generate actionable managerial recommendations based on analytical results. LEARNING METHODS The course combines multiple learning methods, including lectures, group discussions, and hands-on data analysis practice. 2 READING LIST • Suggested textbooks: Field’s books offer a solid conceptual understanding of statistics and provide clear, step-by-step guidance for conducting analyses. o Field, Andy (2024). Discovering statistics using IBM SPSS statistics. 6th edition. Sage publications. Note: The NTHU Library has the 2013, 2018, and 2024 editions available. For this course, any of these editions is acceptable. o Field, Andy, Jeremy Miles, and Zoe Field (2012). Discovering statistics using R. Sage publications. o Or, Field, Andy (2021). Discovering Statistics Using R and RStudio. Sage Publications. Note: The NTHU Library has the 2012 and 2021 editions available. For this course, any of these editions is acceptable. • Academic articles The reading list of academic articles will be provided in the first week. SOFTWARE We will use RStudio for this module. AI USAGE Conditionally open; specify generative AI usage in project output. TARGET STUDENTS Open to: Graduate students only. 3 GRADING • Group work • Group project (5000 words max.) 30% • Group presentation (25 mins max. + 20-25 mins Q&A) 20% • Individual work • Individual class exams 40% • Individual class attendance and engagement 10% Note: Peer evaluation For group projects and presentations, peer evaluation will be used to ensure a fair assessment of each member’s participation and contribution. Peer evaluation results will directly affect the grades awarded for the group report and presentation. Details of the evaluation process will be announced later in the course. Note: Class attendance The TA will keep records of attendance, including sick leave, absences, late arrivals and early departures. • Sick leave: No points will be deducted for sick leave. However, sick leave without medical documentation will be counted as an absence. • Absence: Each absence would result in a 6-point deduction from the attendance score (100/16 weeks=~6 per class). Exceptions may be granted for approved circumstances, such as representing NTHU in official athletic competitions. • Late arrival or early departure: Arriving more than 10 minutes late or leaving more than 10 minutes before the end of class will result in a 3-point deduction from the attendance score for each occurrence. Note: Class engagement The TA will track students’ class engagement, including activities such as asking questions and answering questions. All students will begin with a baseline engagement score of 70. Additional points will be awarded based on the frequency of participation as follows: • 0 times: 70 • 1 – 3 times: 75 • 4 – 6 times: 80 • 7 – 10 times: 85 • 10 – 13 times: 90 • 13 – 15 times: 95 • More than 15 times: 100 4 COURSE PLANNING Week Date Topic & Activity 1 Sep. 10 • Course introduction • Link “research objectives” to “conceptual models” (1) 2 Sep. 17 • Link “research objectives” to “conceptual models” (2) • Group activity: practice to generate research objectives and link the objectives to conceptual models for the group project 3 Sep. 24 • Link “conceptual models” to “questionnaires” • Group activity: practice to develop three conceptual models for the group project and find the items/ questions for the variables, respectively, in the models 4 Oct. 01 • Measurement development: reliability & validity (1) • Group activity: practice what is learned today 5 Oct. 08 • Measurement development: reliability & validity (2) • Group activity: practice what is learned today 6 Oct. 15 • Individual class exam: measurement development (1st hour) • Moderators: theory (1) • Group activity: find a proper moderator for the group project 7 Oct. 22 Note: There is no class this week. Ou has a business trip to Japan. 8 Oct. 29 • Moderators: analyses (2) • Group activity: practice what is learned today 9 Nov. 05 • Moderators: analyses (3) • Group activity: practice what is learned today 10 Nov. 12 • Individual class exam: moderators (1st hour) • Mediators: theory (1) • Group activity: find a proper mediator for the group report • Expected group work by week 10: Submit the three conceptual models and the questionnaire to the TA by 17.00 on November 12. After receiving feedback, revise the questionnaire accordingly and begin data collection, with a minimum of 300 respondents required. 11 Nov. 19 • Mediators: analyses (2) • Group activity: practice what is learned today 12 Nov. 26 • Mediators: analyses (3) • Group activity: practice what is learned today • Additional analysis if time allows: multiple mediators; mediated moderation analysis 13 Dec. 03 • Individual class exam: mediators (1st hour) • Communicate the group project report and group presentation 14 Dec. 10 Individual group meetings (30 mins per group) 15 Dec. 17 Group presentations for groups 1-3 (tentative) 16 Dec. 24 Group presentations for groups 4-6 (tentative) Note: Submit the group project by 17.00 on December 31st 2026 (tentative) 5 WEEK 1 (Sep. 10) • Learning outcomes o Have a better understanding of what this course will deliver to you and expect from you o Carefully consider whether this course aligns with your learning motivation and objectives o Understand the role of “research objectives” in the marketing project o Learn how to link “research objectives” to “conceptual models” in the marketing project • Activities o Introduce yourself to your group members o Share your expectations for this course WEEK 2 (Sep. 17) • Learning outcomes o Learn the role of “research objectives” (continued from Week 1) o Learn how to link “research objectives” to “conceptual models” (continued from Week 1) o Understand three types of conceptual models in the marketing project ▪ Main-effect-only model: independent variables + one dependent variable ▪ Moderation model: independent variables + one dependent variable + one moderator ▪ Mediation model: independent variables + one dependent variable + one mediator • Activities o Select a brand and identify relevant “research objectives” for the brand o Link research objectives to appropriate models WEEK 3 (Sep. 24) • Learning outcomes o Recap the three types of conceptual models introduced in Week 2 o Learn to carefully select variables in conceptual models: ▪ Specific ▪ Measurable ▪ Data-collectable o Learn how to find items/ questions that measure the variables from academic articles o Learn how to select appropriate scales for the items/ questions • Activities o Select a brand and develop three “conceptual models” relevant to the brand. This activity is particularly designed to help you prepare for your group project. o If time allows, identify items/ questions that measure the variables in your models. Note: The items/ questions should be drawn from articles published in reputable journals. What do we mean by a “reputable journal”? Let’s discuss in the class. 6 • Prepare for Week 4: o Each person will install RStudio. o Ou will provide step-by-step installation instructions for Windows and Mac, respectively. WEEK 4 (Oct. 01) • Learning outcomes o Complete steps 1 – 4 in measurement development: • Define the variables • Find items/ questions from academic articles • Use exploratory factor analysis (EFA) to drop bad items/ questions • Assess reliability using Cronbach’s 𝛼 and composite reliability • Activities o Complete steps 1 – 4 in the measurement development process o During the final hour, each group will practice what they have learned in today’s session. • Software required: RStudio WEEK 5 (Oct. 08) • Learning outcomes o Complete the two validity tests in step 5 of measurement development: ▪ Average variance extracted (AVE) and shared variance ▪ Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) • Activities o Complete step 5 in the measurement development process. o During the final hour, each group will practice what they have learned in today’s session. • Software required: RStudio 7 WEEK 6 (Oct. 15) • Individual class exam: During the first hour, students will take an individual exam. The purpose of the exam is to assess students’ understanding of the concepts and calculations involved in measurement development covered in Weeks 4 and 5. the extent to which the students understand the concepts and calculations of measurement development in weeks 4 and 5. • Learning outcomes o Understand the role of moderators from a theoretical perspective o Understand the role of moderators from a strategic perspective • Activities o Discuss the role of moderators from theoretical and strategic perspectives. o During the final hour, each group will identify an appropriate moderator for its group project. WEEK 7 (Oct. 22): There is no class, as Ou has a business trip to Japan. WEEK 8 (Oct. 29) • Learning outcomes o Develop a better understanding of linear regression o Learn how to conduct moderation analysis when the moderator is measured on a non- nominal scale (e.g., ordinal, interval, ratio) • Activities o Recap liner regression o Conduct moderation analysis with a moderator measured on a non-nominal scale o During the final hour, each group will practice what they have learned in today’s session. • Software required: RStudio WEEK 9 (Nov. 05) • Learning outcomes o Develop a better understanding of how to correctly interpret the impact of a moderator. This week’s example focuses on switching costs as a moderator measured on a non- nominal scales. o Learn how to conduct moderation analysis when the moderator is measured on a nominal scale (e.g., gender). 8 • Activities o Conduct moderation analysis with a nominal-scale moderator. o During the final hour, each group will practice what they have learned in today’s session. • Software required: RStudio WEEK 10 (Nov. 12) • Individual class exam: During the first hour, students will take an individual exam. The purpose of the exam is to assess the extent to which students understand the role of moderators covered in Weeks 6, 8, and 9. • Learning outcomes o Understand the role of mediators from a theoretical perspective o Understand the role of mediators from a strategic perspective • Activities o Discuss the role of mediators from theoretical and strategic perspective. o During the final hour, each group will identify an appropriate mediator for the group report. WEEK 11 (Nov. 19) • Learning outcomes o Learn how to conduct two different approaches to mediation analysis: ▪ Baron & Kenny (1986), using RStudio ▪ Zhao, Lynch & Chen (2010), using RStudio ▪ Begin with simple models to build a clear understanding of mediation analysis • Activities o Conduct mediation analysis following Baron & Kenny (1986) o Conduct mediation analysis following Zhao, Lynch, & Chen (2010) o During the final hour, each group will practice what they have learned in today’s session. • Software required: RStudio 9 WEEK 12 (Nov. 26) • Learning outcomes o Learn how to conduct two different approaches to mediation analysis: ▪ Baron & Kenny (1986), using RStudio ▪ Zhao, Lynch & Chen (2010), using RStudio ▪ Continue with some complicated models • Activities o Conduct mediation analysis following Baron & Kenny (1986) o Conduct mediation analysis following Zhao, Lynch, & Chen (2010) o During the final hour, each group will practice what they have learned in today’s session. • Software required: RStudio WEEK 13 (Dec. 03) • Individual class exam: During the first hour, students will take an individual exam. The purpose of the exam is to assess the extent to which the students understand the role of mediators in Weeks 10, 11, and 12. • Learning outcomes o Develop a better understanding of how to write and communicate the group project. o Develop a better understanding of how to present the group project. o Develop a better understanding of mediated moderation analysis. (tentative, we might have done this in Week 12.) • Activities o When discussing how to write and present the group project, please actively ask questions about any aspects of the two assessments that you are unsure about. o If time allows, practice mediated moderation analysis. (tentative, we might have done this in Week 12.) • Software required: RStudio WEEK 14 (Dec. 10) Each group will have a 30-minute meeting with me in my office. The meeting schedule will be announced in Week 11. All group members are expected to attend. If you are unable to attend, please inform me in advance and provide a reason for your absence. 10 WEEK 15 (Dec. 17): tentative Groups 1–3 will present their group project. Each group will have 25 minutes for the presentation, followed by 20–25 minutes for questions and discussion. Students from the non-presenting groups are expected to attend, actively participate in the discussion, and ask questions during the Q&A session. WEEK 16 (Dec. 24): tentative Groups 4–6 will present their group project. Each group will have 25 minutes for the presentation, followed by 20–25 minutes for questions and discussion. Students from the non-presenting groups are expected to attend, actively participate in the discussion, and ask questions during the Q&A session. WEEK 17 (Dec. 31): tentative Please submit your project to the TA by 17.00 on December 31, 2026. Projects must be submitted in Microsoft Word (.doc or .docx) format. 11 READING LIST Suggested textbooks: Please see page 2 in the syllabus. Weeks 2 & 3: Conceptual models Customer metrics or value to customer metrics (V2C) Gupta, S., & Zeithaml, V. (2006). Customer metrics and their impact on financial performance. Marketing Science, 25(6), 718-739. Main effects (independent & dependent variables) Vogel, V., Evanschitzky, H., & Ramaseshan, B. (2008). Customer equity drivers and future sales. Journal of Marketing, 72(6), 98-108. Moderators Ahearne, M., Gruen, T. W., & Jarvis, C. B. (1999). If looks could sell: Moderation and mediation of the attractiveness effect on salesperson performance. International Journal of Research in Marketing, 16(4), 269-284. (2017). The impact of positive and negative emotions on loyalty intentions and their interactions with customer equity drivers. Journal of Business Research, 80, 106-115. docs.text: 1 ISS5066: Programming for Business Analytics (Graduate) Jaewon Yoo Assistant Professor Institute of Service Science National Tsing Hua University Fall 2026 Course Duration: Sep. 2026 – Dec. 2026 Classroom: TSMC Bldg. R421 Class Time: Thursday, 14:20 pm- 17:20 pm TA: TBD Office number ：(03) 5162543 Instructor email: jaewon.yoo@iss.nthu.edu.tw COURSE DESCRIPTION: This course leverages R to equip students with the skills required for robust business data analysis. The course is designed to address both practical programming skills and the conceptual understanding necessary to apply data science effectively in business contexts. Specifically, by the end of the semester you will be able to wrangle and visualize data, turning messy datasets into tidy, analyzable form and communicating them through clear graphics; evaluate causal claims and use simple and multiple linear regression to reach defensible conclusions; and quantify statistical uncertainty through sampling, the bootstrap, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing, all with professional tools (R, RStudio, git, GitHub, and R Markdown or Quarto). As a graduate course, the emphasis goes beyond applying these methods to evaluating and producing rigorous empirical research: posing original questions, defending an identification strategy, and carrying an analysis to publishable-style depth. By the end of this course, students will not only be proficient in handling complex business datasets but will also appreciate the importance of meticulous data analysis. Even as agentic AI now writes much of the code, the essential skill has shifted from writing it to directing and verifying it: without the underlying building blocks, you cannot tell when an analysis is wrong, and you end up steered by the tool rather than steering it. The course thus builds programming and visualization foundations first, then turns to statistical inference for business analytics. This course welcomes students from any background who are interested in developing data analysis skills applicable to the business sector. It is the graduate counterpart to the undergraduate section (ISS4066), with coursework and assessment held to a higher standard: the final project must use self-collected or non- trivial data, address identification and threats to inference, and reach greater analytical depth, and grading is calibrated to this higher bar. For graduate students, it also builds a foundation for more advanced business-analytics coursework, including causal-inference courses such as Experiments and Causal Inference (ECI; ISS5099). Students may not receive credit for both sections. RECOMMENDED TEXTBOOKS: We will use the following books in this class. Students are expected to complete the assigned reading before joining class, which will assist in understanding the lecture materials and foster in-class discussions. Students can purchase either a hard copy or e-book version of the books. 2 Be aware that it might take time for the textbooks to be delivered so if you plan to take the course, please make sure to place your order early enough so the books arrive in time. 1. [MD] Ismay, Chester and Albert Y. Kim. 2022. Statistical Inference via Data Science: A ModernDive into R and the Tidyverse. 2. [QSS] Imai, Kosuke and Nora Webb Willaims. 2022. Quantitative Social Science: An Introduction with Tidyverse, 2022. Princeton University Press. 3. [IMS] Mine Cetinkaya-Rundel and Johanna Hardin. 2021. Introduction to Modern Statistics. OpenIntro. 4. [AAG] R for Everyone: Advanced Analytics and Graphics, 2nd Edition by Jared P. Lander, O'Reilly Media, 2017. 5. [VT] Visualize This: The Flowing Data Guide to Design, Visualization, and Statistics by Nathan Yau, John Wiley & Sons, 2011. SOFTWARE TOOLS: Students will use the R statistical programming language to write and run the codes for the assignments and in-class exercises. R is an open-source language that can be used free of charge and can be downloaded from https://www.r-project.org/. For improved productivity and convenience, students will also use RStudio, a widely used integrated development environment (IDE) for R which is available at https://www.rstudio.com/products/rstudio/ for download. You can also use Visual Studio Code to edit your code, which can be downloaded at https://code.visualstudio.com/. COURSE EVALUATION: Grading Policy Performance in this course is assessed through a blend of practical assignments, participation, and quizzes, designed to gauge your proficiency in understanding of the materials we will cover throughout the semester. Here are how each portion of course contributes to the overall grade: Category Percent of Final Grade Final Project 50% Assignments 15% Problem Sets 10% Quizzes & In-Class Exercises 5% Attitude/Participation 10% Attendance 10% Course Requirements 3 1. AI Use Policy*: Students are permitted and expected to use AI tools, including large language models and agentic coding assistants (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini), for assignments and the final project. You are fully responsible for everything you submit. The final project is designed so that a high-quality result requires genuine understanding; AI accelerates competent work but does not substitute for it. However, it is imperative that the final submission predominantly reflects the student's understanding and personal input. To maintain academic integrity, students who choose to use AI tools must adhere to the following guidelines: a. Thorough Explanation: Students must provide a detailed explanation of how the AI tool was used in the completion of the assignment. b. Original AI Responses: Alongside their submission, students are required to submit the original responses generated by the AI tool. c. Critical Evaluation and Personal Input: Students should critically evaluate the AI- generated content and clearly indicate the portions of the work that have been modified or expanded upon with their own insights and understanding. d. Proper Attribution: Proper attribution should be given to the AI-generated content used, clearly indicating the sections that are AI-generated. ** Remember, attempting to cheat the system by heavily relying on AI-generated content without substantial personal input is ultimately the student's loss, as it undermines the learning process and personal growth. 2. Academic Honesty and Plagiarism*: All work submitted for academic evaluation must be the student’s own. The penalty for violation of academic integrity will result in a zero for that assignment for the first time. Subsequent violation(s) will result in a failing grade for the course. Plagiarism will also not be tolerated. Academic dishonesty comprises of, but is not limited to, the following: • Cheating: Copying from other students’ quizzes and assignments or allowing others to copy from one’s own. • Plagiarism: Using other people’s original work without giving appropriate credit or acknowledgment to the authors or sources. • Self-plagiarism: Submitting a piece of work in more than one course without the explicit permission of the instructors involved. • Misrepresentation of authorship: Submitting work as one’s own, which has been prepared by or purchased from others. Students will be asked to upload their submission materials to Turnitin.com, an online plagiarism checker, to ensure academic integrity. Read more about online submission on http://learning.site.nthu.edu.tw/p/412-1319-7120.php?Lang=en. 3. Attendance: All students are expected to attend every class. Please bring your own hard copy of the course materials, which will be distributed by the instructor before class. If you have any urgent reason to miss a class, you are still responsible for the materials covered during the class and are expected to complete the required work. Attendance will be taken on a regular basis and will count towards your participation score (10%). Class missing will cause about 1% loss of final grade. Students who miss a class should inform me or the TA prior to the class via email or phone call. 4. Final Project*: In lieu of in-class examinations (typically two midterms and a final), the final research project is the primary summative assessment of this course. It is completed in teams and 4 includes a final in-class presentation with Q&A; a grading rubric will be provided. This is an open- ended data analysis project on a topic of your interest. Whether you are fascinated by voting trends in presidential elections, racial disparities in policing, NBA salary distributions, or the box-office economics of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, the core steps should involve: 1) develop a clear research question; 2) locate and prepare data that can address that question; 3) apply the analytical techniques covered in the course to answer the question. You should be able to present your findings in a format suitable for a general audience. The aim is to produce a polished, portfolio-ready project that demonstrates the skills you’ve acquired to prospective employers. Your deliverable will be a publicly accessible article or webpage that includes: a concise overview of the research question and dataset; a visualization that directly addresses the question; a table or figure presenting a regression model and a plain-language explanation of the results; and a brief paragraph discussing the study’s limitations, threats to inference, and how the analysis could be improved (for instance, by collecting better data). Finally, the piece must link to a GitHub repository containing all code used to load, clean, analyze, and visualize the data and to generate the article. The data collection and cleaning must be meaningful -- it’s not sufficient to simply use a pre- cleaned data from an R package. At the graduate level, self-collected or non-trivial data is required, though beware you may need to undergo the Institutional Review Board (IRB) review process to be able to use the data for your final project. Milestone Course Week Creating a GitHub Repository 4 Data and Proposal 6 First Visualization 9 First Analysis 11 Final Report 15 5. Assignments: There will be a total of FIVE assignments throughout the semester. The assignments will be relevant to our class topic and most likely will require you to run and report a statistical method we will cover in class. For instance, after we cover ordinary least squares (OLS) estimation, students will be asked to run a dataset (to be provided by the instructor) and report the results in a simple article format. Students will be required to write a brief report using R Markdown/Quarto for the assignment. Each assignment is worth 3% of the final grade. Assignments are to be submitted on the due date. Late submissions will be penalized 1 percentage point of the assignment’s weight per day (e.g., for an assignment worth 3% of the course grade, turning it in 2 days late caps the attainable score at 1%). 6. Problem Sets: Throughout the semester, you will be required to complete problem sets that make up 10% of your final grade. These problem sets will consist of a mix of exercises taken from the recommended textbooks and are designed to reinforce your understanding of key concepts covered in class. 7. Quizzes & in-class exercises: To keep the learning momentum going, students will be asked to complete multiple quizzes about the course materials throughout the semester. In order to foster learning, students will also be given in-class exercises, some of which will be graded & will count towards the final letter grade. 5 8. Attitude/participation: In class, the most important thing for the students is to stay active and engaged about the topic being discussed. Positive contributions to class discussions will increase your score towards attitude. When we discuss a topic in class, effective discussions are only possible if everyone is well prepared. Please, be prepared to open and engage in discussions with your opinions and thoughts. TENTATIVE WEEKLY SCHEDULE: Week Topics Prepare before class In-class deliverable #1 The nuts and bolts of R programming: • Review of programming structures • Different types of programming errors • Let’s take a touR! • Operators for R programming • What can we do with R? Recap of Basic Statistics: • Probability and inference • Random variables (r.v.s) • Probability distributions • Expectations? Spread? * Read AAG Chap 1 and 2 after class. Read: MD Ch 1 AAG Ch 4.3, 5, and 6 VT Ch 1 and 2 Install R & R Studio Self-introduction on Canvas general discussion board Complete Swirl R Tutorials 1: Basic Building Blocks 2: Workspace and Files 3: Sequences of Numbers #2 Data Types and Structures: • Numeric, character/string, logical, dates & times • Vectors, Matrices, and arrays • Lists and data frames Data Visualization for Exploratory Analysis I: • Building plots by layers • Histograms and boxplots • Grouped data * In-class group exercises Read: MD Ch 2 AAG Ch 3, 4, 7.1, 9, & 10 AAG Ch 27 and 28 VT Ch 3 and 4 Read a handout for ‘Reporting Tools (R Markdown and Quarto)’ #3 User-Defined Functions in R: • Creating & nesting fn. • Local vs. global var. • Scoping rules in R • Creating binary operators Data Visualization II • Principles of analytic graphics * In-class group exercises Read: AAG Ch 7.2 and 11 VT Ch 5 and 6 AS1 (The Nuts and Bolts of R Programming for Business Analytics) Complete group formation survey 6 #4 Data Wrangling: • Operating on rows • Operating on columns • Operating on groups • Creating barplots Read: AAG Ch 14, 15, and 16 VT Ch 7 MD Ch 3 #5 Causality: • What is it? • Randomized experiments • Calculating effects • Observational studies Read: QSS Ch 2.1-2.5 #6 Relationships and Importing/Tidying Data: • Z-Scores and standardization • Correlation • Pivoting data longer • Joining datasets Read: AAG Ch 11 MD Ch 4 QSS Ch 3.5-3.6 AS2 (Visualization & Causality: Air Pollution and Job Training Program) #7 Prediction: • Predicting election outcomes • Loops • Evaluating the predictions • Time-series plot * Review: causal effect estimation for AS2 Read: AAG 4.7 and 12 VT Chap 8 and 9 #8 Regression: • Prediction • Modeling with a line • Linear regression in R • Model fit Read: MD Ch 5 QSS Ch 4.1 and 4.2.1- 4.2.4 #9 More on Regression: • Multiple regression • Categorical independent variables * In-class group exercises Read: MD Ch 6.1-6.2 QSS Ch 4.2.6-4.3.2 AS3 (Regression & Prediction: Ethnic Bias and Voter Turnout) #10 Sampling and Sampling Distribution: • Sampling exercise and framework • Random var. and probability distributions • Normal variables and the central limit theorem Read: MD Ch 7 #11 Bootstrap and Confidence Intervals: • Resampling from our samples • Bootstrap CIs for a difference in means • Bootstrap CIs for a difference in ATEs • Computing and interpreting CIs Read: AAG Chap 18 and 19 MD Ch 8 IMS Ch 12 #12 Hypothesis Testing: • Hypothesis testing using [infer] • Two-sample tests • Two-sample permutation tests • Issues with hypothesis testing • Power analysis Read: MD Ch 9 IMS Ch 11 AS4 (Bootstrapping: Rags to Riches TV & Economic Mobility) 7 #13 Individual meeting by appointment. (no in-class meeting) #14 Models of Uncertainty: • Using the normal for inference • CI for experiments • Inference for linear regression Read: IMS Ch 13 AS5 (Hypothesis Testing) #15 Inference for Linear Regression: • Uncertainty estimation for regression • Presenting OLS regressions • Wrapping up the class Read: QSS Ch 7.3 #16 Final Project Showcase and Course Wrap-up: • Teams present their projects at stations in a showcase (gallery) format • Peers visit and evaluate other teams Showcase materials ready Final project showcase; peer evaluations Notes: The course schedule is subject to change if necessary (AAG, VT, MD, QSS, and IMS, refer to ‘Recommended Textbooks’ in Page 1; AS: assignment). Assignments are due at the beginning of the class on the submission date.

docs.text: Cross-cultural Marketing Communication (跨文化行銷溝通) Institute of Service Science, National Tsing Hua University Fall Semester, 2026 COURSE INFORMATION MEETING TIME Monday, 9:20 am to 12 pm LOCATION CTM (TSMC) ROOM 430, OR ONLINE DEPENDING ON THE PANDEMIC SITUATION INSTRUCTOR Chen-Ya Wang (王貞雅) Office: 855 TSMC Building E-Mail: cywang@iss.nthu.edu.tw Office hours：By appointment Teaching Assistant: COURSE DESCRIPTION In an increasingly interconnected global business environment it is crucial that marketers recognize how a better understanding of cultural differences can help improve performance. This course offers a framework for analyzing cultures within global marketing. A cross-cultural approach (i.e., comparisons of national marketing systems and local consumer behavior in various countries), as well as an intercultural approach (i.e. the study of marketing/service interaction between people from different cultures) are adopted. This course is helpful for those who wish to improve their cultural awareness or start their career outside their native countries. COURSE OBJECTIVES By completing this course and its requirements, students are expected to: 1. identify and describe the multiplicity of cultures as they relate to marketing communications; 2. explain principles, concepts and theories of marketing that can be applied in the global marketplace; 3. compare and contrast current/practical marketing issues as a result of cultural focus or negligence; 4. use theoretical frameworks and real-world learnings to design marketing communication strategies with a cultural mindset; 5. develop communication and presentation skills in a multi-cultural environment. LEARNING METHODS This course is based on a combination of lectures, classroom discussions, experiential activities, case studies, and marketing projects. MATERIALS Reading materials will be assigned each week. Please see the reading list on EEclass. STUDENT LEARNING ASSESSMENT Class Participation (incl. in-class quizzes, activities and discussions of articles/cases) 33% Team Article Presentation 14% Experiential Exercises 8% Country and Case Presentation 15% Final Team Project 20% Exam 10% (Letter Grade) Definition A+ (All goals achieved beyond expectation) Exceptional A (All goals achieved) Superb A- (All goals achieved, but need some polish) Excellent B+ (Some goals well achieved) Very Good B (Some goals adequately achieved) Good B- (Some goals achieved with minor flaws) Acceptable to Adequate C+ (Minimum goals achieved) Barely adequate *Please note that B is already a good grade in this class. ACADEMIC HONESTY I assume that all students do their own work and credit all work or thought taken from others (including those ONLINE!). Plagiarism will result in a huge reduction of your final course grade of even “F”. Since plagiarism is a matter of fact, not of the student’s intention, it is crucial that acknowledgment of the sources be accurate and complete. Always provide references and be sure to put quotation marks if your paragraph is exactly someone else’s work. CLASS SCHEDULE * This course schedule may be subject to change. docs.text: 服務設計 Designing for Service Course Syllabus – Fall 2026 國立清華大學（National Tsign Hua University） 余德彰(Der-Jang Yu)，林文綺（Wen-Chi Lin），廖慧萍（Hui-Ping Liao） ▓服務設計與創新系列課程的設計構想 服務創新課程由必修改為選修，服科創所時的 1.服科導論，2.服務創新，3.服 務設計之序列架構不再存在，本規劃將一樣具有創新導向、設計思維的兩門課 區分為二，服務設計著重「接觸點」與「旅程線」的設計創新，服務創新著重 「創新面」的共感轉換，兩者分學年開設，避免內容重疊的困境。 ▓服務設計 描述服務、活動、互動、體驗與結構化敘事技術的關係，聚焦在「接觸點」與 「旅程線」的基礎設計創新,著重在接觸點上的物件,資訊,互動設計，以及旅程 線的活動規劃與服務轉型價值掌控，操作技術力以點的設計思考方法，線的服 務設計規劃為目標，建構學習者對服務設計的掌握力。透過結構化敘事基礎， 進行酷創新採集,轉換應用,建構學習者對服務接觸點體驗與轉型挑戰的服務旅 程整合因應能力。 □服務創新 描述創新的趨勢、演化、突變與擴散，聚焦在環境「創新面」的感知與因應,以 創新情境與活動知識的共感，及導引綜變的因應為核心, 透過結構化敘事基 礎，進行酷創新採集,轉換應用,建構學習者對服務創新趨勢變化感應與挑戰的 服務整合因應能力，結構面包含品牌體驗式創新，科技破壞式創新，社會修補 式創新；操作技術面著重酷獵共感，場域團隊的知識綜變，服務劇本轉化的因 應與創新能力。 選課方式： 服科所學生請以服科所規定。其他科系可以無需考慮任何擋修問題，有興趣與 老師在第一週洽談後即可加簽。 1) 課程說明 Course Description and Overview 本課程目標是在服務「接觸點」的互動設計與服務「旅程線」的體驗與轉型設 計。內容著重服務設計技術:包含以服務為軸，連結實體商品，活動體驗與行為 轉型的設計空間，設計思考的理解方式,體驗與轉型的設計原型，團隊共創導引 技術，服務設計呈現技術，以及 AI 協作共創。課程結合設計思考實驗課與服務 設計實務專題，學習者將建立作品與完整設計能力。 ▓服務設計課程設計構想 從農業，工業到服務業，人類生活中，價值交換內容的樣貌一直在改變，體驗 經濟（B. Joseph Pine II、James H. Gilmore）描述了原料，商品，服務，體 驗以及轉型的演化架構，協助我們以服務為線，將設計標的區隔成實體功能與 活動體驗，提供了目標的樣貌，協助了操作方法的區隔。 服務設計重點在以顧客（Customer）為中心，描述服務、活動、互動、體驗、 創新的關係，透過結構化敘事，聚焦在接觸點與旅程線的設計創新，例如接觸 點上的物件，資訊，互動設計，旅程線的活動規劃與轉型體驗，操作「接觸 點」的設計思考方法，「旅程線」的服務設計規劃，並以體驗與轉型原型的設 計，建構學習者對服務設計與價值遞送的掌握力。 服務設計也要包含供應端服務者，服務者也是人，顧客經由旅程接觸體驗服 務，服務者則是周而復始地在接觸點提供相似的服務給不同顧客；好的設計， 能夠協助服務者提供雙方都滿意的接觸體驗與服務價值遞交。 服務設計旅程線 今年度，課程將以＂轉型＂主題，建立將主題場域由服務，體驗，提升到轉型 價值的轉型服務設計，課程將以圖書館為場域，將圖書館由當下的借還書服 務，閱讀空間體驗，提升到有 AI 協助的轉型賦能圖書館。 課程分為基本概念與理論框架，設計工具與主題演練，以及專題策展三階段： 階段一，以服務設計為主軸，介紹服務設計與案例，劇本導引與設計思考，活 動理論與關係人網絡，體驗經濟與轉型設計，田野研究與文化酷獵。 階段二，分設主題與分組，結合作坊式設計思考實驗課 L1-L4 操作，建立學習 者設計思考與服務設計基本操作能力，透過切換不同關係人視角，結合主題演 練服務探旅，顧客旅程，服務介面，服務藍圖，一步一步引領學生進入服務設 計過程。此階段亦邀請主題場域專家,相關應用與設計專家分享經驗,協助同學 發展設計。 實驗課將結合專家演講,小組共創,發表討論, 以兩週為一單元進行。實驗課主 軸與工具如下: L1: 內隱與外顯,場景九宮格, 5W1H 活動九宮格,情境與概念表單。 L2: 用戶與原型,第三人稱觀察,代言人 PERSONA, HMW 腦力書寫,實體紙原型。 L3: 價值與數媒, 第二人稱訪談, 價值階梯, 創新矩陣, 數位互動原型。 L4: 體驗與旅程, 第一人稱探旅, AEIOU, 顧客旅程, 微電影體驗原型。 階段三，透過展品製作，布展，展出測試，完成兼顧顧客端與供應端引導轉型 服務設計原型與藍圖一組，並於最後整合發表。 本學期專題「2030 大學圖書館讀者轉型 AI 協作服務」將與清華大學圖書館合 作，探討未來圖書館運用 AI 協助使用者轉型的服務樣貌;修課同學將可以選擇 圖書館不同使用者使用服務，建立新的服務旅程，並以轉型經濟的核心＂引導 客戶實現願望＂為主軸，結合 AI 協作趨勢,設計圖書館讀者轉型創新服務，產 出成果將於十二月以快閃展形式展出。 清大圖書有多種服務，選課同學將可以擇一進行服務設計與價值轉換創新探 討，積累個人設計作品。 2) 教學方式 Course Format 講課：以理論與案例，說明關鍵知識。 課堂練習：以課堂小練習，演練理論關鍵，內化知識 作業與分享：作業練習，發表分享，外化智慧，組合分享。 作坊實驗課：同化團隊操作，組合智慧，外化洞察，內化技能。 原型製作：樂高微電影，紙原型，互動介面，概念表單，服務旅程圖。 分組專題：以選定場域服務為主軸，結合服務設計所學能力與知識，結合設計 思考方法與劇本導引程序，進行共創，實證所學。 個人作業：針對一場域主題，完成顧客旅程服務地圖設計。 小組作業：期末專題，針對一場域，以 4 人小組方式完成服務旅程再設計，包 含兼顧顧客端與供應端服務設計原型與藍圖一組。 本課程並將於模方式教室上課。 3) 課程教材 Course Materials 本課程將提供自備講義教材。 參考用書： 1. 這就是服務設計，服務設計工作者的實踐指南（2019），Marc Stickdorn 2. 設計思考改造世界（2010），Tim Brown 3. 行為式設計探索手冊（2014），余德彰，南一書局 4. Design Is Storytelling（2017），Ellen Lupton 5. 體驗經濟時代（2013,十年版），B.Joseph Pine II、James H. Gilmore 6. 知識創造的螺旋（2006），野中郁次郎 7. 小處著手厚設計（2023），林文綺，陳學琳與應用劇本 8. The Transformation Economy: Guiding Customers to Achieve Their Aspirations,(2026), B. Joseph Pine II (Author), 4) 課程內容進度 Course Outline and Schedule Session # Topic Area / Theme Read & Do Prior to Class Session Deliverables / Assignments Due / Exams 1w 0908 服務設計是什麼？ 選課 2w 0915 服務設計與服務藍圖 1, 選課 3w 0922 設計思考與劇本導引 2, 4w 0929 活動理論與體驗經濟 3,4,5,8 5w 1006 顧客研究與服務酷獵 7, 轉型酷獵研究 6w 1013 圖書館服務介紹 L1,內隱與外顯 L1,更便利的圖書館 7w 1020 概念與場景 服務概念與情境 8w 1027 轉型科技介紹 L2,用戶與原型 L2,用戶轉型ＨＭＷ 9w 1103 用戶與產品 服務紙原型 10w1110 酷獵共創 L3,價值與數媒 L3,轉型酷獵分享 11w1117 價值與數媒 酷轉型數位服務 12w1124 導引設計介紹 L4,體驗與旅程 L4,顧客旅程圖 13w1201 布展準備展品製作 服務體驗原型製作 14w1208 布展與展示製作 策展 15w1215 展示與測試，修正 策展 16w1222 期末報告 學期報告 5) 成績考核 1. 出席率與參與度（10%） 2. 課堂練習（25%） 3. 個人作業（25%） 4. 小組專題（40%）

docs.text: Course Syllabus (Fall’26) Design for Behavior Change 1 Design for Behavior Change 行為改變設計 Fall 2026 Instructor: Patricia Pei-Yi Kuo Email: pykuo@iss.nthu.edu.tw Schedule: Mondays, 14:20-17:20pm Location: CTM R406 This syllabus is subject to change. Full reading list will be available in the first week of class. Description Smartphone apps are widely designed and used to engage people in positive behavioral changes in recent years, ranging from weight loss, healthy diet and exercise to meditation practice, medication adherence, and eco-friendly behaviors. However, we still do not fully understand whether and how people’s behaviors change through the use of technology (e.g., interventions, smartphone apps, sensors, web-based interface, social media). Nor did we know much how theories in behavioral economics, psychology, and communication could come together to better inform the design of behavior change technologies. How are behavior interventions designed and instrumented, and what makes these interventions successful or unsuccessful? This course is designed to understand these questions. Through in-class lectures, discussions, and activities as well as individual and team assignments, students are expected to present a project at the end of semester in the form of a formal paper, which follows the format of ACM major conferences. The final project/paper can be either research-focus (i.e., hypotheses testing) or design-focus (i.e., functional prototype) that addresses a key question in the design of behavior change technology. Course Objectives Students who take this course will be able to: 1. Learn what empirical study is, and know the major publishing venues of behavior intervention research. 2. Learn the fundamentals of behavior change research, as well as relevant theories, techniques, and design methods. 3. Get a grasp of how researchers from different fields conduct behavior change interventions through technology. 4. Understand how technology is designed and used in behavior change interventions, and the types of data collected in the interventions. Grading and Assignments (Details available in the first week of class) • Individual Assignments: 45% • Group Assignments: 55% Course Syllabus (Fall’26) Design for Behavior Change 2 Required Readings • There is no required textbook for this class. Readings will be assigned by the instructor. • Complete list will be available in the first week of class. Policy Regarding Use of AI Students may use AI (e.g., ChatGPT) to assist their learning and assignments for this class. However, each student is required to submit two written statements to indicate how AI is used: (1) to prepare their assignments, and (2) to assist any learning activities throughout this course. Tentative Schedule Week Date Topic 1 Sept. 7 Course Introduction and Team Building 2 Sept. 14 Design Fundamentals 3 Sept. 21 Technology Overview (Web, Mobile, Sensing, and Wearable Technologies) 4 Sept. 28 NO CLASS (Teacher’s Day) 5 Oct. 5 Theories Fundamentals I 6 Oct. 12 Theories Fundamentals II 7 Oct. 19 Mid-Term Project Presentations 8 Oct. 26 NO CLASS (Taiwan Restoration Day) 9 Nov. 2 Behavior Change Research in HCI 10 Nov. 9 Guest Speaker Talk + In-Class User Testing 11 Nov. 16 Group Project Refinement 12 Nov. 23 Nudging 13 Nov. 30 Sustainability 14 Dec. 7 Persuasion 15 Dec. 14 Mental Health 16 Dec. 21 Final Project Presentation

docs.text: 1 ISS5095: Maximizing Impact of Marketing Strategies and Nudges Instructor: Yi-Chun Ou Class time: 9.00 – 12.00 Wednesdays email: ycou@iss.nthu.edu.tw Class location: 406 TSMC Building Office location: 828A TSMC Building Office hour: by appointments COURSE DESCRIPTION The course is divided into two parts. The first focuses on maximizing the impact of marketing strategies, while the second examines the use of nudges. Marketing strategies aim to create value for both customers and firms. Customer value includes satisfaction, loyalty, engagement, experiences, and overall well-being, while firm value is reflected in outcomes such as revenue, profitability, and customer lifetime value (CLV). Given the complexity and dynamism of the business environment, effective marketing decisions should be guided not only by managerial experience but also by empirical evidence from data analysis. This course introduces approaches for identifying effective marketing strategies and collecting relevant evidence to support marketing decisions. Beyond firm performance, marketing can also contribute to customer and societal well-being. The second part of the course explores nudges and their applications in promoting healthier lifestyles, enhancing well-being, and improving broader societal outcomes. COURSE GOALS The scope of marketing strategies and nudges is broad and cannot be fully covered in a single course. Therefore, this course focuses on the B2C (business-to-customer) context, with particular emphasis on customer management. In the selection on nudges, particular attention is given to promoting healthier lifestyles and contributing to societal well-being. LEARNING MATERIALS • Academic articles in marketing (see the weekly reading list below). I might provide additional articles one week before the class. • Kotler, P., & Keller, K. (2012). Marketing Management (14th edition). Pearson Education Limited. (optional) Note: You may also use later editions (15th or 16th). The 14th edition is assigned because it is freely available online. The textbook provides fundamental concepts of marketing management, which remain largely consistent across editions. I strongly encourage you to read it for self-study, especially if you are new to marketing. 2 COURSE EVALUATION • Class attendance and engagement in class discussions: 20% • Three individual exams (close book): 50% • Final-term group presentation: 30% Note: Peer evaluation For group presentations, peer evaluation will be used to ensure a fair assessment of each member’s participation and contribution. Peer evaluation results will directly affect the grades awarded for the group presentation. Details of the evaluation process will be announced later in the course. Note: Class attendance The TA will keep records of attendance, including sick leave, absences, late arrivals and early departures. • Sick leave: No points will be deducted for sick leave. However, sick leave without medical documentation will be counted as an absence. • Absence: Each absence would result in a 6-point deduction from the attendance score (100/16 weeks=~6 per class). Exceptions may be granted for approved circumstances, such as representing NTHU in official athletic competitions. • Late arrival or early departure: Arriving more than 10 minutes late or leaving more than 10 minutes before the end of class will result in a 3-point deduction from the attendance score for each occurrence. Note: Class engagement The TA will track students’ class engagement, including activities such as asking questions and answering questions. All students will begin with a baseline engagement score of 60. Additional points will be awarded based on the frequency of participation as follows: • 0 times: 60 • 1 – 3 times: 75 • 4 – 6 times: 80 • 7 – 10 times: 85 • 10 – 13 times: 90 • 13 – 15 times: 95 • More than 15 times: 100 3 TARGET STUDENTS • Open to: Graduate students only. • Prerequisites: • Basic knowledge of marketing concepts, including STP, the 4Ps, and customer metrics. • Familiarity with basic empirical methods, such as regression analysis. Meeting both prerequisites is essential for successfully following the course. Students who do not meet one or both requirements will need to engage in additional self-study outside of class to keep up. AI USAGE Conditionally open; specify generative AI usage in course output. 4 COURSE PLANNING Week Date Topic 1 Sep. 09 • Introduction of the course • Customer values & 4Ps • Introduction of meta-analysis • Basic calculations of meta-analysis (1) 2 Sep. 16 • Basic calculations of meta-analysis (2) • Relationship marketing • Customer trust • Role of AI in building customer relationships and trust 3 Sep. 23 4 Sep. 30 • Individual exam about contents covered in Weeks 1, 2, and 3 on September 30th, the first hour of the class • Influencers (including celebrities) • Digital marketing (including keywords and social media) 5 Oct. 07 6 Oct. 14 • Individual exam about contents covered in Weeks 4 and 5 on October 14th, the first hour of the class • Luxury consumption • Multi-channel management • Loyalty programs 7 Oct. 21 8 Oct. 28 • Application of AI in marketing • What is the value for humans at work in a coming AI world? 9 Nov. 04 • Individual exam about contents covered in Weeks 6, 7, and 8, the first hour of the class • Introduction of nudges 10 Nov. 11 Sport Day (no class) 11 Nov. 18 Marketing is not only about profits: consumer well-being in healthy lifestyles (1) 12 Nov. 25 Marketing is not only about profits: consumer well-being in healthy lifestyles (2) 13 Dec. 02 Marketing is not only about profits: society well-being 14 Dec. 09 Meeting in groups: Answer questions regarding group presentations 15 Dec. 16 Group presentations & submit peer evaluation results: 1, 2, 3 (tentative) 16 Dec. 23 Group presentations & submit peer evaluation results: 4, 5, 6 (tentative) 5 WEEKLY READING LIST Weeks 2 and 3: Relationship marketing and customer trust Relationship marketing Khamitov, M., Rajavi, K., Huang, D. W., & Hong, Y. (2024). Consumer trust: Meta-analysis of 50 years of empirical research. Journal of Consumer Research, 51(1), 7-18. Palmatier, R. W., Dant, R. P., Grewal, D., & Evans, K. R. (2006). Journal of Marketing, 85(3), 240-255. 8 THREE INDIVIDUAL EXAMS Exam Instructions • The exam is a paper-and-pencil, closed-book examination. • The exam will last one hour. • At the beginning of the exam, you will receive the exam questions and answer sheets on site. Purpose of the exam • You will be asked to reflect on and apply the concepts learned in class. Expectations • Your answers should be based on empirical evidence and research findings (i.e., articles discussed in class), rather than personal speculation. • To support your answers effectively, make extensive use of the knowledge, theories, and concepts covered in class. 9 FINAL-TERM GROUP PRESENTATION GUIDELINES Each group will deliver a presentation on topics introduced in weeks 9, 11, 12, and 13, that is, nudges. Tasks • Select two companies. • One that implements nudges to promote healthy lifestyles • One that contributes a better society or world • Introduce each company and describe the specific nudge it implements in detail. • Evaluate the effectiveness of each nudge in achieving its intended objective. • If the nudge is effective: • Explain why it works, using evidence from academic articles and relevant theories. • If the nudge is not effective: • Explain why not. • Propose an improvement and justify why your suggested nudge would be more effective. Brief example • Select a company • Example: Peloton, https://www.onepeloton.com/. • Research the company’s activities related to customer wellbeing • Example: https://www.engadget.com/2019-01-21-living-with-peloton-bike.html • The article mentions several nudges, including being able to view the performance statistics of other attendees in the same class. • Evaluate the effectiveness of each nudge in achieving its intended objective. • Viewing others’ performance statistics provides feedback on my own progress and highlights areas for improvement, serving as a strong motivation to continue exercising. • Beginners may feel motivated when they see that most attendees perform better than they do. However, this comparison can also be discouraging. Therefore, it is worth considering a tailored nudge specifically for beginners using Peloton and explaining why it could be effective. 10 • Propose a nudge aimed at beginners, with the objective of encouraging them to continue exercising. • Retaining beginners (i.e., those with lower fitness ability) is often challenging, as they are more likely to drop out compared to advanced bikers (i.e., those with higher fitness ability). Research shows that improving either performance or happiness is key to retaining gym-goers (Fishbach and Choi 2012; Hertel, Niemeyer and Clauss 2008). To enhance performance, Peloton could encourage beginner to join mixed-level classes, where they train alongside advanced bikers. The presence of more skilled participants may motivate beginners to push themselves and improve. To enhance happiness, Peloton could encourage beginners to join same-level classes, where they exercise with peers of similar ability. This reduces negative social comparisons and helps beginners feel more comfortable and satisfied. Thus, the proposed nudge is the design of classes – either mixed-level or same-level. Peloton could ask beginners about their primary goal when joining classes. If the goal is performance improvement, assign them to mixed-level groups; if the goal is happiness and comfort, assign them to same-level groups. The proposed nudge can be explained by social comparison theory (Brewer and Weber 1994; Buunk and Gibbons 2007). In mixed-level classes, beginners observe that they perform worse than advanced bikers, which may motivate them to catch up and thereby improve their performance. In contrast, in same-level classes, beginners are less likely to feel inferior, which can enhance their happiness and overall exercise experience. Reference list Brewer, Marilynn B. and Joseph G. Weber (1994), “Self-evaluation effects of interpersonal vs. intergroup social comparison,” Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 66(2), 268–275. Buunk, Abraham P. and Frederick X. Gibbons (2007), “Social comparison: The end of a theory and the emergence of a field,” Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 102(1), 3–21. Fishbach, Ayelet and Jinhee Choi (2012), “When thinking about goals undermines goal pursuit,” Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 118(2), 99–107. Hertel, Guido, Grit Niemeyer, and Andrea Clauss (2008), “Social indispensability or social comparison: The why and when of motivation gains of inferior group members,” Journal of Applied Social Psychology, 38(5), 1329–1363. 11 Rules for group presentations • Duration: Each group presentation should last 20–25 minutes. Presentations shorter than 20 minutes or longer than 25 minutes will be marked down. After the presentation, there will be 20 minutes of Q&A. Groups that are not presenting are required to ask questions. • Equal participation: Each group member must present for an approximately equal amount of time. For example, in a four-person group with a 25-minute presentation, each member is expected to present for about 6 minutes. Significantly shorter contributions are not acceptable. • Non-participation: Any group member who does not present will not receive a presentation grade. • Assessment criteria in group presentations Criteria Detail Content 1. Introduction is attention-getting, lays out the problem well, and establishes a framework for the rest of the presentation. 2. There is an obvious conclusion summarising the presentation. 3. Appropriate amount of material is prepared, and points made reflect well their relative importance. 4. Material included is relevant to the overall message/purpose and has a consistent style. 5. Information is presented in a logical sequence. Presentation 1. Speakers use a clear, audible voice. 2. Delivery is poised, controlled, and smooth. 3. Good language skills and pronunciation are used. 4. Visual aids are well prepared, informative, creative, effective, and not distracting. 5. Length of presentation is within the assigned time limits. 6. Information is well communicated. 7. Speakers are professional in their delivery.

docs.text: Mindfulness for Well-Being & Wise Decisions, Fall 2026 (11510ISS 571701) Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) Offered by Andrew Yeh, Qualified MBSR Teacher & Profs. G Shmueli (ISS) and Y-C Wu (KPC) This evidence-based course provides participants with mindfulness training to enhance awareness, focus, manage stress, and improve decision-making in high-pressure environments. Cultivating mindfulness supports thriving in dynamic study and work environments while maintaining balance and clarity in one’s personal and professional life. The mindfulness-based stress reduction program (MBSR) originated from the stress reduction clinic at the University of Massachusetts Medical School and later transformed into the Center for Mindfulness at UMass. Thousands of scientific studies have confirmed the MBSR program helps with: ● Increasing focus and work efficiency ● Reducing stress ● Enhancing emotional awareness and regulation ● Improving sleep quality ● Alleviating symptoms of anxiety, depression, panic, etc. ● Easing chronic pain and enhancing quality of life ● Boosting immunity Cultivating mindfulness brings healing and profound transformation, allowing us to reclaim our lives rather than just existing in an ivory tower or self-imposed cage. Mindfulness practice enables us to draw from and enjoy the source of our own lives with our own strength. It helps us regain the ability to choose and self-affirm, nurturing a sense of groundedness and joy from within. For over 40 years, MBSR training has continued to expand into various fields such as medicine, psychology, education, business, sports, and even politics. This MBSR course is the most important and critical prototype of contemporary mindfulness training. Mindfulness training programs have been adopted by many international and Taiwan corporations including: *This course uses a pass/fail grading system per Article 27.1.5 of the academic regulations. It only counts for credit hours and is not included in the calculation of the GPA. Course format: 1 credit pass/fail* Requirements: Full attendance: 11 weekly sessions (9/9-12/9), Day of Mindfulness (11/7), (max 2 missed sessions after add/drop period); Weekly practice journal & class surveys. Resources: Will be distributed in class Optional reading: Full Catastrophe Living by Jon Kabat-Zinn Suitable Participants (priority given to international students) ● Those seeking to enhance emotional awareness and management skills ● Wanting to improve focus and work efficiency ● In high-pressure work or living environments ● Wishing to improve interpersonal relationships ● Experiencing sleep problems ● Easily prone to tension, anxiety, worry, and panic ● Prone to depression, low mood, and negative thinking ● Facing chronic fatigue or chronic pain issues ● Desiring self-care and tranquility of body and mind ● Eager for self-growth and deeper self-understanding Course Features | In-person ● Small class teaching, catering to each student ● In-person teaching for authentic interaction ● Group dynamics for shared exchange and growth ● Exclusive group for ongoing inquiries and discussions ● Weekly classes for steady progress ● Practice resources: free, abundant, uninterrupted ● Exclusive certification, shared learning, and continued practice Course Outline 9/9 Preparatory Class: Embarking on the treasure hunt Understanding what mindfulness and mindfulness-based stress reduction are Understanding the path of mindfulness learning Mindfulness acquaintance 9/16 Class #1: Are you kind to yourself? Learning to cultivate a gentle connection with oneself Discovering habits and new possibilities Body scan, mindful eating 10/7 Class #2: Gentleness starts with oneself Static body awareness. How to perceive stress and determine its development Body scan, breath awareness 10/14 Class #3: Happiness doesn't necessarily come from external sources Static body awareness. Accumulating emotional deposits. Seeing things we typically take for granted Mindful yoga, walking meditation 10/21 Class #4: Approaching with gentleness, seeing more Dynamic and static body-mind awareness. Gently and safely dismantling stress Mindful yoga, sitting meditation 10/28 Class #5: The tranquil power from within Dynamic and static body-mind awareness Giving oneself a vast sky Five layers of sitting meditation 11/4 Class #6: Can you really communicate? Deconstructing the elements of communication, learning simple and effective communication methods Mindful communication Day of Mindfulness: 11/7 (Saturday) Enhancing the power of mindfulness awareness Learning uninterrupted awareness. Developing into one's own best friend Various exercises 11/18 Class #7: Let's delve into theory and research From habitual reactions to mindful responses Deconstructing the development process of stress Mindful yoga, sitting meditation 11/25-12/9 Class #8-10: Gathering the treasures of wisdom and awareness Review and outlook.
