docs.text: 1 Qualitative Research Methods ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The Road Not Taken (by Robert Frost in 1916) Two roads diverged in a yellow wood, And sorry I could not travel both And be one traveler, long I stood And looked down one as far as I could To where it bent in the undergrowth; Then took the other, as just as fair, And having perhaps the better claim, Because it was grassy and wanted wear; Though as for that the passing there Had worn them really about the same, And both that morning equally lay In leaves no step had trodden black. Oh, I kept the first for another day! Yet knowing how way leads on to way, I doubted if I should ever come back. I shall be telling this with a sigh Somewhere ages and ages hence: Two roads diverged in a wood, and I— I took the one less traveled by, And that has made all the difference. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Ronald Coase (1988, p 185): “In my youth it was said that what was too silly to be said may be sung. In modern economics it may be put into mathematics.” (source: The Firm, the Market, and the Law, Chicago, University of Chicago Press.) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Thomas Cook, a methodologist, claims in1995: Qualitative researchers have won the qualitative-quantitative debate: • Won in what sense? • Won acceptance ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 2 Class Time: Monday. 14:20 ~17:10 Classroom: R833, TSMC Building Instructor Shih-Chang Hung, NTHU Chair Professor of Strategy and Innovation I'm in cubicle 827 on the eighth floor of the TSMC Building I. I read my e-mail frequently via iPhone. Send your messages to schung@mx.nthu.edu.tw. Telephone: Work: (03) 574-2448 (http://mx.nthu.edu.tw/~schung/) Objectives • Introduce some issues and problems in the philosophy of social science. • Introduce the means of assessing the key assumptions underlying the selection and use of qualitative (and quantitative) methods. • Introduce a range of qualitative research methods, including naturalistic inquiry, interpretive practice, case study, narrative analysis, grounded theory approach, comparative method, particularly as they applied to field of organization and management. • Introduce the use of a mixed methods design that combines qualitative and quantitative analyses. Course Format The course will be organized as a doctoral seminar. Our primary activities will include critical discussion of assigned articles and how these relate to our own nascent and ongoing research activities (in English/Chinese). I view the research seminar as a lively place in which we encourage and constructively develop everyone’s ideas. Effective seminars require participants to engage in the following behaviors: • You will be expected to have completed the required essential readings before each session. You may also want to read the supplementary readings associated with the session. • Read something each week that is NOT required in the lists provided. • Actively participate in the class by contributing commentary on the assigned readings (but also respect others’ air time). Willingness to constructively engage the ideas presented by others. 3 Skills The course will also give you a chance to practice the generic research skills that are valued by supervisors and employers, including communication skills, time controls, paper reviews, network building, and team working. Class Design The class includes discussions over classic books and scholarly papers. Roundtable Discussion As outlined in the course schedule (p.16-17), we will focus on one conceptual paper and one empirical article each week, discussed in two separate 75-minute sessions. For each session, one student will be randomly assigned by the chair to open the discussion with a 10-minute critical overview of the focal paper. Each participant will then have approximately 5–10 minutes to offer comments, critiques, and questions about the paper. Your paper critiques should assess the strengths and weaknesses of both the paper itself and the tradition(s) in which it is situated. With respect to our course purpose, you should also particularly assess the adequateness of research methods used. For suggested areas to address in your comments, please refer to Appendix 1: The Reviewer Guidelines of AOM. Note: Beginning in Week 3, each student should complete a pre-class note of no more than one-page words of text INDIVIDUALLY and submit it to eeclass before 11:00 pm the day before each lecture. The report should briefly describe (1) the progress made during the week and, where relevant, reflect on how the assigned readings inform the development of the project, (2) research problems or challenges encountered, (3) planned progress for the following week. 4 Assessment 1. 40% by class performance 2. 10% by individual pre-class note of each week 3. 50% by a term project of your own – in which you apply one or more of the analyses being conveyed this semester. Instructor will evaluate this. This will demonstrate your understanding of the course topics. The best measure is actually completing the project and getting it published (or at least submitted to a renowned conference) after the course has concluded. SMJ, 43(3): 447-475. 16 12/21 • Term-paper presentation 17 Appendix A: The Reviewer Guidelines of AOM REVIEWER GUIDELINES* With the opening of the Centralized Reviewer System and the enthusiastic response, we would like to thank all of you who have reviewed in the past and welcome those of you who are new to reviewing. With that said we offer these guidelines as suggestions which we encourage you to take to heart as the quality of the Annual Meeting Program is based upon the reviews you provide for the Division and Interest Group Program Chairs. Setting the Tone of the Review  Please keep your comments constructive. If the problems you identify cannot be fixed, try to provide the authors with constructive ideas for how they might improve upon their submission as they develop their research. It is also important to try and identify the strengths of a manuscript to help the author(s) improve their work.  One of the greatest services that Division reviewers perform is the development of the research of members who submit their work. Identify areas of weakness in a manuscript, but also provide specific guidance on how the authors might address the limitations you have noted. The more specificity you provide in your review, the more likely it is that the authors will benefit from your efforts.  Authors deserve to be treated with respect, regardless of your evaluation of their work. Remember, you are representing the particular Division with your review and ultimately the AOM.  Please try to be open-minded to different authors using different theoretical frameworks. Try to judge manuscripts based on how well they stimulate thinking and discussion. Also, keep in mind that many AOM members come from disciplinary backgrounds and research traditions with diverse theoretical and methodological orientations. Review Format  You must submit your review within the timelines provided. There is no slack in our schedule. Please see the annual meeting website (http://meetings.aomonline.org/) for more information.  Provide a structured review by separating and numbering comments. Also, where appropriate, cite specific page numbers, passages, tables, and figures in your review.  If you are uncertain about your comments in terms of some aspects of your review, please do your best to determine the accuracy of your position. Remember that 18 inaccuracies in your review reflect on the division you are reviewing for as a whole as well as on AOM.  Do not provide information in your review that reveals your identity and do not seek to discover the identity of the authors. This protects the integrity of the “double-blind” review process.  A good review is typically 1 single-spaced page in length. This year through the Central Reviewer System, we hope to increase the number of reviewers for each Division and Interest Group (DIG), in order to decrease the number of submissions each reviewer had to evaluate. When you signed up to review for a DIG, you commit to reviewing up to 3 papers. It is our overall goal to have you review fewer submissions, and provide higher-quality, division reviews. General Areas to Cover  In addition to commenting on the theoretical development of a submission and the technical correctness of the methodology, you should also consider the overall value-added contribution the submission offers. Does the submission pass the so what test? Also, consider whether the submission has any practical value, and comment on its implications for the practice community. Specific Areas to Consider The following points are some suggested criteria that might help you structure your evaluations of the submissions sent to you.  Introduction ✓ Is there a clear research question, with a solid motivation behind it? ✓ Is the research question interesting? ✓ After reading the introduction, did you find yourself motivated to read further?  Theory ✓ Does the submission contain a well-developed and articulated theoretical framework? ✓ Are the core concepts of the submission clearly defined? ✓ Is the logic behind the hypotheses persuasive? ✓ Is extant literature appropriately reflected in the submission, or are critical references missing? ✓ Do the hypotheses or propositions logically flow from the theory?  Method (for empirical papers) ✓ Are the sample and variables appropriate for the hypotheses? ✓ Is the data collection method consistent with the analytical technique(s) applied? 19 ✓ Does the study have internal and external validity? ✓ Are the analytical techniques appropriate for the theory and research questions and were they applied appropriately?  Results (for empirical papers) ✓ Are the results reported in an understandable way? ✓ Are there alternative explanations for the results, and if so, are these adequately controlled for in the analyses?  Contribution ✓ Does the submission make a value-added contribution to existing research? ✓ Does the submission stimulate thought or debate? ✓ Do the authors discuss the implications of the work for the scientific and practice community? *These guidelines were from the Organizational Behavior Division Reviewer Guidelines which were adapted from reviewer guidelines developed by Catherine Daily and Albert A. Cannella Jr. for the Business Policy and Strategy Division and for use in a BPS Professional Development Workshop on reviewing sponsored by the Academy of Management Review (AMR) and the Academy of Management Journal (AMJ). Don Bergh, Javier Gimeno, Bruce Avolio, and David Ketchen also contributed to the revision of these guidelines. We would like to thank both the BPS and OB Divisions for their willingness to share these reviewer guidelines for the benefit of everyone. 20 Appendix B: Readings for AI in Qualitative Research Bechky, B. docs.text: TSE 5002 Foundation of Quantitative Methods National Tsing Hua University Fall 2025 Instructor: Eric S. Lin Contact Information: Office: CTM 712, Email: slin@mx.nthu.edu.tw, Phone: 574-2729 Time and Location: Monday 9:00-noon, Center of Innovative Incubator 2F-A10 Office Hours: By appointment Course Webpage: Course materials will be available on the web through eeclass. Teaching Assistant: Raktisud You are lucky to have XXX to be your TA. Teaching Assistant Hours: TBA TA will hold the office hours and also be available for consultation on homework. Course Description: TSE 5002 introduces a range of quantitative tools that are commonly used to inform public policy issues. It provides an introduction to descriptive statistics, probability theory, statistical inference, and decision analysis. Our goal is that by the end of this course you will be able to: 1. Take a data set and a broad descriptive policy question (such as “What has happened to income distribution in Taiwan in the last 30 years?”), figure out what statistical analysis would be most appropriate to answer the question, conduct such an analysis, and present the findings in a way that is accessible to policymakers. 2. Identify real world policy situations in which the tools of probability can be used, identify which tools are most relevant, and critically consume policy analysis in which probability is used. 3. Critically consume policy studies/papers/reports in which statistical analysis is used. 4. Use the decision analysis framework as one tool to make personal and professional decisions, and to think about policy problems. Syllabus Fall 2024 The course content is divided into four broad units: (1) Descriptive Statistics, (2) Prob- ability, (3) Statistical Inference, and (4) Regression. Although the aim will remain on the underlying theory, students will be given several opportunities to gain “hand on” experience with real data set through homework assign- ments. I would encourage students to make use of my office hours (or TA’s office hours) during the semester and not wait until the day before the exam. If you are having difficulty with concepts early on, then it is likely that your difficulties will snowball and that there will be insufficient time to deal with your puzzles close to the exams. So please make use of my office hours to sort out difficulties as they arise. Prerequisites: High school algebra/Calculus preferred but not required Suggested Textbook: Basically, I will hand out my own lecture notes which are the summary of textbooks. You may find a similar textbook to the following:  Moore, David S., McCabe, George P., Craig, Bruce A., 2021, Introduction to the prac- tice of statistics (10th Edition), Macmillan Learning. Of course, there are lots of textbooks related to this course. If you have enough time, it would be also beneficial to check out some of the following reference books. References: Note that you don’t need to buy the following books. The book list is just for your reference.  Gujarati, D. N., 2003, Basic Econometrics, McGraw-Hill.  Wooldridge, J. M., 2003, Introductory Econometrics: A modern approach, South- Western. It is a very popular undergraduate level textbook adopted in US. This book gives a huge amount of empirical examples and illustrates econometric concepts intuitively.  Maddala, G. S., 2001, Introduction to Econometrics, 3rd edition, Wiley. This book is well written and in general is deeper than our textbook. You could also find some fancy topics in Maddala’s book such as bootstrap, Jackknife and GMM.  Kennedy, P. A., 1998, A guide to Econometrics, 4th edition, MIT Press. This book tries to verbally explain difficult econometric ideas and avoids heavy math. – 2 – Syllabus Fall 2024  Pindyck, R. S. and L. R. Rubinfeld, 1998, Econometric Models and Economic Forecasts, McGraw-Hill. Ths is my econometric textbook when I was a junior. It is quite easy to read.  Ramanathan R., 2002, Introductory Econometrics with Applications, 5th edition, South- Western. This book provides a number of practical applications. It is also self-contained. In Chapter 14, the author demonstrates the various steps involved in carrying out an empirical research project.  Johnston and DiNardo, 1997, Econometric Methods, 4th edition, McGraw-Hill. If you are sort of familiar with matrix algebra, it is a nice book to build up the foundation of econometrics. It also serves the bridge to compensate the gap between undergraduate and graduate level econometrics. Software: You are welcome to use any econometric packages such as STATA, R, or Python. Grading: Several problem sets will be passed out during the semester. Although there are benefits to be obtained from working in groups I would advise against students free-riding off other students. There will be two midterms and a final. Note that overdue assignment will NOT be accepted unless accompanied by a medical certificate. The same is true for the exams. docs.text: 1 TSE – Taipei School of Economics and Political Science Syllabus – 2024 FALL [Version May 25, 2024 / with dates to be updated] PERSPECTIVES IN INTERNATIONAL POLITICAL ECONOMY : (國際政治經濟) The Age of Disruption Instructor: Yves Tiberghien (Professor, Dept. of Political Science, UBC and Visiting Professor, TSE) Email: yves.tiberghien@ubc.ca Twitter: @Yves_Global Instructor Bio: https://politics.ubc.ca/persons/yves-tiberghien/ Course Schedule: TBC, lecture room A10 TBC Course Description: This course focuses on the foundations of international political economy, both theoretically and substantively. We initially discuss the various theoretical approaches to IPE, as well as key debates in trade, finance, currency, and investment questions. It also applies the theories and frameworks of IPE to the great questions of our time: the role of governance in markets, changing political economy of development, overcoming the resource curse, the transition of global economic order and hegemonic transition, climate political economy and the green technology revolution, digital and AI political economy, global sanction politics, and others. The session brings all frameworks down to the level of concrete empirical policy questions. Context: This course offers the tools and methods to understand the current remaking of the global economic order since 2008. The time for incremental changes within a stable structure is over. 2 The current battle is over the structure itself. Some pillars remain resilient, and are even expanding, owing to innovative entrepreneurship. But most are fragmenting, decaying, or being redrawn through shifting domestic forces and strategic competition. Will the postwar global order survive? And what explains the different trajectories of key regimes of globalization? We face an age of unprecedented global disruptions and systemic risks. Global governance constitutes one of the key challenges in current international relations and policy- making. As demonstrated by the Covid-19 pandemic, climate change, or the global financial crisis of 2008, global forces often overwhelm a political system that is primarily rooted in fragmented national sovereignty. As the global challenges facing the nations of the earth become more pressing, it becomes critical to address the classical political dilemmas of collective action, global commons, and asymmetry of benefits and costs. Are the dominant players in the system able to make progress in this large battle? The age of a stable US-dominated order is over. We have entered a period of great competition for global rules and norms, a battle between connectivity and fragmentation, and a confrontation between old powers and new rising powers. We are also facing a perfect storm that combines globalization-induced dislocations and a democratic crisis in US and Europe; a large-scale Russian war in Ukraine with ripple effects across the world; a climate change crisis challenging our entire economic model; the greatest pandemic since 1919; a powerful AI-centered/digital technological revolution; the greatest shift in the balance of power in over a century (over 20% of economic power shifting hands from advanced Western democracies to emerging countries between 2000 and 2018); the massive and threatening rise of China; and a US President bent on unraveling the economic and security institutions patiently built since 1944. Asia and soon Africa are rising across the board in all sub- regions, recovering a voice that was lost since pre-colonial times, ushering a much more diverse and multipolar world. According to the IMF’s current forecasts, over 60% of world economic growth will take place in Asia between now and 2030. The two dominant powers, the US and China, are locked into an ever-worsening spiral of trade conflict and security competition, a process made worse by misperceptions and emotional reactions and threatening to engulf the world economy. Is the US intent on destroying the rules-based order it nurtured for decades, in order to stop the rise of China? Or is the US just seeking to adjust rules and the division of benefits? Is China intent on uprooting the Western liberal order, or is China just seeking to gain a bigger voice within existing economic and global institutions, while retaining its historically- derived governance? The course will include a variety of activities, including lively lectures, guest speakers, movie excerpts, discussions, and debates. Invitations to global online events will be included. The instructor will be available for further discussion in person or by email. Key Words: Global trade, great transformation, disruptions, systemic crisis, technological change, global governance, Covid-19 Crisis, G20, global finance, Digital governance, AI, 5G, climate change, 3 rise of China, development (including AIIB), SDGs and Agenda 2030, global rules, globalization, global trade (TPP, RCEP) Learning Outcomes / Course Objectives 1. Understand the origins of the modern global economic system and its historic phases 2. Understand and be able to present arguments according to the various key theoretical models of IPE 3. Understand and be able to work with key debates regarding global trade, global finance, global currency, global investment, and global economic norms. 4. Understand the concept and pillars of the global economic order 5. Explain theoretical dilemmas of global governance in the current age; Unpack the process of creating global governance (comparing different arenas); Develop a pathway to analyze and solve governance problems; 6. Explain the particular historical juncture of our current period in a larger comparative perspective with a focus on the interplay between the US, the EU, Japan, and large emerging powers (China, India, Brazil) among others. 7. Provide a detailed overview, from the perspective of global governance and a changing balance of power, of five issue areas: global finance, development/SDGS, climate change, pandemic governance, and digital governance 8. In addition, students will be actively involved in the course through participation and debates and will thus improve their analytical and presentation skills. Professional Skills - Analytical and theoretical skills - Management: project management; team work - Communication: oral and written; multiculturalism, negotiation - Performance: research and analysis, critical thinking, creative thinking; and problem- solving - Entrepreneurial Spirit Assessment and Grade Distribution: Session Participation: 15% Session Presentation: 15% Short Paper (Summit Report) 20% October 23 Think Piece Paper (10-12 pages): 50%. [due Jan 20] Required readings (per syllabus) consist of selected book chapters and articles. These readings are available as PDF pieces. 4 The course will operate as a combination of both lively lectures (with text available on the website) complemented with occasional documentaries AND session discussion and debates. From the third or fourth session onward, each session will start with a student-led presentation on the topic and a first round of student-led discussion to unpack key issues in an interactive way. This discussion will be followed by a lecture and further discussion. Readings are important to complement the lectures and material covered in session. You are expected to finish the readings by the night before our session. Participation: Given the interactive nature of this course (half lecture, half discussion), I give a lot of importance to participation. I will moderate discussions to ensure that everyone has a chance to participate. Participation grades will be given both on quantity and quality of interventions (but mostly quality). I will encourage lively debates and confrontations of ideas. Session Presentation Participants will be divided into groups. Each group will be in charge of taking the lead for the seminar beginning session 3 or 4. The group will open the seminar with a 15-20mn (MAX) lively presentation exposing the key questions of the given week and reviewing key approaches and empirical results to answer these questions (based on the readings assigned for this week). Participants will then put 1 or 2 questions to the session and will moderate the ensuing 30-minute discussion. This first part will not exceed 55 mn in total (presentation+ discussion). A common grade will be assigned to the group members. Short Paper (5-7 pages, double-spaced): Summit Report You may join any global summit or significant workshop (mostly online, live or recorded) from a range of options related to global governance or global order: global online summits, global institutional summits, Paris Peace Forum, global think tank events, global NGO event, academic workshops. I will send you many invitations to global summits, but you are not limited to those. It should be a workshop that goes beyond a single talk by one speaker to hear a range of views. Your report will include the following elements: - 1. Introduction on scope, contribution and potential limits from the summit - 2. Summary of key takeaways from the summit, salient ideas, moments - 3. Analysis and Discussion in reference to some readings, theories, frameworks, and discussions of this course (ie a contextual analytical discussion). This could extract bigger trends and lessons in either decay, disruption, or resilience or innovation in the broad global governance system. - 4. Concluding part with your own voice covering either major implications or ideas for future research, or presenting your policy proposal to address issues discussed at this workshop and take them to a new dimension. 5 Think Piece Paper (10-12 pages, double-spaced): Think pieces have 2 major goals: first to develop a personal interpretation of IPE issues by presenting your own argument and defending it in a few pages; second, to demonstrate your mastery of the readings and facts presented in lectures. The questions are given by the instructor. (pick one from a choice of 5). Your paper should be an essay. Specifically, the paper must do the following three things: 1. Present an analytical argument that is a clear answer to the question 2. Address some of the literature related to the question (possible answers) 3. These little computer 33 chips provide the processing power for everything from cars and iPhones, to unmanned drones and missiles. In Beijing's Made in China 2025 industrial strategy, through which China seeks to move up the value chain to become a high-tech superpower, semiconductor self-sufficiency was one of the targets. Beijing is falling far behind on this target. MIC 2025 stated the aim of meeting 70 per cent of China's demand through domestic production by 2025, but, seven years on, it is only meeting 20 per cent of its domestic needs (by one estimate). The world's leading manufacturer of semiconductors is in fact in Taiwan. The Taiwanese Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dominates more than half the global market, and controls 90 per cent of the cutting edge 5 to 10 nanometre sector (in this industry, size matters; the smaller the chip, the better). Even American companies like Intel outsource a substantial amount of production to TSMC. A tech arms race is underway. In order to control the supply of this small but vital component, China and the US are desperately funnelling money into their own national champions, whilst 'kneecapping' each other's efforts, as my guest Nigel Inkster tells me on this episode. He's the former director of operations and intelligence at MI6 and author of The Great Decoupling: China, America and the Struggle for Technological Supremacy . docs.text: 1 Civilizations, Empires and World Order Professor Amitav Acharya Introduction The 21st century is witnessing the end of the “great divergence” between the West and the Rest, which began with the rapid ascent of Western Europe from the 17th century AD onwards and the corresponding decline of the once mighty and wealthy civilizations, such as those of China, India, and Islam. As the global power and idea shifts reshape dynamics of world politics civilizational identities are asserting themselves, creating fears of what Samuel Huntington called a “clash of civilizations”. At the same time, the relative decline of the West, the crisis in the US- led liberal hegemonic order and the increasingly global role of rising powers such as China and India in world affairs are creating new possibilities of both conflict and mutual learning and cooperation between the West and the Rest. Against this backdrop, it has become ever more important to revisit the concepts of “civilization” and “world order”, to examine them from a historical and global perspective, to analyze their interaction and inter-relationships through the ages, and to draw lessons for the present and the future. Aside from its intellectual and analytical purpose, this course has a normative inspiration: to promote greater diversity and inclusion in international studies. According to its foundational narrative, the field of International Relations (IR) was “born” in the UK, and “raised” in the US; hence its labelling as an “American social science” (in Stanley Hoffmann’s phrase),. The conventional study of international relations relies heavily on concepts and practices developed in Europe and the US. This course (due to lack of time, it has a primary focus on China, India and Islam, but brings in others) challenges the Western-centric narrative of IR and opens the door to a Global International Relations (Global IR). While conventional IR uses the nation-state as the unit of analysis, the Global IR approach takes civilizations as the basis unit to explore the multiple types of international systems or world orders, including those that predate the Westphalian system and the rise of the West. If one approaches IR (or “world politics” or “international studies”) with the nation-state as its core unit of analysis, one has less than 400 years of history to play with. This is also the period of the rise and dominance of the West. If one studies IR and related fields from the perspective of civilizations, then one has over 4000 years of human history to reflect on and analyze. In this broad sweep of history, many civilizations have risen, fallen, and reemerged. No civilization can claim a monopoly over ideas or approaches to peace, security, diplomacy, development, human rights, environmental protection, or other related subject-matter of IR. By taking a broad historical perspective, this course aims to uncover the forgotten or marginalized agency of non- Western civilizations in the making of the modern world order, and stress the multiple, global origins of international relations and world politics. This “Global IR” approach not only helps us to better understand the contemporary dynamics of world politics, but also promotes inclusiveness in our increasingly complex, diverse and multicultural world. Learning Objectives 2 In completing this course, students should have developed: 1. Broad familiarity with the history of civilizations and world orders, especially the major civilizations such as China, India, Islam and their impact on the world orders of their times; 2. Ability to analyze the key factors behind the rise of the West and the role played by non- Western civilizations in contributing to it and recognize the historical and cultural forces that have shaped the contemporary world order and will shape the future; 3. Understand and appreciate the multiple foundations of theories and concepts of the discipline of International Relations (IR) and question the present state of IR as a Eurocentric or Western-centric field of study; 4. Enhanced critical thinking, including ability to interpret and present international affairs from multiple cultural and philosophical perspectives; 5. Understand and analyze the key forces shaping world politics today, including the role of emerging powers such as China and India, trends in global governance, conflict and cooperation among nations and states; 6. Sensitivity to, and respect for, diversity and inclusion in the study international affairs. Texts: 1. Henry Kissinger, World Order (New York: Penguin, 2014) 2. Amitav Acharya, The End of American World Order, 2nd edn. (Cambridge, Polity, 2018) Assignments: A. Mid-Term Essay (20%): The “Great Divergence”: Causes, Consequences and Legacies (Deadline Oct 5) The Great Divergence refers to the rise of Western Europe vis-à-vis Asia after the 15th century AD. Your essay should answer the following three questions: • Why did the “great divergence” occur? • Would the West have developed its “killer apps” without imperialism and racism? • What were the principal Eastern contributions to the rise of the West? B. Final Essay (40%) On the topic decided by you after approval from the professor. This must fall within the scope of the syllabus. (Deadline, last day of Class) C. Participation (40%) This will take into consideration regular, punctual attendance; active participation in discussions (asking questions to professor and presenters, commenting on their views as well as those of other students participating in discussions). Schedule: Topics and Readings Class 1. docs.text: Keywords: China, BRI, Global South, infrastructure, SEZs, extractive industries, environmental impact Course Title: China and the Global South TSE Fall Semester 2026-27 Draft 6-26[some readings might be swapped out, as this is a field that is changing all the time] Julia C. Strauss Class time: Thursdays, 9-12 Lecture Room: Office: Office Hours Wednesdays 1-3 pm and by appointment online E-mail: js11@soas.ac.uk Description As China is an increasingly important player in world politics, its profile as a non-traditional donor to other developing countries has risen. Yet there is a great deal of (mis)information and at best only partial understanding of its “rise” for the Global South. This weekly seminar seeks to overcome a range of (mis)perceptions about China and the Global South that are regularly (re)told and (re)presented in the open media and in think tanks outside China. In Week 2 we take a macro view of what is and is not different about China’s approaches to development and aid and we disaggregate “China” as comprising a multiplicity of actors who “go out” to the Global South in search of investment, aid, and employment in quite different sectors. Weeks 3-6 concentrate on what China makes available to the Global South in terms of infrastructure and investment; Week 7 turns specifically to the question of the impact of China’s rise as a development actor in the Global South on environment and biodiversity. Weeks 8-9 deal with the indirect impact of China’s footprint in the Global South: the ways in which food imports from the Global South have (re)shaped domestic consumption, and how migrants to and from the Global South are changing perceptions. Throughout the class we will focus on the ways in which neither China nor countries in the Global South are unified: each is comprised of an ever shifting range of different political, social, and economic actors. After Week 10, we will shift to discussion and presentation of students’ final projects. If the class is small, we will add an additional unit on China’s “soft power” initiatives in the Global South in Week 11; if the class is medium sized or large, we will commence with student presentations of their final projects in Week 11. In Weeks 13-14, there will be no class; this is the time for students to concentrate on their final projects, which will be due the last regular day of class before exam week. Course Objectives For students to: 1) Develop greater understanding of the drivers behind China’s sets of relationships with the Global South 2) Develop critical awareness of the rhetoric and claims for and against China’s growing relationships with the Global South through the BRI 3) Hone critical ability to analyse particular instances of China’s projects in the Global South 4) Develop critical and writing skills in policy analysis through the writing of short policy briefs and a longer piece of policy analysis Course Delivery Until the last week in November, will be face to face, and we will meet weekly. Once we shift to “Flipped learning” in the last two weeks of the semester before the examination period, there will be no regularly scheduled class, but I will continue to be available for consultation remotely. Until Week Eleven, the normal format of the seminar will be that I will lecture for a bit more than an hour, followed by a short break, and the rest of the time will be given over to student presentation, discussion, and other exercises TBA. Weeks Eleven and Twelve will be devoted to student presentation of their final projects and discussion. Weeks Thirteen and Fourteen are “Flipped Learning” from then until the Friday before the beginning of Exam Week, you should be working on your policy report/ final project. There will be no final exam. Course Requirements A) Reading Requirements All students will be expected to have done the reading for the weekly seminar an advance of the class meeting itself. I try to mix up longer, often more academic articles or book chapters with shorter policy or opinion pieces. But if you are to get much at all out of this class, then you need to come to class prepared, and this means having engaged with the reading and the topic before the seminar! B) While there are no specific textbooks for this class, and the topic is changing so rapidly that I will almost certainly have to swap out individual readings as new ones become available, there are several book length treatments of the topic that are especially noteworthy that I hope that the library will procure: 1. Min Ye, The Belt Road and Beyond: State-Mobilized Globalization in China: 1998–2018 (Cambridge University Press, 2020) 2. David Lampton, Selina Ho, and Cheng-chwee Kuik, Rivers of Iron: Railroads and Chinese Power in Southeast Asia (University of California Press 2022) 3. Miriam Driessen, Tales of Hope, Tastes of Bitterness: Chinese Road Builders in Ethiopia (Hong Kong University Press, 2019) 4. Austin Strange, Chinese Global Infrastructure (Cambridge Elements, 2024), https://www.cambridge.org/core/elements/chinese-global- infrastructure/35932BF8AEADDEFF1E96B19B13300FAE (free download) C) Writing Requirements 1. One short (500-750 words) critical response paper: due by the end of Sunday 20 September(10 %) 2. One short (1,000- 1,250 word ) policy brief : due end of Week Eight before class on Friday 29 October (15%) 3. One abstract/ short bibliography for final essay/ policy report : not formally assessed but necessary to finalize your topics. DUE BEFORE the end of MONDAY 11 November . This will not be graded, but is important for feedback prior to your presentations. 4. One policy report OR regular analytical academic essay on a topic involving China and the Global South that covers some aspect of China’s investment/ aid/projects/ trade/ migration / environmental impact etc. You do not have to choose a topic that is explicitly covered in this class, but it should broadly align with the themes of the course and not be primarily focused on either military or security issues. (5,000-7,000 words), due BEFORE the beginning of regular exams on FRIDAY 18 December 2026 5. (50%) D) Oral Requirements 1. One 20 minute oral + ppt presentation on your chosen topic for your final policy report/ paper, date TBA in either Week 11 or Week 12 (15%) 2. Regular participation and preparation in seminar discussions. (10%) This breaks down into two components: a. Taking on presentation of the seminar readings for the week and participating in other exercises b. Regular attendance in class (attendance will be taken from Week Three, and without a reasonable excuse, deductions will be made for non-attendance) c. Regular and meaningful participation and discussion even when you are not a presenter Statement on Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in this class Artificial Intelligence is an increasingly powerful, and also easily misused, tool that researchers and writers at any level now cannot afford to ignore. I encourage the critical use of AI in this class (it is very helpful for organizing thoughts, sifting through references and bibliography, and checking text. However, the uncritical and unrestricted use of AI can equally lead to very large problems (false or misleading information, “tilt” towards what is popular rather than what is well referenced and well argued, overreliance on what is current and trendy rather than what has depth and might be older). Think of AI as an autocompletion and sorting tool: it can help you sort and get through routine tasks quickly, but it cannot substitute for either your thinking or the parameters that you put in when you ask it to do something. Therefore, the critical use of AI in this class is not only permitted, but encouraged. However, I do require that you indicate exactly when and how you use AI in all your written work. docs.text: 1 Sept 1, 2026 Government and Politics in Asia (a two-credit course) for Fall Semester 2026 Instructor: Tun-jen Cheng (tjchen@wm.edu or tjcheng7@gmail.com) Teaching Assistant: Klay Si Thu Aung Class hours: 9-11 am Tuesday Taiwan time, Fall 2026 Office hours: Tuesday afternoon 1-3pm in person for weeks 1-4, weeks 14-16 Wednesday evening 6:30-8:30 pm, online remote, for weeks 5-13 Appointment required for all office-hour meetings (details below). Description: For half a century Asia has been the most vibrant economic region on earth. It is essential to understand political underpinnings and consequences of this region’s economic transformation. Covering East Asia, Southeast Asia, and South Asia, this course is structured thematically. Within each theme, however, we will focus on specific countries that are either standing alone or in paired or multiple comparisons, thereby combining thematic analysis and country specificities. Part I provides a historical and contemporary overview of Asian politics, examining dynasty legacy, colonial rule, decolonization, and state- and nation-building. For Part II, this seminar addresses salient aspects of regime dynamics in the context of economic development which is the most important goal for a country upon gaining political independence. Topic issues for these five sessions include regime type and economic growth, drivers, processes, and problems of democratic transitions, as well as patterns of political evolution. For Part III, this seminar dwells on political institutions and processes in Asian democracies, covering constitutional forms of government, political parties, political participation, political polarization, and contentious politics. The final part is devoted to a few leading issues of governance in resilient authoritarian polities, including the implicit social contract, the political and economic conundrum, and intractable agency problems. Course requirements, grade distribution, and important dates: 20% Attendance and participation 30% Midterm assignment (due 5pm Oct 28, 2026, Wednesday, Week VIII) 50% Term paper (due 5pm December 23, 2026, Wednesday, Week XVI) September 21 last day for add-and-drop November 21 last day for course withdrawal Reading materials for the course: All required readings are book chapters or journal articles. They will be available to you in softcopy. Note that a few book chapters are from the following three Routledge Handbooks: Tun-jen Cheng and Yun-han Chu, eds., Routledge Handbook of Democratization in East Asia, 2018; Paul Brass, ed. Routledge Handbook of South Asia Politics, 2012; Jeffrey Haynes, ed., Routledge Handbook of Democratization, 2010 [in which Southeast cases are predominant examples]. You are encouraged but not obliged to read any recommended readings. 2 Weekly Topics Very important note: The instructor will inform you before each session which items in the required readings are for you to peruse, which other items are for you to skim through only. In average you are actually reading 2 or 3 items per week (not 5 or 6 as the syllabus seems to suggest). Part I. Pre-colonial Legacy, De-colonization, State-Building, and Nation-Building Sessions 1 & 2. Sept 8 & Sept 15 Topics: Course Mechanics and an Overview of Asian Politics: Patterns, Distinct Features, and Puzzles; Pre-colonial and Colonial Legacies, Decolonization, State- Building and Nation-Building Required readings: Nayan Chanta, “When Asia was one,” Global Asia 2003, pp.58- 68; Chun-in Moon and Seung-won Suh, “Burden of the Past: history, identity, and nationalism in Northeast Asia,” Global Asia 2004, pp.34-48; Yuhua Wang, The Rise and Fall of Imperial China, Princeton University Press 2022, ch.1, pp.3-29. Recommended readings: Selections from Ebrey, Walthall, and Palais, East Asia, Houghton Mifflin 2009, pp.257-261, 296-303; Ian Talbot, “India and Pakistan: Colonialism, Nationalism, and Independence”; in Paul Brass ed., Routledge Handbook of South Asian Politics 2010, pp.27-41. Part II Regime Dynamics and Economic Development Session 3. Sept 22 Topic: State Capacity and Economic Development--Colonial Legacies Do Matter Required readings: Atul Kohli, State-Directed Development, Cambridge University Press, 2004, Ch 1 Introduction pp.1-26; Ch 2 The Colonial Origins of a Modern Political Economy: The Japanese Lineage of Korea’s Cohesive-Capitalist State, pp. 27-61, and Ch 6 “Origins of a Fragmented-Multiclass State and a Sluggish Economy: Colonial India,” pp.221-256. Recommended readings: Nicola Mastrorocco and Edoardo Teso, State Capacity as an Organizational Problem: the US experience, NBER August 21, 2023; Guo Xu, “The Cost of Patronage: Evidence from the British Empire,” American Economic Review 2018. Session 4. Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, 2025; Steve Levitsky and Lucan A. Way, “What Comes After Democracy Breakdown?” Foreign Affairs Today, Feb 11, 2025; Steve Levitsky, Lucan A. Way, and Daniel Ziblatt, “How Will We Know When We Have Lost Our Democracy?” May 8, 2025, the New York Times; Pepper Culpper and Taeku Lee, “When Populism Can Be Good,” Journal of Democracy, April 2026, pp.79-90; Sheri Berman, “Democracy’s Problems Should Be No Surprise,” Journal of Democracy, April 2026, pp.35-48. Highly recommended: Kachan Chandra, “The Future of Multiracial Democracy: Majoritarianism without Majorities,” Journal of Democracy 2024, 35:4, pp.46-62. Questions for this full discussion session: What factors, forces and institutional guardrails prevented Indira Gandhi’s full and long dictatorship? Are these good old democracy safeguards working now? Are European electoral dynamics (most notably, the most recent local elections in Britain and the latest election in Hungary) helpful to our evaluation of India democracy under Narendra Modi? Part III Democratic Institutions and Processes in Asia 4 Session 8. Not So Fast,” Taiwan Journal of Democracy December 2019, pp.1-30 and his “Regime Type and Pandemic Policy: Hybrid Exceptionalism in Malaysia,” Taiwan Journal of Democracy December 2020, pp.31-56. Details about office hours: dates, modes and logistics Tuesday 1-3 pm in person for weeks 1-4, weeks 14-16 (that is 9/8, 9/15, 9/22, 9/29, 12/8, 12/15, 12/22) Wednesday evening 6:30-8:30 pm, online remote, for weeks 5-13 (that is, 10/6, 10/13, 10/20, 10/27, 11/3, 11/10, 11/17, 11/24, 12/1) Appointment required, email mail me to make it two days ahead Midterm assignment: Pick a topic on political development or an essential aspect of political dimension of economic development in as many Asian nations as possible. Or you can pick two comparable cases. You can even do just one country. But no matter how many country cases you have, make good use of a database available in the field, and write a well-focused piece that is both theory-informed and empirically substantiated. Final term paper: You can pick a new topic or delve more in-depth into the topic that you have already dwelled on in your midterm paper. If you choose to refine/deepen your midterm paper, you should give one page description on the difference between the midterm and the final, as well as submit two versions of your final paper, one highlighting the portion of additions and changes, one being the clean copy. Consultation and mechanics of two writing projects: You are encouraged to come to my office hours for consultation for your topical choice. On both written assignments, you must provide appropriate citation for all thoughts, words, or ideas that are not your own (this includes the ideas of peers). An electronic file summarizing the Chicago Manual citation style will be posted on our eeclass platform. The midterm assignment should be approximately 2,000 words in length and the term paper approximately 4,000 words in length. Both should be submitted via email attachment in both Word and PDF formats. Both are to be turned in on time by 5 pm on the due date. AI policy: Using generative AI for this class is strongly discouraged but not prohibited. Disclosure of its use is required. Expectations: • Class participation is a required part of the course. Please attend all classes and contribute towards discussion. • Writing, writing, writing: Learning to write well, to make a coherent and well researched argument, is one of the key skills you should get out of the grad school or, if you are an undergrad, a grad level course. • Current Events: A good theory, thesis, or analytical framework is a tool for digesting current events. Current events in turn allow us to assess the utility and limitation of the analytical tool. This is a very exciting time in Asian Politics with many daily changes in the region. I therefore strongly recommend that you follow current events in Asia by reading a major news source with good international coverage (i.e. BBC news, New York Times, The Economist etc.) or a news source from a subregion (i.e. Indian Express, Dawn, ToloNews etc.). This will help you get more out of the reading, by making class discussions more productive and improving the quality of your analytical thinking.

docs.text: 1 Asian Development in Global Historical Perspective 歷史與全球觀點下的亞洲發展 Fall 2026 Instructor: R. Bin Wong, Distinguished Research Professor of History, UCLA Course Code TSE 602800 Email address: wong@history.ucla.edu Place: Time: Wednesdays 1:20 pm – 4:20pm (Weeks 1-6 and Weeks 8-12) OH: Wednesdays 10:00 am -12:00PM (& by appointment if unable to attend OH). Course Overview This course focuses on Asian economic development within a global context of industrialization & trade beginning in the late eighteenth century, moving through the 19th & 20th centuries, and looking forward into future 21st-c. possibilities. Each of the course’s four units devotes time to relationships between economic development and the natural environment in order to place our contemporary concerns about climate change in historical perspective and prepare future paths of economic and environmental change. Late 20th-century scientific research began to accumulate evidence confirming multiple ways in which the benefits of economic growth came at serious costs—air and water pollution, biodiversity loss, and climate change. We therefore consider how the processes of modern industrialization that began less than 250 years ago depend on natural resources in ways unimaginable for most of the 300,000 years of human history. We begin in Unit I looking at Asian Development in the 19th-20th c. world of economic change and move in Unit II to placing Asian development within a global economic and environmental framework. The first half of the course brings us to the late 20th century and the recognition of limits to growth that leads us to Unit III where 21st-century efforts to foster sustainable development confront the challenges of achieving sustainability transformations. Unit IV concludes the course’s concern for understanding how economic activity depends on natural 2 resources with a focus on energy development that is foundational to the economic security and wellbeing of people across Asia and the rest of the world. Central to this course are the economic and political principles and practices that together form the political economies of the past, present, and possible futures we seek to create. This course aims to make your study of political economy prepare you to consider the type of 21st-century political economy you want to see emerge. Course Format 1. We meet in Weeks 1-6 and Weeks 8-12. Each three-hour session will include both lecture and discussion components. Weekly Study Guides with questions that highlight key themes to think about as you prepare the upcoming meeting’s readings will be posted to the class website at least a week in advance of the class meeting. Students are encouraged to take notes that summarize your understanding of the articles or portions of books that makes up each week’s readings. Having these notes will help you participate actively in each class as well as help you prepare the written work assigned in this course. Please be aware that you have readings to prepare before our first class meeting. 2. Readings for each class meeting can be found on our class website course syllabus links. 3. Please consider sending me an email by Tuesday evening regarding any questions you may have about any of week’s readings that I will try to address in my opening remarks. The more communication we have, the more effectively the course will succeed in teaching you ways to understand economic development. 4. Students will write and submit digitally three Response Essays that address one or more of the questions raised on the weekly study guides. The first Response Essay (1000 – 1500 words) will cover Units I & II and be due on October 21st (Week 7) at 1:00 pm. The second and third Response Essays (750-1250 words each) will cover Units III and IV respectively and be due on Saturdays (1:00 pm ) of Weeks 9 and 12. 5. These Response Essays along with the Study Guide notes you take on the weekly readings should prepare you for class lecture and discussion; they should also provide much of the basis for you to write your Final Papers. 6. Citations Format for the Response Essays and Final Paper should be made in a social science format of brief in-text citations (Author or Lead Author followed by “et al.”, then 3 publication date followed by page number(s)” and a bibliography organized by author or lead author’s last name followed by publication date and the title of book, book chapter or article; if you cite any PPT lecture material, in-text citation should be PPT title and slide number(s) and in the bibliography as “my name, week number, and PPT Title.” 7. The Final Paper assignment will be a 1,750-2,500-word double-spaced (7-10 pp) essay response to some selection of course themes. While I will offer you some themes for your final papers during Unit III, you can either select among the themes I suggest or propose your own theme. You’re encouraged to do some additional reading for your final paper. In past years, some students have incorporated materials regarding their home countries as part of the preparation of their final papers. Finally, I ask that you inform me by email the topic you choose for your final paper no later than Wednesday November 12th. Final papers are due Week 14 on Thursday December 11th by 5:00 pm TST. 8. Grading Please inform me if for any reason you will not be attending class as this is the norm typical in graduate school training (which a few students in the past did not realize). While there is no grading of class participation, there is an expectation of oral engagement with course material during class each week and if you’re not able to attend a class session, you’ll be expected to write some brief responses to the Study Guide Questions. Each Response Essay counts as 20% of your final course grade and the final paper 40% of your final course grade. The papers will have numerical grades converted to a final letter grade according to: A+ (97–100), A (93–96), A- (90–92), B+ (87–89), B (83–86), B- (80–82), C+ (77–79), C (73–76), C- (70–72), D+ (67–69), D (65–66), D- (below 65). To summarize, each paper gets a numerical grade with the sum of the numerical grades adding up to a potential maximum of 100 points. Ethics Statement on Generative Artificial Intelligence Grounded in the principles of transparency and responsibility, this course encourages students to leverage AI for developing their understanding of course materials. In accordance with the published Guidelines for Collaboration, Co-learning, and 4 Cultivation of Artificial Intelligence Competencies in University Education, this course adopts the following policy: Conditionally Open If you use generative AI in any of the four writing assignments, you must briefly explain how you used generative AI to develop your understanding of specific concepts, themes, arguments, and research methodologies in the readings. This explanation should be given below your paper title. If usage is discovered without proper disclosure, instructors, the institution, or relevant units have the right to reevaluate the assignment or report or withhold scores. I have not used generative AI to develop course materials or format. List of Unit Subjects, Session Themes, and the Readings I. Asian Development in the 19th-20th c. World of Economic Change A. Origins, spread, and limits of Industrialization (Week 1 September 9) Readings: Allen 2011, “Why the industrial revolution was British.” Allen 2014, “The spread of manufacturing.” Jun, Lewis, Kang, 2008 “Korean Expansion and Decline from the Seventeenth to the Nineteenth Century: A View Suggested by Adam Smith.” Elson, 1993 “International Commerce, the State and Society: Economic and Social Change.” B. Capitalism: Fossil fuels, the Environment & the Geopolitical World Order (Week 2 September 16) Readings: Wrigley, 2013 “Energy and the English Industrial Revolution.” Tello-Aragay & Jover-Avellà, 2014 “Economic History & the Environment” Sugihara, 2017 “Monsoon Asia, Intra-regional trade and fossil fuel-driven industrialization.” Wong, 2021 “Modern Capitalism’s Multiple Pasts and Its Possible Future” II. 20th c. Asian Development in Global Economic & Environmental Frames A. Asian Economic Growth (Week 3 September 23) 5 Readings: Fukao and Settsu, 2021 “Japan-Modern Economic Growth in Asia.” Grove and Kubo, 2022 “Handicraft and Modern Industries.” (China) Wu and Fan 2014 “China’s Economic Reform: Processes, issues, and prospects (1978-2012)” in Chow and Perkins eds., Routledge Handbook of the Chinese Economy Huff, 2021 “Growth and Globalization Phases in South East Asian Development.” B. 20th century Energy and Environment (Week 4 September 30) Readings: Bankoff, 1995 “Coming to terms with nature--state & environment in maritime Southeast Asia” McNeill, 2007 “Social, Economic, and Political Forces in Environmental Mattick, Williams & Allenby, 2010 “Historical Trends in Global Energy Consumption” Meadows et al 1972 The Limits to Growth chapter 1 C. 20th-century Knowledge & Beliefs About Development (Week 5 October 7) Readings: Donella Meadows et al 1972 The Limits to Growth Chs 2 & 3; Dennis Meadows, 2007 “Evaluating Past Forecasts--reflections on one critique of Limits to Growth” III. Late 20th-c. Recognition of Limits to Growth & Early 21st-c. Efforts to Foster Sustainable Development A. Limits to Growth & the Pursuit of Sustainable Development (Week 6 October 14) Readings: Meadows et al 1972 Chs 4 & 5; Gale 2018 Ch 1 & Ch 3 Week 7 1st Paper Assignment due October 21 at 1:00 pm B. 21st c. views of sustainable development (Week 8 October 28) Readings: Gale Ch 4 “Deriving sustainability value from sustainable development”, Herrington 2022 “The Limits to Growth Model—still prescient 50 years later.”, Berkes, Colding & Folke, 2000 “Rediscovery of Traditional 6 Ecological Knowledge as Adaptive Management”; “ Shao 2025 “Systematic Review of Doughnut Economics” C. Sustainability Value and Leverage Points for Sustainability Transformation (Week 9 November 4) Readings: 2018 Gale Ch 8; 2017 Abson Leverage Points; 2019 Fischer & Riechers Leverage Points Perspective; 2021 Linnér and Wibeck Drivers of sustainability transformations--leverage points, contexts, & conjunctures Week 9 2nd Paper Assignment due November 7 at 1:00 pm IV. Asian Energy & Sustainable Development in Geopolitics & the Global Economy A. SDGs: Asia in Global Perspective & Systems Thinking (Week 10 November 11) Readings: 2018 Gale Ch 5 pp 123-127; 2025 ESCAP Asia & the Pacific SDG Progress Report (vi-vii, 26-31)—2020 Fortier Connecting the SDG Dots Through Systems Thinking (7 pp), 2014 Weitz et al A Nexus Approach—Formulating Integrated Water, Energy, and Food SDGs (15 pp) B. Asian energy development, especially in & by China (Week 11 November 18) Readings: 2024 IEA China’s evolving footprint (10 pp); 2025 Nedopil China BRI 2024 investment report; 2023 Liu et al China BRI energy (24 pp) ; 2025 Chiengkul Toward greener BRI (22 pp) C. Energy Transitions, Connectivity in Asia, and the Importance of Solar Energy (Week 12 November 25) Readings: 2024 ESCAP Energy connectivity for sustainable development in Asia & the Pacific [assigned reading pp. 7-28, pp. 42-58 (through 4.1), pp. 60-75 (through 5.1.1 “Digital twin technologies”)]; 2025 McKibben, “Solar is Liberation”; “2025 Powering Transitions—The Future of Energy Storage in the Indo-Pacific”; 2026 “China and India power Asia-Pacific’s growth in global solar expansion”; “2026 Carbon Brief Solar overtakes gas power in Asia for first time ever”: “2026 Southeast Asia’s Solar Panel Boom – The Diplomat”; “2026 Powering South Asia’s clean energy transition ESCAP” Week 12 3rd Paper Assignment due November 28 at 1:00 pm 7

It examines recent advances in the theories of growth and structural transformation, with a focus on applying these frameworks to understand cross-country income differences in the world economy and the role of public policy in shaping them. The use of macroeconomic data is also emphasized. Learning Outcome: Based on different dynamic macroeconomic models, we try to understand the driving forces behind the development process of an economy and the related policy implications. This allows us to identify the sources of world income differences. docs.text: Bureaucracy and Economic Development Vorada Limjaroenrat Taipei School of Economics and Political Science 1 Course Information 1.1 General Course Info Course Title: Bureaucracy and Economic Development Course Term: Fall 2026 Professor: Vorada Limjaroenrat Class time: Monday 13.20-16.20 am (Room A08). Office hour: Wednesday 15.00-16.00 am TA: Charles Tsai 1.2 Course Description The success of government policy depends heavily on the bureaucracy. Bureaucrats are responsible for policy implementation and, in practice, serve as the operational arm of the state. Their actions can foster economic and social development, but they may also produce undesirable outcomes, including repression, inefficiency, and corruption. This raises central questions: How do political institutions and incentive structures shape bureaucratic behavior and performance? How can insights from labor and political economy be used to improve effectiveness, accountability, and bureaucratic performance? This course addresses these questions through the lens of labor and organizational eco- nomics. It begins by introducing the role of bureaucracy in state capacity and economic development. The second part focuses on the personnel economics of the state, examining how governments recruit, motivate, evaluate, and retain public servants. Students will apply core economic frameworks, including principal-agent theory, signaling, and screening mod- els, to analyze problems of selection, incentives, and bureaucratic performance. The third part shifts the focus from individual bureaucrats to the organization of the state. We ex- amine how accountability, organizational structure, management, and political institutions influence bureaucratic effectiveness and public service delivery. Throughout the course, we study evidence from a wide range of institutional settings, including democratic and authoritarian regimes, high- and low-income countries, and diverse public sectors such as policing, education, taxation, and the judiciary. Emphasis is placed on integrating economic theory with recent empirical research to understand how bureaucratic institutions shape state capacity and long-run development. 1 Students are expected to have prior coursework in microeconomics and applied econo- metrics, or to have completed a related applied economics course. Enrollment is limited to students in at least the second year of an MA program/PhD. 1.3 Grading policies Midterm exam (20%);seminars presentation and participation (20%); attendance (10%); final project (20%); final exam (30%). More details will be discussed and announced on the first class. 2 Reference List Part 1: Bureaucracy and Economic Development 1.1 Conceptual Issues (Week 1) Conceptual: rethinking policy and bureaucracy in economic development.  **Besley, T., Burgess, R., Khan, A. and Xu, G., 2022. Mostly Harmless Econometrics: An empiricist’s companion. Princeton university press.  Cunningham, S., 2021. Causal Inference: The mixtape. American Economic Review.  **Do, Nguyen, and Tran (2017). One Mandarin Benefits the Whole Clan: Home- town Favoritism in an Authoritarian Regime. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics. North- Holland, 2017. 467-514.  Guo Xu, Erika Deserranno, Diana Moreira, Edoardo Teso, “Bureaucracy” VoxDevLit, 8.1, September 2023 2.3 Selection & Recruitment (Week 5-6) Who enters bureaucracy?; adverse selection, signaling, screening.  **Akerlof, G. A. (1970). The Market for "Lemons": Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism. Quarterly Journal of Economics.  Ashraf, N., Bandiera, O., & Lee, S. S. (2018). Losing Prosociality in the Quest for Tal- ent? Sorting, Selection, and Productivity in the Delivery of Public Services. American Economic Review.  Bai, Ying and Ruixue Jia. 2016. docs.text: 1 Political Economy of the Semiconductor Industry Course Outline The semiconductor industry has become strategically important in economic growth and international relations. This course is designed to demystify the complexity of the global semiconductor industry in terms of technological development, market competition, geopolitics, and interactions of national policies. It is an interdisciplinary course bringing together the knowledge of engineering, management, economics, and political science. The course is divided into four parts and to be taught by four instructors, with each instructor covering a part of the course. The rest of the time will be used for examination and guest lectures. The four parts are (1) development of the semiconductor industry and technology, (2) characteristics and evolutions of the global semiconductor market, (3) geo-politics and geo-economics in the semiconductor industry, (4) technology policies pertinent to the semiconductor industry in East Asia. The detailed contents of each part are listed below. Part 1: Development of the Semiconductor Industry and Technology (Chintay Shih) Part 2: Global Semiconductor Market (Kenneth Kin) Part 3: Geo-politics and Geo-economics (Tain-Jy Chen) Part 4: Technology Policies (Chan-Yuan Wong) Class Plan Thursday, R6-R8 14:20 – 17:10 Week Date Instructor To pic 1 2026/9/10 Tain-Jy Chen Introduction 2 2026/9/17 Part 1 - Chintay Shih Semiconductor industry dev. (3) 5 2026/10/8 Part 2 - Kenneth Kin Global semiconductor market (1) 6 2026/10/15 Part 2 - Kenneth Kin Global semiconductor market (2) 7 2026/10/22 Part 2 – Kenneth Kin Global semiconductor market (3) 8 2026/10/29 Part 3 – Tain-Jy Chen Geo-politics and Geo-economics (1) 9 2026/11/5 Part 3 – Tain-Jy Chen Geo-politics and Geo-economics (2) 10 2026/11/12 Tain-Jy Chen Midterm presentation 11 2026/11/19 Part 4 - Chan-Yuan Wong Technology policy (1) 12 2026/11/26 Part 4 - Chan-Yuan Wong Technology policy (2) 13 2026/12/3 Guest Lecture: Burn Lin Chip Peace/Lithography 2 Week Date Instructor To pic 14 2026/12/10 Part 4 - Chan-Yuan Wong Technology policy (3) 15 2026/12/17 Part 3 – Tain-Jy Chen Geo-politics and Geo-economics (3) 16 2026/12/24 Part 3 – Tain-Jy Chen Open Grading Policy Homework #1: Short essay for technology policy, evaluated by Professor Wong (20%) Midterm presentation: Topics to be assigned and evaluated by Professors Shih, Kin, Chen (30%) Final Essay: Evaluated by Professor Chen (35%) Class Participation: 15% Part 1 Development of the Semiconductor Industry Description: Topic 1: Introduction to semiconductor industry development and global value chains. Topic II: How Taiwan developed its semiconductor industry (1975-1994). Topic III: Important technological breakthroughs in the semiconductor industry. Reference: • John Matthews 1995, High-tech Industrialization in East Asia: the Case of the Semiconductor Industry in Taiwan and Korea. Taipei: CIER. • Tain-Jy Chen and Chin-Tay Shih, 2026, Taiwan’s Semiconductor Miracle: From Periphery to Core, Oxon and New York: Routledge. • Shih, W., Shih, C., and Chien, Chen-Fu (2008), Horizontal specialization and modularity in the semiconductor industry, Harvard Business School Case Study (9-609-001). • Shih, W., Chien, Chen-Fu, Shih, C., and Chang, J. (2009), The TSMC Way: Meeting Customer Needs at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., Harvard Business School Case Study (9-610-003). • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_transistor • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microprocessor • 張如心， 『矽說台灣』 ， 潘文淵文教基金會， 天下文化出版， 2006 Part 2 Global Semiconductor Market Description: This course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the global semiconductor market and supply chains. Students will gain an in-depth understanding of the political and economic factors that drive the semiconductor industry, including market trends, supply chain dynamics, and the role of Taiwan in the industry. The course will cover key topics such as the semiconductor market by industry, by technology, and by region; the semiconductor supply chains; and future challenges and opportunities in the semiconductor industry. Through lectures, 3 case studies, discussions, and projects, students will develop a strong foundation in the political economy of the semiconductor industry and its role in global economics. Learning Outcomes: Upon completion of this course, students will be able to: • Understand the political and economic factors driving the global semiconductor market • Analyze trends in the semiconductor industry by industry, technology, and region • Understand the dynamics of the semiconductor supply chain • Assess the role of Taiwan in the semiconductor industry • Identify future challenges and opportunities in the semiconductor industry Course Topics: • Overview of the Global Semiconductor Industry • Market Trends by Industry, Technology, and Region • The Semiconductor Supply Chains • The Role of Taiwan in the Semiconductor Industry • Future Challenges and Opportunities in the Semiconductor Industry Recommended Reading: • Chris Miller, 2022, Chip War: The Fight for the World’s Most Critical Technology, London: Simon and Schuster. • Stephen Witt, 2025, The Thinking Machine: Jensen Huang, NVIDIA, and the World’s Most Coveted Microchip, New York: Viking Book. Part 3 Geo-politics and Geo-economics Topic I: Foundry Model: The origin of the foundry model; why Taiwan came to adopt the foundry model; the impacts of the foundry model and TSMC’s success. Topic II: US-Japan trade conflicts: Trade war on semiconductors; SEMATECH (US industrial policy to revitalize the semiconductor industry); the impacts of geopolitics on the semiconductor Topic III: China’s rise: China’s rise in the semiconductor industry; industrial policy; role of the state; US-China technology war and threats on globalization. Topic IV: DRAM: Role of DRAM in the semiconductor industry; US-Japan competition; Japan-Korea competition; China’s challenge. Topic V: Moore’s Law: Effects of Moore’s Law; Barriers to Moore’s Law and technology progress; Scale economies and industry structures. docs.text: 1 COURSE SYLLABUS COURSE TITLE: International organizations in global politics Autumn 2026 • Credit: 2 • Time: T7T8 (Tuesday 15:30~16:20, 16:30~17:20) • Room: A10, TSE • Level: MA / MGPE Core • Instructor: Gerald Chan, e-mail: cgcw@mx.nthu.edu.tw; gerald.chan@auckland.ac.nz • Office: C03, TSE • Office hour: Wednesday 13:00~15:00 or by appointment • Teaching assistant: TBA COURSE DESCRIPTION This course assesses the significance of international organizations in global politics. It focuses on the theoretical approaches to the study of international organizations, including the origins and development of these global bodies, especially the growth of regional organizations after the Second World War. The course explores the changing roles, functions and norms of these organizations working in such areas as security, economics, environment protection, human rights, public health, resource scarcity, science and technology, and social justice. How does the rise of Asian countries, in particular China, affect inter-state relations and the workings of international organizations? KEYWORDS International organizations, global issues, political economy, norms, rules, Asia, China LECTURE DATES & TOPICS Sep 8 Introduction Sep 15 Lecture 1 (L1): Globalization Sep 22 L2: Global governance Sep 29 L3: International organizations Oct 6 L4: Peace and security Oct 13 L5: Trade and finance Oct 20 L6: Environmental protection Oct 27 L7: Human rights Nov 3 L8: Humanitarian intervention Nov 10 L9: Public health 2 Nov 17 L10: Resource security Nov 24 L11: Poverty Dec 1 L12: Development Dec 8 L13: The digital world Dec 15 L14: Summary and conclusion Dec 22 Exam AIMS AND OBJECTIVES At the end of the course, we should be able to: 1. understand international relations and organisations in their many facets; 2. make a distinction between globalisation as a process and as an ideology; 3. examine the roles and functions of international organisations in conflict and cooperation; 4. assess the impact of the rise and fall of great powers on globalisation and global governance; and 5. probe a little into the future shape of globalisation. TEACHING METHOD Weekly lectures and/or tutorials/seminars ASSESSMENT Three pieces of assessment (details to be arranged or confirmed): 1. 50% research essay a. Topic on some aspects of globalisation, global governance, or international organisation (to be discussed) b. Word limit: 3,000 words (plus or minus 10%) c.
