docs.text: Constitutionalism in Asia/Syllabus/TSE/Fall 2026 1 SYLLABUS CONSTITUTIONALISM IN ASIA Professor Jiunn-rong Yeh 葉俊榮 Email: jryeh@ntu.edu.tw TA: Nguyen Vo My Tam Email:nguyenvomytam11@gmail.com Wednesday, 10:20-12:10 Taipei School of Economics and Political Science I. INTRODUCTION Constitutinal order has been the foundation of socio-economical and political development. The rise of Asia, in economic, politcial and technological terms, has demonstrated the institutioal relevence of constituional governance. Constitutionalism has increasingly taken root in Asia in the forms of democratice governance, human rights and rule of law. With the rise of Asia and growing economic powers therein, attentions have been paid to the embedded constitutional institutions and culture that serve as the foundation of economic and political governance. In particular, constitutional review to check government functions is now being performed in most, if not all, of Asian states by courts of general jurisdiction or specialized constitutional courts. This course seeks to explore the constitutional foundations of development dynamics in the region including that of Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, Mongolia, China, Hong Kong as well as Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Singapore, India and Nepal. The thematic discussion in this semester will include constituitonal culture, constituional making history, government and seperation of powers, constitutional change, judicial review, equality and equal protection, free speech, and socio-economic rights. II. OBJECTIVES This course seeks to advance the following three objectives 1. To deepen the understanding of constitutional context of socio-economic-political development in Asia. 2. To provide more dynamic and contextual perspectives on the theory and practice of human rights protection and democratic governance. Constitutionalism in Asia/Syllabus/TSE/Fall 2026 2 3. To compare and analyze contemporary constitutional order in Taiwan and her peer states in Asia. III. READING MATERIALS Core Readings ⚫ Wen-Chen Chang, Li-ann Thio, Kevin YL Tan & Jiunn-rong Yeh, (2014), Constitutionalism in Asia: Cases and Materials, Hart Publishing. ⚫ Jiunn-rong Yeh, (2016), The Constitution of Taiwan: A Contextual Analysis, Hart Publishing. IV. SCHEDULE Week 1: 9/9 Asian Constitutionalism: Purpose and Basis Introduction of the course: Themes, Formates, and Methodology Constitute Project: https://www.constituteproject.org/. Comparative Constitutions Project: https://comparativeconstitutionsproject.org/. 1. Jiunn-rong Yeh, (2010), The Emergence of Asian Constitutionalism, 4 National Taiwan University Law Review, No. 3, pp. 39-53. 2. Li-ann Thio, (2021), Varieties of Constitutionalism in Asia, 16 Asian Journal of Comparative Law, No. 2, pp. 285-310. Week 2: 9/16 Constitutionalism and Methodology Contemporary constitutional discourse has been foundationally shaped by the understanding of liberal constitutionalism and more recent divergent development in democratic transition and globalization in terms of transitional and transnational constitutional discourse. The understanding of these changing contours and comparison among them is foundational to comparative constitutional law. 3 Jiunn-rong Yeh and Wen-Chen Chang, 2009, The Changing Landscape of Modern Constitutionalism: Transitional Perspective, 4 National Taiwan University Law Review, No.1., 145-183 4 Jiunn-rong Yeh & Wen-Chen Chang, 2011, The Emergence of East Asian Constitutionalism: Features in Comparison, American Journal of Comparative Law Vol. 59 No. 3, pp 805-840. Constitutionalism in Asia/Syllabus/TSE/Fall 2026 3 Week 3: 9/23 Special session: Bruce Ackerman’s Master Lecture Week 4: 9/30 Presidential administration and divided society Many new democracies in Asia have experienced contentious politics. In a winner- takes-all presidential system, political divisions tend to center around the role of the president, as demonstrated in Taiwanese and Korean politics. How constitutional courts adjudicate on contentious presidential politics in new democracies remains a significant issue in comparative constitutionalism. We would look into five constitutional courts in Asia, and compare how courts deal with political disputes arising from presidential politics in Korea and Taiwan 5 Jiunn-rong Yeh, 2011, Presidential Politics and Judicial Facilitation of Political Dialogue between Political Actors in New Asian Democracies: Comparing the South Korean and Taiwanese Experiences, International Journal of Constitutional Law Vol. 8.No. 4. pp.911-949 Week 5: 10/7 No class Week 6: 10/14 Electroal constitutionalism In general terms, there has been routine national elections held in line with constitutional calendar in most of the Asian states. Looking into respective contexts, however, one finds levels of problems confronting Asian states in electoral constitutionalism. Electoral deficit, institutional capacity, and embedded family dynasty structure seems to be prevailing multi-level challenges to constitutionally mandated elections in Asia states. 6 Jiunn-rong Yeh & Wen-Chen Chang, 2025, Changing Dynamics of Constitutional Progress and Regression in Asia: Interplay of Electoral, Civic, and Judicial Constitutionalism, Constitutional Studies, Vol. 11. No. 1. 1-31(PP. 14-24) (part 1) Week 7: 10/21 Constitutional eternity and revisions There has been vibrant politics of constitutional revisions in Asia, with success and setbacks. The drives for constitutional change vary in contexts, some undermine democratic mandates from the constitution. To an extreme, constitutional revisions were even ruled unconstitutional by the Court with judicial strategies questioned when analyzed in context. Constitutionalism in Asia/Syllabus/TSE/Fall 2026 4 6 Jiunn-rong Yeh & Wen-Chen Chang, 2025, Changing Dynamics of Constitutional Progress and Regression in Asia: Interplay of Electoral, Civic, and Judicial Constitutionalism, Constitutional Studies, Vol. 11. No. 1. 1-31 (PP. 1-14)(Part 2) Week 8:10/28 Judicial strategies in applying the political question doctrine: The Philippines, Japan, Taiwan Many Asian states confront politically charged issues in the constitutional actuality, many of those demand judicial resolution. Where and how the courts resort to the political question principle in handling these highly contentious issues? Were there judicial strategies involved? 7Jiunn-rong Yeh, 2016, Judicial Strategies and Political Question Doctrine: An Investigation into the Judicial Adjudications of the East Asian Courts, in Legal Thoughts betwen the East and the West in the Multilevel Legal Order (Chang-fa Lo, Nigel N.T. docs.text: TSE 604900: Institutions and Economic Development Course Description The purpose of this course is to analyze institutions, and how institutions affect economic development. In addition to general analyses, institutions of China and China’s development are discussed with some details. The institutional component introduces analytical concepts and theoretical frameworks with historical and contemporary contexts. The economic component addresses economic development and political economic issues. It is a largely self-contained course on institutional economics, political economics, and Chinese political economy. Basic microeconomics and macroeconomics, development economics, political science, Chinese political economy are beneficial, but not as prerequisite knowledge. Basic Text Chenggang Xu (2026), Lecture Notes (PPT) (to be distributed during lectures). If the class size is moderate, evaluation will be based on each student’s final essay. If the class is larger, evaluation will be based on group work, including a group presentation and within-group self-evaluation. In your essay or presentation, you must demonstrate your understanding of the essential course materials by applying them to substantive issues. You may challenge the arguments and evidence presented in the lectures and required readings if you hold different views. However, any such challenge must clearly identify the point of disagreement and explain the reasons for it, supported by well-reasoned counterarguments and properly sourced evidence. Otherwise, your answer will be treated as reflecting a failure to understand the course materials. docs.text: 1 Trade and Regulations in the Digital Age Fall 2026 W6W7, TSE Professor Shin-yi PENG sypeng@mx.nthu.edu.tw Overview This course examines international trade and regulations in the context of the digital economy. Newspaper headlines frequently highlight global trade challenges in the digital age, from disputes over semiconductor tariffs and national security-based 5G standards to AI and data nationalism measures that restrict cross-border data flows. Governments are facing dilemmas between, on the one hand, maximizing opportunities stemming from the digital economy and, on the other, managing the associated risks and pursuing public policy objectives such as privacy and cybersecurity. The course begins by exploring regulatory frameworks for information and communication technology (ICT) products, with a particular focus on international trade rules and related disputes. It then turns to data-related domestic regulations, analyzing their impact on global trade and the balance among trade liberalization, industrial innovation, and digital sovereignty, particularly a nation’s right to regulate amid rising geopolitical tensions. Students will also study the role of international trade rules under the World Trade Organization (WTO), free trade agreements (FTAs), and digital economy agreements (DEAs) in shaping the digital economy. They will examine the interests of key stakeholders in international negotiations and identify areas where new trade rules and policies may be needed. The course is designed to provide interdisciplinary perspectives on trade issues. The instructor will interpret trade rules in clear and straightforward terms, making them accessible to students from diverse academic backgrounds. Through real world disputes, the course develops understanding of key regulatory concepts and their underlying economic and political rationales. 2 Schedule (Provisional) Week 1 (9/9) Introduction and Overview ICT Industrial Policy, Geopolitical Trends and Trade Rules Week 2 (9/16) Tariff War over Technology Export Controls on ICT Products Week 3 (9/23) Digital Economy and National Security Class Exercise: Trade Disputes Over ICT Products Week 4 (9/30) Data-Driven Economy and the Right to Regulate Week 5 (10/7) Privacy, Cybersecurity and Global Trade Governance Week 6 (10/14) Data Nationalism and Data Localization Class Exercise: Multistakeholder Role-Playing Meeting on Data Localization Issues Week 7 (10/21) Digital Platform Governance – Digital Trade Market and Competition Week 8 (10/28) Digital Platform Governance (Continued) - Social Media Content Moderation Week 9 (11/4) Digital Platform Governance (Continued) - Video Streaming Services and Cultural Diversity Weel 10 (11/11) No Class due to the University’s Annual Sports Day Week 11 (11/18) Digital Trade Rules in FTAs and DEAs Week 12 (11/25) Digital Inclusion, Investment and Sustainability Week 13 (12/2) Review and Reflections Class Exercise: Trade Negotiations Simulation 3 Week 14 (11/26) Trade Governance in the Age of AI Week 15 (12/15) Student Presentations Week 16 (12/23) Student Presentations Assessment Class participation (50%) Research paper (50%) • Due date: Wednesday, 30 December 2026 • Length: Approximately 4,000 - 5,000 words

docs.text: TSED Comparative Public Policy Fall 2026 Instructor: Jonghoon Lee Time: Thu 13:20 - 16:20 Email: Place: Section#: Credit Hours: 3 Office Hours: , or by appointment. Course Description: This course examines how public policies are formulated, adopted, implemented, and evaluated across different political and institutional contexts. Moving beyond a single-country focus, the course takes a comparative perspective on public policymaking in advanced democratic, developing democratic, and authoritarian systems. Students will analyze how political institutions, state capacity, eco- nomic structures, interest groups, bureaucracies, and international pressures shape policy outcomes across countries. The course is organized into three parts. The first part introduces major theories and frameworks of the policy-making process: including institutions, agenda settings, decision-making, implementation, and external pressures. The second part applies these frameworks to substantive policy areas such as welfare states, regulation, industrial policy, globalization, immigration, and emerging technological and environ- mental challenges. The third part examines comparative policy processes across different political systems and regional contexts, including presidential, parliamentary, and authoritarian regimes, with focused case studies from Taiwan, Korea, Japan, China, Southeast Asia, the United States, and Europe. The course is designed for students pursuing careers in government, international organizations, busi- ness, and research, and aims to develop both analytical and practical policy analysis skills. No advanced quantitative background is required, although students will be introduced to comparative policy research and evidence-based policy analysis throughout the semester. Course Learning Outcomes: At the conclusion of this course, students should be able to: • Understand major theories, concepts, and frameworks in comparative public policy and the policy process. • Analyze key stages of the policy process, including agenda setting, policy formulation, implementation, and evaluation. • Evaluate how governments respond differently to major policy challenges such as inequality, regulation, globalization, immigration, technological change, and climate governance. • Apply comparative policy frameworks to real-world cases from East Asia, Southeast Asia, North America, Europe, and other regions. Course Keywords: Public Policy; Policy-Making Process; Policy Implementation and Evaluation; Com- parative Politics; Political Institutions. 1 Comparative Public Policy Fall 2026 Text Books and References: • The assigned readings are yet to be updated. • Required readings will be provided by the instructor online. Evaluation: Participation (10%), Weekly Reading Summaries (20%), Discussion Leaders (20%), Research Presentation (20%), and Final Paper (30%). • Participation (10%): All students are expected to participate actively and thoughtfully in class. Active participation includes asking questions, responding to questions posed by the instructor or other students, and contributing to class discussion in ways that demonstrate careful engagement with the assigned readings. High-quality participation does not require having a fully developed critique. Rather, it requires demonstrating that the student has read the assigned materials carefully and is prepared to engage with them analytically and constructively. • Weekly Reading Summaries (20%): From Week 2 through Week 14, students are required to submit four short reading memos over the course of the semester. Each memo should be approximately 75 words. For each submission, students should write two brief memos based on two assigned readings: – Summary memo: This memo should identify the research question, explain why the question is important, summarize the main argument, and describe the key findings of the article. – Extension memo: This memo should go beyond a summary by offering a critique, comparison, contrast, or extension of the article. Students may discuss theoretical limitations, empirical design, measurement, case selection, alternative explanations, or connections to other readings and policy debates. Weekly reading summaries must be submitted by Tuesday at 5:00 PM. Submissions received after the deadline will be considered late and will be subject to the course’s late work policy. The instructor may select some student memos to help motivate and structure in-class discussion. Selected memos are intended to generate collective discussion, not to single out individual students. • Seminar Presentations (15%): Each student is required to present one assigned seminar article to the class during the semester. Presentation slots will be assigned in Week 2. The presentation should be 12–15 minutes long and should clearly address the following questions: – What is the main research question the author(s) seek to answer? – Why is this question important? – What answer or argument do the author(s) provide? – What evidence do the author(s) use to support their argument and conclusions? – Do the author(s) find the results they expected to find? If not, how do they interpret the findings? To receive full credit, students should organize their presentation around these five questions, demon- strate a clear understanding of the article, and stay within the allotted time limit. Strong presentations will not only summarize the article but also help the class understand its theoretical contribution and relevance to broader course themes. • Research Presentation (20%): In Week 15, students will present their final paper projects to the class. This assignment consists of two components: the presentation itself, worth 15%, and discussant comments, worth 5%. Each presentation will be assigned one discussant. Presentations should be 8–10 minutes long, followed by 3–5 minutes of comments from the assigned discussant. One week before the presentation, the presenter must share an extended draft of their final research paper with the assigned discussant. The purpose of this requirement is to give the discussant enough time to read the project carefully and prepare constructive comments. The presentation should address the following questions: 2 Comparative Public Policy Fall 2026 – What is the main research question? – Why is this question important? – What argument or answer does the paper propose? – What evidence, cases, data, or research design will be used to support the argument? The discussant should provide constructive feedback on the presenter’s project. Discussant comments should address the clarity and significance of the research question, the strength of the argument, the appropriateness of the research design or evidence, and possible ways to improve the final paper. Discussants are not expected to solve all problems in the project, but they should identify the most important strengths, weaknesses, and next steps for revision. To receive full credit, presenters must clearly organize their presentation around the four questions above and stay within the allotted time limit. Discussants must demonstrate that they have carefully read the presenter’s draft and provide thoughtful, specific, and constructive feedback. • Final Paper (35%): Students will write a final research paper on a topic related to comparative public policy. The paper should develop a research project up to the research design stage. Students are not expected to conduct empirical analysis or present empirical findings. Instead, the final paper should include a clear research question, a statement of the paper’s contribution, a review of relevant literature, a theoretical argument, and a proposed research design. Students are strongly encouraged to visit office hours throughout the semester to discuss possible topics, refine their research questions, and receive feedback on the development of their projects. The final paper assignment consists of the following components: – Week 4: Paper Topic Submission (5%). Students will submit a brief topic statement of no more than one-half page. The statement should identify the research question, explain why the question is important, and provide a preliminary argument or expectation. – Week 7: Research Proposal (10%). Students will submit a two- to three-page research proposal. The proposal should build on the topic statement by adding a preliminary literature review. Students should situate their research question within the existing literature and explain the significance and potential contribution of their project. – Week 10: First Draft Feedback. Students may submit a partial or full draft of their paper for instructor feedback. This submission is voluntary and will not be graded, but students who submit a draft by the deadline will receive feedback intended to help improve the final paper. – Week 16: Final Paper Submission (20%). Students will submit the final version of their research paper. The final paper should present a well-developed research question, explain the importance and contribution of the project, engage relevant literature, develop a theoretical argument, and propose an appropriate research design. A strong final paper should not simply describe a policy issue. It should identify a clear puzzle, explain why the puzzle matters, show how existing scholarship helps but does not fully answer the question, and develop an argument that can be evaluated through a feasible research design. • The overall class grade will be the following: 3 Comparative Public Policy Fall 2026 Grading Disputes: If a student wishes to dispute a graded assignment, the student can send the instructor a one-page memo within one week of receiving the graded assignment. The memo should respond to the feedback on the assignment from the instructor. The instructor will carefully review the assignment and its grade, given that the memo provides a reason to do so. After regrading, students must accept the reviewed grade, even if the grade is lower than the original assignment. Late Work Policy: Late work is defined as any assignment submitted after the established deadline. Work submitted as makeup work for an excused absence is not considered late and is exempt from this policy. For unexcused late submissions, the assignment grade will be reduced by one letter grade if submitted within one day after the deadline. Work submitted more than one day late will receive an additional one- letter-grade reduction for each additional week it is late. Attendance Policy: Students are expected to attend class and complete all assignments. Students who are unable to attend class and complete assignments must request leave from the instructor in advance, except for psychological leave, menstrual leave, and maternity leave. Leave requests for midterm and final exams are not permitted, except in cases of official duties, illness, childbirth, bereavement, force majeure, or other extenuating circumstances. Such requests must be sup- ported by appropriate documentation and approved by the instructor. Exceptions may be granted at the instructor’s discretion. A late application may be submitted within 7 days of the absence, only in cases of extenuating circum- stances, and must be accompanied by the necessary documentation. See National Tsing Hua University Regulations for Student Leave of Absence for further details. Rules on the Use of AI: This course adopts a conditionally open policy on the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI). Students must clearly specify whether, how, and for what purpose they used AI tools in producing any course output. Students remain fully responsible for the accuracy, originality, integrity, and intellectual quality of all submitted work. Generative AI tools are not permitted for the following assignments or activities: reading assigned articles, preparing weekly reading summaries, serving as discussion leaders, and preparing research pre- sentations. These assignments are designed to evaluate students’ own reading comprehension, analytical interpretation, synthesis of scholarly arguments, and ability to lead academic discussion. Generative AI tools may be used for the final paper, but only as a limited research and writing aid. The final paper may not be written entirely or substantially by AI. Acceptable uses may include brainstorming research questions, improving grammar or clarity, organizing an outline, identifying possible weaknesses in an argument, or receiving feedback on draft prose. Students may not present AI-generated text, ideas, citations, data, or analysis as their own original work without proper acknowledgement. Students are also responsible for verifying all claims, citations, quotations, and references, since AI tools may produce inac- curate, fabricated, or misleading information. When AI tools are used in the final paper beyond minimal spelling, grammar, or formatting assistance, students must include a brief disclosure statement either in a footnote or the acknowledgments section. The disclosure should identify: (1) the name of the AI tool used, (2) the date or approximate period of use, and (3) a concise description of how the tool was used. For example: “I used ChatGPT on March 15, 2026, to receive feedback on the organization and clarity of an early draft. All arguments, evidence, citations, and final wording are my own.” Failure to disclose substantive AI use, use of AI for assignments where it is prohibited, or submission of AI-generated work as one’s own may be treated as a violation of the course’s academic integrity policy. Please refer to American Journal of Political Science AI Policy for a useful example of emerging academic norms regarding AI disclosure, human accountability, and limits on AI-generated scholarly work. 4 Comparative Public Policy Fall 2026 u Part I: Foundations of Comparative Public Policy This part introduces the core concepts and theoretical frameworks used to study public policymaking across countries. docs.text: 1 Comparative Health Insurance Systems Instructor: Professor Jui-fen Rachel Lu Email：rachel@gap.cgu.edu.tw Class meeting time: Mondays, 16:30-18:20 Classroom：CII 育成 A08 Session date time contents Instructor 1 09/07 16:30-18:20 Course introduction & Introduction to global health statistics databank RLU 2 09/14 16:30-18:20 Introduction to global health systems RLU 3 09/21 16:30-18:20 Principles of insurance RLU 4 09/28 16:30-18:20 No class - Happy Teacher’s Day RLU 5 10/05 16:30-18:20 The Control Knob Framework RLU RLU Global Experiences RLU 6 10/12 16:30-18:20 Social insurance system: Germany RLU 7 10/19 16:30-18:20 Social insurance system: Japan RLU 8 10/26 16:30-18:20 No class – National holiday RLU 9 11/02 16:30-18:20 Mid-term presentation RLU 10 11/09 16:30-18:20 Single-payer social insurance system: Taiwan RLU 11 11/16 16:30-18:20 Tax-financed health system: Canada & UK RLU 12 11/23 16:30-18:20 Mixed model: US RLU 13 11/30 16:30-18:20 Mixed model: Singapore RLU 14 12/07 16:30-18:20 Role of private insurance RLU 15 12/14 16:30-18:20 Equity vs. efficiency RLU 16 12/21 16:30-18:20 Final presentation RLU 2 Comparative Health Insurance Systems Instructor: Professor Jui-fen Rachel Lu Email：rachel@gap.cgu.edu.tw Class meeting time: Mondays, 16:30-18:20 Classroom：CII 育成 A08 Course Description The development of healthcare systems is a complex process deeply rooted in a nation’s unique cultural, political, and economic history. While each system possesses distinct characteristics, international experiences provide critical benchmarks for reform and policy innovation. Since the implementation of its National Health Insurance (NHI) program in 1995, Taiwan has established one of the world's most significant social programs, fundamentally reshaping its healthcare landscape. This course is designed to provide students with a rigorous analytical foundation for understanding diverse health insurance systems globally, using Taiwan’s NHI as a central reference case. The curriculum begins by introducing global health statistics and the fundamental principles of insurance, followed by the application of the Control Knob Framework— focusing on Financing, Payment, Organization, Regulation, and Persuasion—as a diagnostic tool for system performance. The second half of the course facilitates a deep dive into major international models, including social insurance systems (Germany and Japan), tax-financed health system (Canada and UK), and mixed models (the United States and Singapore). A critical component of this analysis includes examining the role of private health insurance and how it functions alongside or within public systems to address gaps in coverage, financing, and service delivery. Throughout the term, students will explore the essential trade-off between Equity and Efficiency, applying metrics such as the Gini Index and Kakwani Index to evaluate the fairness of financial burdens and resource distribution. The course culminates in a comprehensive comparative study where students apply these analytical frameworks to examine the challenges of a selected country in relation to the Taiwanese experience. Course Objectives By the end of this course, students will be able to: 1. Analyze Global Health Data: Utilize international health statistics databanks (such as OECD and World Bank HEFPI) to compare health system performance across nations. 3 2. Apply the Control Knob Framework: Identify and evaluate the five primary "control knobs" (Financing, Payment, Organization, Regulation, and Persuasion) that policymakers use to adjust health system outcomes. 3. Evaluate Insurance Models: Differentiate between major health insurance structures, including Social Health Insurance (SHI), National Health Insurance (NHI), and mixed market models. 4. Assess Equity and Efficiency: Critically examine the trade-offs between optimal resource allocation and social justice, using quantitative indicators like the Kakwani Index to measure the progressivity or regressivity of healthcare financing. 5. Conduct Comparative Research: Design and present a formal comparative analysis that evaluates the strengths and weaknesses of an international health system against the framework of Taiwan’s NHI. ◎ Assessment： Mid-term assessment 30% Final assessment 40% Class participation 30% ◎ Office hour： By Appointment ◎ Useful data sources 1. OECD Health Statistics 2026. 2. World Bank, HEFPI (Health Equity and Financial Protection Indicators) 3. Asia Pacific Observatory Health Systems in Transition series. 4. The Commonwealth Fund. 5. European Observatory Health in Transition series. ◎ Recommended reference books 1. Johnson JA, Stoskopf CH, 2009, "Comparative Health Systems", 1st edition, Jones & Bartlett Publishers. 2. Roberts M, Hsiao WH, Berman P, Reich MR, 2008, “Getting Health Reform Right – A Guide to Improving Performance and Equity”, Oxford University Press. (Hereafter as RHBR).

docs.text: Fall 2026 TSE608900 Political Economy of Authoritarianism Class Information: • Time: Fridays, 10:00-12:00 • Place: A08 Instructor: • Name: Hans H. Tung (hanshtung@mx.nthu.edu.tw; hanstung@ntu.edu.tw) • Office Hours: By appointment. 1 Course Design and Objectives Over the past three decades, the study of authoritarian politics has undergone a re- markable transformation. Rather than viewing dictatorships simply as political systems characterized by coercion, repression, and the absence of competitive elections, schol- ars increasingly recognize that authoritarian regimes possess sophisticated institutions and incentives that shape their economic performance, political stability, and long-term survival. Contemporary dictatorships are not merely governments that rule by force; they also rely on ruling parties, legislatures, bureaucracies, information systems, fiscal institutions, and carefully designed policy instruments to coordinate elites, manage so- cial conflict, and promote economic development. At the same time, these institutions create new constraints and dilemmas, forcing rulers to balance political survival against economic efficiency, credible commitments, and state capacity. This course introduces students to the political economy of authoritarianism through the analytical tools developed in economics and political science. Rather than exam- ining authoritarian governments solely from a historical or descriptive perspective, the course emphasizes theory-driven explanations of how political institutions shape eco- nomic policies and how economic incentives influence political outcomes. Throughout the semester, students will engage with both formal theoretical models and cutting- edge empirical research, learning how scholars formulate hypotheses, identify causal 1 mechanisms, and evaluate competing explanations using comparative evidence, histori- cal analysis, and modern quantitative methods. The organization of the course reflects several major intellectual turns in the con- temporary literature. We begin with an institutionalist perspective, examining how authoritarian institutionsˆaincluding ruling parties, legislatures, elite power-sharing ar- rangements, and succession rules-help dictators solve commitment problems, reduce elite conflict, and maintain political stability. We then turn to an informational per- spective, exploring how propaganda, censorship, surveillance, and strategic information manipulation shape the interactions between rulers and citizens. Together, these two perspectives provide complementary explanations for why many authoritarian regimes prove far more resilient than traditional theories once predicted. Building upon these theoretical foundations, the course investigates a series of sub- stantive policy domains in which political and economic incentives intersect. Topics including the manipulation of official statistics, redistribution, industrial policy, trade policy, and land reform illustrate how economic policies frequently serve political objec- tives such as coalition building, regime legitimacy, and elite management. Conversely, they also demonstrate how political institutions influence governmentsˆa ability to pro- mote economic development, allocate resources efficiently, and respond to social de- mands. The course further examines the development of state capacity through fiscal institutions and taxation before concluding with the political economy of media con- trol and information governance, an increasingly important area as digital technologies transform both authoritarian governance and citizen resistance. The selection of readings reflects two principles. First, students will be exposed to influential theoretical contributions that have fundamentally reshaped the study of authoritarian politics, alongside recent frontier research published in leading journals in economics and political science. Second, the syllabus deliberately integrates stud- ies from different regionsˆaincluding China, Russia, Vietnam, Morocco, Taiwan, Mexico, Peru, and several cross-national analyses-to encourage students to distinguish between general theoretical mechanisms and country-specific institutional contexts. By combin- ing conceptual rigor with empirical diversity, the course aims to equip students with a systematic understanding of how authoritarian regimes function, why they vary across countries, and how political institutions and economic forces jointly shape one of the most important forms of government in the contemporary world. Requirements 1. Active Participation: Each student is expected to complete all the required reading each week and to contribute to the collective discussion. Keep such questions in mind as you read articles and books listed in the syllabus: • What are the central issues at stake in this literature? • What are the major arguments of the works under study? • How do they relate to the debates in the field? 2 • How valuable and viable is the theory or argument that each puts forth? • Which scholarly disputes have been resolved? • What good further work lies ahead? 2. Class Presentation: We will have presenters (the number depends on the enroll- ment) for each week between Week 2 and Week 14. In this 15-minute presentation, you should include: • Your understanding of what issues the selected articles and books are dealing with and how they solve these issues • Your suggestions for alternative solutions • Two questions for class discussion 3. A Research Proposal: Each student is also required to submit a research proposal on a topic of his/her own choice (Feel free to talk to me for some advice before you start writing.). In your proposal, you need to justify your choice of topic (i.e., why is it puzzling?), define your research question (e.g. what is the dependent variable of interest?), develop a theoretical argument and testable hypotheses (e.g. what is your explanation?), identify your data sources, and specify your methodology. Your research proposal should not be more than 10 pages, double-spaced, and use times font no smaller than 12 point. The due date of your research proposals is 19, 2026. 4. A Final Project Presentation: Each student has to present his/her research proposal in front of the class in Weeks 15 or 16. docs.text: 1 11510TSE 609000 | Global Political Thought Instructors: Prof. Brian Chen (National Chengchi University) & Prof. Leigh Jenco (Department of Government, LSE) Description: We know that politics happens in all times and places. So does political theory—which we might understand as a practice as well as a field of study that reflects on political concepts, norms and goals. But typically the study of political theory in the academy has not been as global as its practice suggests. This course asks how we might think about politics if we take seriously a much wider, global range of thought about politics and try to bring all of these ideas across time and space into conversation on big questions: why do we need politics? How does a political community come into being in the first place? Who might act effectively for positive change in our communities, in our countries, and on the planet itself? We begin and end the course with some thinking about methodology: how do we bring different voices into conversation in a way that makes sense of their contribution? Is this necessary to do, or is it mere cultural “appropriation”? docs.text: Advanced International Political Economy Doeun Kim Fall 2026 E-mail: doeunkim@mx.nthu.edu.tw Course Website: https://eeclass.nthu.edu.tw/course/36542 Office Hours: TUE 11:00 - 13:00 or by appointment (Room C09) Class Hours: TUE 14:20 - 17:20 TA: Luigi Volponi (luigi.volponi96@gmail.com) TA Office Hours: WED 11:00 - 12:00 Course Description This course introduces graduate students to international political economy (IPE), a dynamic field that examines how political power, interests, interactions, institutions, and information shape eco- nomic policies and outcomes and, conversely, how international economic forces reshape political actions in the world arena. Beyond surveying foundational concepts, key theories, and influential scholarship, the course pushes students to think critically about real-world phenomena through an IPE lens. By the end of the semester, students will have a solid grounding in the major topics of IPE, the ability to engage with them from multiple theoretical angles, and the analytical tools to ask and pursue important research questions. The course, structured into six modules, covers trade (flow of goods), foreign direct investment (flow of capital), migration (flow of people), finance (flow of money), and emerging issues, includ- ing environment, backlash against globalization, supply chain, and technology. Students engage with these topics from diverse perspectives and at multiple levels of analysis. More specifically, we will explore the following questions: • What are the central issues and debates in IPE? • Who are the key actors in IPE, and what interests and incentives shape their behavior? • How do these key actors interact? • What are the political consequences of economic change in the global economy? • How does globalization reshape domestic politics, and how do domestic political forces in turn shape foreign economic policy? • In what ways do political institutions — domestic and international — structure outcomes in the global economy? 1/16 Advanced International Political Economy • Under what conditions do states cooperate on international economic issues, and why does cooperation sometimes fail? • How do international institutions shape the behavior of states, firms, and other subnational actors? The class is organized into two main components. First, the student discussion leader will provide a brief (five-minute) overview of the week’s theme and assigned readings. Building on this sum- mary, the instructor will guide the session by (re)introducing the topic and situating it within the broader literature. This will be followed by an in-depth class discussion. All students are expected to complete the assigned readings in advance and come prepared to engage actively. The second component focuses on application and empirical exploration. The session will transi- tion to an empirical exploration segment, in which the instructor may introduce relevant methods or students will work with datasets to complete short analytical tasks. These in-class exercises will involve basic coding and empirical analysis and should be submitted by the end of the class. The primary programming language used in the course is R. No prior knowledge is required. Detailed plans for in-class assignments will be provided during class. Requirements • Discussion leader x 1 (5%) • Presentation on a suggested reading x 1 (5%) • One-page reading memo x 3 (15%) • Class participation (10%) • Weekly in-class assignments (15%) • Research proposal (20%) • Final research paper (30%) Discussion leader x 1 Each student will serve as a discussion leader once during the semester. Assignments will be determined during the first class. Each week, one student will be designated as the discussion leader. The discussion leader is responsible for preparing a 5-minute summary of the overarching theme of the week’s readings (no slides). This summary should highlight the main arguments of each required reading and explain how the readings relate to and inform one another. Presentation on a suggested reading x 1 Each student will present a summary of one of the suggested readings during a designated week of the semester, followed by a short Q&A session with the class. The selection of the reading must be approved by the instructor via email. The presentation should be 10–15 minutes long and cover the paper’s research question, its relationship to other papers in the required weekly readings, main argument, methods, results, implications, and your own thoughts on the paper. Please prepare slides for the presentation. The 15-minute time limit will be strictly enforced. 2/16 Advanced International Political Economy One-page reading memo x 3 Each student is required to submit a one-page reading memo three times during the semester, to be submitted by 12 noon the Monday before class. Assignments will be determined during the first class. The week assigned for serving as discussion leader should not overlap with the week of the one-page reading memo. The memo may consist of either a critical reading of two or more assigned readings, or an in-depth discussion of a single assigned reading. More specifically, the memo should include: (1) the research questions and main arguments of the paper(s); (2) how the paper(s) relate to the overarching theme of the week or connect to readings from other weeks; (3) the measurements and methods the authors use to support their main argu- ments; and (4) your critical evaluation of the readings, including potential ways to expand them into a more developed research project. Weekly in-class assignments In every class, students will work in groups on a basic empirical analysis exercise. The exercise must be completed during class and submitted before the end of the session. While no prior knowledge of R is required, students are strongly encouraged to read the assigned chapters of R for Data Science in advance. Research proposal Around the middle of the semester, students will submit a research proposal and have a one-on- one meeting with the instructor. The research proposal is intended to serve as a foundation for the final research paper. The proposed research should address a topic related to international political economy. Students are required to attend at least one office hour or schedule an appointment with the instructor prior to submission, ideally by Week 4, to confirm their research question/topic. The research proposal should not exceed two pages in length (excluding the bibliography) and should include, but not be limited to, the following elements: • research question (importance and background) • dependent and independent variables • relevant literature • theory and hypotheses • scope of analysis • case study or empirical analysis plan More detailed instructions will be provided closer to the due date. Final research paper The final research paper should build on the research proposal and should include either a case study or empirical analysis. If you choose a case study, the selection of cases should be clearly justified. If you are using a large-N approach, presenting correlations or OLS results is sufficient. Null results are also acceptable. The paper should not exceed 15 pages in length. More detailed instructions will be provided closer to the due date. 3/16 Advanced International Political Economy Resources You may use whichever tool you are most comfortable with for preparing your documents (e.g., Microsoft Word, Quarto, Overleaf, etc.). However, I strongly encourage you to move away from Microsoft Word and become comfortable preparing and publishing your work in LaTeX. For your assignments and research proposals, I recommend using one of the following templates: Option 1, or Option 2. Office Hours Office hours will be held every Tuesday from 11:00 to 13:00. The sign up form is available at https://doeunkim.org/officehour.html or you can go to https://doeunkim.org and click on "Of- fice Hour". You must use your NTHU account to sign up for office hour. AI Policy Students are welcome to use generative AI tools to support and enhance their learning in this course. However, these tools should be used responsibly. Students are responsible for critically evaluating any AI-generated content they use, verifying its accuracy, and ensuring that their submitted work genuinely reflects their own understanding, analysis, and ideas. For each assignment in which AI tools are used, students must briefly disclose how and for what purpose they used them (e.g., "I used ChatGPT to proofread the assignment for grammar and clarity."). Throughout the semester, including during class discussions and one-on-one meetings, students may be asked to explain their submitted work, discuss the materials and sources on which it is based, and elaborate on their reasoning and arguments. Students should therefore be prepared to demonstrate their understanding of the material and to explain and defend the ideas presented in their work. * I reserve the right to modify the syllabus to better serve the learning objectives of the course. 4/16 Advanced International Political Economy Reading List Part 1: Introduction Week 1. docs.text: Conflict and Peace Seung-hun Lee Fall 2026 Web: https://seunghunlee918.github.io E-mail: seunghunlee@mx.nthu.edu.tw TA: TBD TA mail: TBD Class Hours: Thurs. 9AM-12PM Office Hours: Thurs. 2-4PM (Sign up here) Classroom: Innovative Incubation Hall A09 Office: Innovative Incubation Hall C06 1 Course Description Conflicts encompass a broad range of violent events that disrupt the economic and social stability of individuals and states, including crime, political violence, civil wars, and inter-state wars. Peace refers to the absence or resolution of conflict and the institutional and economic progress that helps prevent it. The existence of capable states that can prevent and mitigate conflict is crucial for peace. With the global rise in conflicts, it is essential to understand their origins and explore pathways to peace. This course covers topics in the political economy of development related to conflict and peace. The course will be organized around four key questions: What causes conflict? What are its consequences for individuals and states? How do individuals respond to conflicts? How can a state develop the capacities that allow it to maintain peace? Each class will consist of discussions on seminal papers, with two students taking turns presenting two selected papers. Throughout the semester, assignments will build the ability to critically engage with scholarly work, assess its claims, conduct empirical analysis, and develop original research that addresses gaps in the literature. 2 Prerequisites (MA students: Speak to me in person) • Familiarity with statistical inference: Students will assess empirical research and write a virtual paper demonstrating argumentation based on data. • (Not required, but helpful) Graduate-level micro/macroeconomics: Frameworks often in- volve game theory, constrained optimization, and principal-agent problems. 3 Lecture Materials and topics I will upload slides no later than the day before the lecture. Papers that will be discussed in the class will be presented in the latter half of this syllabus. There are no designated textbooks for 1 Conflict and Peace, Fall 2026 this course. However, the following books are recommended for understanding how economists and political scientists study conflicts and peace • Daron Acemoglu, James A. Robinson (2012), Why Nations Fail: The Origins of Power, Prosper- ity, and Poverty, Crown Business • Jean-Marie Baland, François Bourguignon, Jean-Phillipe Platteau, and Theirry Verdier (2020), Handbook of Economic Development and Institutions, Princeton University Press • Timothy Besley, and Torsten Persson (2011), Pillars of Prosperity: The Political Economics of Development Clusters, Princeton University Press • Chris Blattman (2022), Why We Fight: The Roots of War and the Paths to Peace, Viking The four topics covered in this course are as follows: 1. Cause of conflicts: Conflicts occur in many places, especially in developing countries. How do economic incentives drive individuals and states into conflict? How do political and ethnic dynamics lead to conflict? How and why do people engage in criminal activities? 2. Consequences of conflicts: Conflicts may undermine development prospects or trigger shifts that promote long-term progress. How do they affect the economic and non-economic out- comes of individuals? How do they shape economic development? How do they alter the institutional development of the state? 3. Response to conflicts: Individuals respond to conflicts by either fighting back or migrating. How do we overcome the collective action problems required to fight back? What causes people to migrate? How do migrants integrate to new settings? How do individuals and societies recover? 4. State capacity: An effective state can mobilize fiscal and human resources to prevent conflict and promote development. Why do some states fail at this? How do capable states build and maintain fiscal capacity? How do they manage personnel capacity? 4 Grading Policy Snap presentation (10%) Each week, two students will give a 15-minute presentation on two papers from the reading list (marked with double asterisks), with each student presenting one paper. The presenter will be chosen at random on the day of the class. Thus, everyone must prepare presentation slides for the two papers. Each presentation can use up to 8 slides (excluding title) covering: 1) moti- vation and research questions, 2) background, 3) data and empirical strategy, 4) key findings, 5) mechanisms, and 6) a critical self-assessment. This component evaluates students’ engagement with class materials and their ability to com- municate research clearly. Overly long or off-topic presentations are discouraged. 2/15 Conflict and Peace, Fall 2026 Replication exercise (20%) This exercise involves reproducing key findings from an empirical paper and submitting a report. Most empirical papers include data and code to allow others to verify the credibility of their results. Each student is expected to use R or Stata to replicate a paper of their choice and check if the findings are reproduced by writing their own code. Students are recommended to replicate results of any paper on the reading list. You may choose to replicate a paper that is not on the reading list, but you must get approval from me in this case. The papers should have a publicly available dataset and be published in a reputable academic journal. After completing the replication, each student should submit a report covering the following: • Are the data accessible? Some recent papers use administrative data, which are accurate but often restricted. Others construct datasets by merging publicly available sources. Report how much of the data is accessible to you and how much is not. • Do the key findings replicate? Focus on replicating the most important tables or figures that support the paper’s core claims. Are your results similar or different? If different, how so? You must also submit your code (R or Stata) to demonstrate your independent effort. For those that used AI tools (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini etc.) in this assignment, AI prompts must also be submitted (i.e., queries that you typed in the AI interface, but not the artifacts or answers generated by the AI). Failing to submit the code (and the AI prompts for those who used it) will result in a grade of zero for this assignment • Make your own extensions: Try alternative regression specifications, different choices of independent variables, sample restrictions, or falsification tests. You can use the original dataset or combine it with other sources. If extensions are not feasible due to data limita- tions, outline a detailed plan for how you would conduct the research differently. Take-Home Final Exam (20%) There will be a cumulative exam focusing on the papers discussed in class, specifically those marked with single or double asterisks in the reading list. The questions will assess your un- derstanding of the theoretical frameworks covered and ask you to connect an empirical find- ing—either provided in the exam or drawn from the reading list—to a relevant theory. Furthermore, one of the quesetions will be a guided referee report. You will be asked to read an unpublished working paper and assess its academic and empirical merit, following the questions that provide you with the tools or framework to be able to do so. Virtual Paper (50%) Your assignment is to develop a viable paper plan that clearly motivates the research question, explains the background, data, and empirical strategy, and includes some preliminary results. The paper does not need to be complete—a half-finished but original and exciting project is preferred over a complete yet uninteresting one. The draft counts for 30% of your grade. You’ll deliver a 20-minute presentation of your virtual paper in the final class, which counts for 10%. 3/15 Conflict and Peace, Fall 2026 The paper should be written in a scholarly article format. For instance: 1. Introduction: What is your research question? Why is it important from a scholarly or policy standpoint? 2. Literature review: What is the gap in the relevant literature? How are you filling that gap? 3. Background: What is the relevant information on the context that you are studying? 4. Data: What data source are you using or planning to use? Why should it be that dataset? 5. Empirical strategy: What statistical methods do you use? How do they allow for causal inference? What are the potential threats to that inference? 6. Preliminary results: What are the statistical relationships that you have found so far? 7. Mechanism and falsification tests: What factors may explain your main results? What are your plans to address potential factors that may nullify your findings? You will regularly discuss your virtual paper ideas with me. By October 29th, submit a 2-page research proposal outlining your question, contribution, background, and potential data sources. There is no need for results or detailed explanations on empirical strategy and falsification tests at this stage. This proposal counts for 10% of your grade. 5 Course Structure and Logistics Rules regarding collaboration Collaboration is encouraged assuming that (1) each student writes their own assignments, and (2) students must clearly identify their collaborators. Rules regarding AI usage AI tools may be used for assistive purposes only—such as proofreading, grammar checking, and coding support. Using AI assistance is permitted for replication exercise. For those who used AI tools in this task, you must submit both the codes and the AI prompts you have used. However, using AI to generate complete assignments - presentations and take-home exams, in particular - is strictly prohibited. All submitted work, especially the virtual paper, must be original writing and analysis. One way to show that you are writing a paper with your own idea is to discuss your ideas with me throughout the office hours openly (without aid of AI). Any use of AI must be properly disclosed to the instructor. Violations will be treated as academic dishonesty and subject to disciplinary action under university policies. Late submission policy Late submissions will not be accepted without prior approval. If you anticipate any issues with meeting deadlines, please contact me as soon as possible to discuss accommodations. 4/15 Conflict and Peace, Fall 2026 6 Schedule and reading list The schedule is tentative and may change. Students are expected to prepare presentations on papers marked with double asterisks. Papers with a single asterisk will be discussed in class. Important deadlines • Presentation on research proposal: October 29th (Submit 2-page draft by email before class) • Replication exercise due date: November 19th, midnight (Submit codes and report by email) • Presentation on the virtual paper: December 17th, in class • Virtual Paper due date: December 31st, midnight (Submit the draft by email) • Final Exam: Week of December 24th, (exact time TBA) 6.1 Course Introduction and empirical analysis: Week 1-2 I will go over course organization, how to do assignments, and introduce the topics covered in this class. We will also discuss empirical frameworks necessary to understand the papers covered in this class. There will also be demonstration using Stata and R Conceptual motivation for understanding why conflicts occur and how to achieve peace • Roots of war: Theories explaining why some entities go to war • Paths to peace: Individual resistance and institutional backdrops that allow for peace Tools for empirical analysis • Conceptualizing Treatment Effects • Ordinary least squares and randomized control trials • Panel regression • Instrumental variable methods • Difference-in-differences, event studies, and regression discontinuity 6.2 What causes conflicts: Week 3-5 Economic incentives behind conflicts • Berman, Eli, Michael Callen, Joseph H. docs.text: TSE Advanced Microeconomic Analysis (Course ID 11410TSED702100) Fall 2026 People and Time Instructor: Wei-Lin Chen (weilinchen@mx.nthu.edu.tw) Teaching Assistant: Jakob Heibel (jakob.heibel@gapp.nthu.edu.tw) Class meetings: Tuesday 234, i.e., 9-12 @CII A9 Discussion Section: TBD Office Hours: TBD Midterm 1: Oct 13, 2026 Midterm 2: Nov 10, 2026 Final exam: Dec 22, 2026 Course Website: https://eeclass.nthu.edu.tw/course/36547 Living update weekly schedule and reading list: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rHtuDpgLRYqZFCT6v-XLqqnjnVQlp0A5efpz0RPBzPE/edit? usp=sharing Course Description This is a required course for Ph.D. students in the economics track at TSE. Students not in the economics track should discuss with the instructor before enrolling in the course. The class introduces fundamental ideas in microeconomics so that students (1) are familiar with the backbones of most modern microeconomic models and (2) are confident in using microeco- nomics in applications. The course consists of three parts, each part taking five weeks. The first part covers consumer theory and choice under uncertainty. The second part covers the basics of game theory, and the third part covers information economics and contract theory. These topics are chosen to provide a foundation for the microeconomic models commonly used in public economics, development economics, labor economics, and political economy. 1 Course Requirements 1. Problem sets (25%) Problems will be assigned each week. My plan is for you to submit your write-up every two to three weeks, depending on our progress. Exact problem set submission dates will be an- nounced in class. Problem sets are graded for completion, and only a “check+/check/check- /no credit” will be offered for feedback. A “check-” or better gives you full credit for the problem set. You are allowed and encouraged to work in groups; if you do, write all group members’ names on the write-up. However, we do not expect to see identical answers from different students. You should make sure that the solutions you submit reflect your own thoughts and understanding. You must hand in independently handwritten solutions. No typed solution will be accepted. Make sure your handwriting is legible. Sloppy work will not receive credit. AI usage policy: You are allowed to use AI to help you solve the problem sets. However, I strongly encourage you not to use AI when attempting to solve the problems or use AI as the last resort. A few notes on this. (a) I think AI is a wonderful resource. But since we are all here, we might as well pick each other’s brains first. I encourage you to discuss with your classmates, and come to office hours and review sections to discuss with the TA and me. At least in my experience, talking to humans is much more effective in (1) clarifying our own thoughts and (2) deepening our understanding of a subject. Plus, the person you discuss with would also benefit from such discussions. I treasure every opportunity that will have positive externalities. (b) The course introduces basic concepts and models in economics. You may not use these every day in your work, but it would be nice to be able to apply them whenever you want. A lifeguard would need an oxygen tank to scuba dive, but they can definitely jump into the ocean at any time without floaties. (c) The midterms and final will be similar to the problem sets but will be closed-book. So it is probably a good idea to practice solving the problems on your own. 2. Midterm exam 1 (closed-book) (20%) 3. Midterm exam 2 (closed-book) (20%) 4. Final exam (cumulative, closed-book) (35%) 5. BONUS (10%) You are highly encouraged but not required to attend the discussion sections. Each week, problems (in problem sets) will be assigned for discussion in the discussion sections. Stu- dents who attend the discussion sections will be randomly selected to demonstrate how they tackle the problems. Bonus points will be given to students who showcase under- standing of how to solve the problems. 2/5 Course Materials No textbooks are required for this course. Lecture slides will be uploaded to the course website on the Sunday before each lecture. In the living update weekly schedule and reading list, I will assign some notes and articles as required readings; I will also list the relevant sections of the following notes and books for each lecture, so you know where to find useful information. The books are available at NTHU libraries. • Nolan H. Miller’s lecture notes. The lecture notes can be freely downloaded at: https: //nmiller.web.illinois.edu/notes.html (M) • Watson, J. (2013). Strategy: An Introduction to Game Theory. W.W. Norton (W) • Mas-Colell, A., Whinston, M., and Green, J. (1995). Microeconomic Theory. Oxford University Press (MWG) • Bolton, P. and Dewatripont, M. (2004). Contract Theory. The MIT Press (BD) The following resources are freely available and may be useful for understanding some lectures. There are many other textbooks. Please feel free to ask me for suggestions if you want to read books written in other styles/covering other topics. • For the first five weeks: Rubinstein, A. (2025). Lecture Notes in Microeconomic Theory: The Economic Agent • For the second five weeks: Osborne, M. J. and Rubinstein, A. (2024). A Course in Game Theory Both can be freely downloaded after registration via https://arielrubinstein.tau.ac.il/books. html Audit Policy Students who want to audit the course should discuss it with me first. Audit students should actively participate in the lectures, are strongly encouraged to attend discussion sections, and are required to submit problem sets. Advice • Practice, practice, and practice. Exam questions will resemble problem set questions, but I encourage you to look for other practice problems. Many textbooks and online sources have exercises. The TA and I are happy to help you learn relevant material that you find independently. What’s better is that you design questions by yourself. That’s a good sign that you are mastering the course materials. • Discuss, discuss, and discuss. Interrupt the lectures whenever you have questions. Most of the time, at least one other person shares the same thought! Discuss problem sets with your classmates, the TA, and me. We are all here to learn with each other! 3/5 • Read the required readings before the lectures. After the lectures, work on the problems and review the readings at the same time. Working on the problems takes precedence over reviewing the readings. • Feel free to come to my office hours. We can talk about the course material, microeco- nomics, research, or other questions you have. Credits The design and the material of this course draw on courses I attended as a student at National Taiwan University and UC San Diego. I am thankful to Hui-Wen Koo, Mark Machina, Joel Watson, and Joel Sobel for introducing me to microeconomics. I thank Nolan H. Miller for sharing the lecture notes online and Maciej H. Kotowski and Jie Bai for sharing their syllabus online. 4/5 Tentative Lecture Schedule Note: We may adjust our pace as we go. The following schedule is a plan for your reference. For weekly readings, check the living update weekly schedule and reading list. # of weeks Topic Main reference 1 Preference and Utility M 3.1, 3.2 2 Demand and Welfare Analysis M 3.3, 3.4 2 Choice under uncertainty M 6 Midterm 1 Representing Games W 2, 3, 4, 5 2 Analysis of Static Settings W 6, 7, 11 2 Analysis of Dynamic Settings W 14, 15, 22 Midterm 1 Adverse Selection and Signaling BD 13.1, 3; MWG 13.A, B, C 1 Screening BD Ch 13.1; MWG 13.D 1 Moral Hazard BD Ch 14; MWG 14.B 1 Monopolistic Screening BD Ch 2; MWG 14.C Final 5/5

docs.text: 1 Taipei School of Economics and Political Science (Fall, 2025) 11421TSED702300 Quantitative Methods II (數量方法二) Instructor: Min-Hua Huang (黃旻華) Class Time: Mon 13:20-16:20 Office Hours: By appointment Location: A09 classroom Email: mhhuang5103@ntu.edu.tw Course Description This course aims to train students with statistical skills to conduct multivariate regression analysis, including linear regression, ordinal logistic regression, multinomial logistic regression, and other advanced regression methods, such as multilevel modeling, panel regression, and psychometrics. The purpose is to equip student with proper capability to proceed causal investigation and able to do empirical research independently. This course will also introduce several large-scale public opinion datasets, including Asian Barometer, Arab Barometer, Afrobarometer, Latino Barometer, and Euraisa Barometer, and many others. Those datasets offer a rich source of information for students to engage in substantial studies in many subfields of political science. Background knowledge and theories that associated with those topics will be also covered in this course. Overall, the training of this course is not restricted to statistical methods, but also cover the realms of data collection and empirical analysis. Course Objective/Requirement This course proceeds with lectures and practical exercises. The topics cover basic mathematical skills (matrix algebra, calculus), probability theory, statistical estimation, regression analysis, hypothesis testing, statistical diagnosis, etc. There are two basic requirements: (1) complete weekly exercises on time; (2) participate in the final exams. Weekly topics will demonstrate how survey questions associate with theoretical concepts and apply to empirical research that results in journal publication. Grading Attendance and Discussion (10%), Weekly Assignments (40%), Midterm (20%), Final Exam (30%). AI Policy This course does not involve the use of AI.
